6.text: A lion was sleeping in the forest when a little mouse ran over his nose. The lion woke up angrily and caught the mouse in his huge paw. “Please let me go,” cried the mouse. “If you do, I will help you one day.” The lion laughed. “How can a small mouse help the king of animals?” But he felt kind that day and let her go. A few weeks later, hunters caught the lion in a strong net. He pulled and shouted, but he could not escape. The mouse heard his roar and ran to him. She began to bite the ropes with her sharp teeth. Soon the net fell apart and the lion was free. “You laughed at me,” said the mouse, “but now you see that even a small friend can be a great friend.”
6.src: adapted from Aesop's Fables, The Lion and the Mouse (public domain)

q.q: Why did the lion let the mouse go?
w: He was not hungry at all

q.q: How did the mouse help the lion?
q.a: She bit through the ropes of the net

q.q: What is the lesson?
q.a: Even small friends can give great help

6.text: Kevin was nervous on his first day at a new school. His family had moved to a different city, and he did not know anybody. In the morning, he sat alone in the classroom and looked at the strange faces. At break time, nobody spoke to him, and he ate his sandwich quietly. Then a girl with a green backpack came to his desk. “Hi, I'm Nora,” she said. “Do you like football?” Kevin's face lit up. “It's my favourite sport!” he answered. Nora invited him to join her team on the playground. Kevin was not the best player, but he ran hard and even scored a goal. After the game, the other children patted him on the back. On the way home he thought, “A new place is only strange until you meet the first friend.” That night he told his mother about every detail of his day, and she smiled.

q.q: Why was Kevin alone at first?
q.a: He did not know anybody in the new city

q.q: How did Kevin make a friend?
What does Kevin learn?
q.a: A new place feels better after you meet a friend

6.text: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's crust. Deep underground, rock is so hot that it melts and becomes magma. Because magma is lighter than the rock around it, it slowly rises. When enough pressure builds up, it bursts out of the volcano, and then we call it lava. A volcanic eruption can be frightening. Hot ash can fill the sky, and rivers of lava can destroy forests and villages. Yet volcanoes also give us gifts. After many years, the ash and broken lava turn into very rich soil, so farmers like to plant crops near volcanoes. Some countries, such as Iceland, use the heat from under the ground to make electricity and warm their houses. Scientists called volcanologists watch active volcanoes with special instruments, and they can often warn people before an eruption, which saves many lives.

q.q: What is the difference between magma and lava?
q.a: Lava is magma that has come out of the volcano
w: Magma is only found in Iceland
Lava is a kind of ash

q.q: Why do farmers like land near volcanoes?
How do scientists save lives?
q.a: They watch volcanoes and warn people

6.text: The Dragon Boat Festival takes place on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month. It remembers Qu Yuan, a poet and minister who lived more than two thousand years ago. He loved his country, but when it was in danger, the king did not listen to him. Sadly, Qu Yuan jumped into a river. The local people rowed out in boats to look for him, beating drums to scare the fish away, and they threw rice into the water so that the fish would not eat his body. Today, people remember this story by racing long boats shaped like dragons. Each boat has about twenty rowers, and a drummer at the front keeps everybody in the same rhythm. Families also eat zongzi, sticky rice wrapped in leaves. At the race, the loud drums, the cheering crowd and the splashing water make an exciting scene.

q.q: Who does the festival remember?
q.a: Qu Yuan, a poet and minister

q.q: What is the job of the drummer in the boat?
q.a: To keep all the rowers in the same rhythm

q.q: What do families eat at the festival?

6.text: Thomas Edison is famous for inventing the practical electric light bulb, but he did not do it on his first try. Edison went to school for only a few months, and his teacher thought he was slow. His mother taught him at home and he read everything he could find. As a young man, he built a laboratory where he and his helpers tested hundreds of different materials to find one that could glow for a long time inside a glass bulb. Again and again the experiments failed. A friend asked him if he felt sad about so many failures. Edison laughed and said, “I have not failed. I have just found ten thousand ways that will not work.” Finally, after trying a carbon thread, the bulb glowed for more than a day. Edison's story teaches us that mistakes are steps towards success, if we keep trying.

q.q: Who taught Edison at home?
What did Edison mean by “ten thousand ways that will not work”?
q.a: Each failed test taught him something
w: He did not like his helpers

q.q: What worked in the end?

6.text:
Teacher: Class, today we are going to the history museum. Please stay together and listen carefully.
Lily: Can we take photos, Miss Wang?
Teacher: Yes, but you must turn off the flash. It can damage old paintings.
Tom: What is the most famous thing in the museum?
Teacher: There is a bronze bell that is more than two thousand years old. When it was made, people did not have any machines.
Lily: How did they make it?
Teacher: They poured hot liquid metal into a mould made of clay. It took many skilled workers and a lot of time.
Tom: That is amazing! May I touch it?
Teacher: No, Tom. Please look with your eyes, not with your hands. Many people want to enjoy it after us.
Lily: Can we buy something in the shop afterwards?
Teacher: Yes, if there is time. But first, let's go and see the bell. Follow me!

q.q: Why must the students turn off the flash?
w: It uses a lot of power
It is against the law in the shop

q.q: How was the bell made?
q.a: Hot metal was poured into a clay mould

q.q: Why can Tom not touch the bell?
q.a: Others want to enjoy it after the class

6.text: A young shepherd boy looked after the village sheep on a hill near the forest. The work was boring, and he often felt lonely. One afternoon, he wanted some fun, so he shouted, “Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is eating the sheep!” The villagers dropped their work and ran up the hill with sticks. But there was no wolf, and the boy laughed at their worried faces. “Do not play such a trick again,” they said angrily. A few days later, he did it a second time, and again the villagers ran to help him. Then, one evening, a real wolf came out of the forest. The boy cried out in fear, “Wolf! Please help me!” But this time nobody came, because they thought he was lying again. The wolf scattered the sheep, and the boy learned a bitter lesson: nobody believes a liar, even when he tells the truth.
6.src: adapted from Aesop's Fables, The Boy Who Cried Wolf (public domain)

q.q: Why did the boy shout the first time?
w: He wanted to leave the hill

q.q: Why did nobody come at the end?
q.a: They thought he was lying again
w: They were afraid of the wolf

q.q: What is the lesson?
q.a: People do not believe a liar, even when he is honest

6.text: Every day, people in the world throw away millions of tonnes of rubbish. Much of it ends up in big holes in the ground or in the ocean, where it stays for hundreds of years. Recycling is a way to give old things a new life. When we put paper, glass, metal and some plastics in the right bins, factories can melt or crush them and make new products. This saves energy and natural resources. For example, making a can from recycled aluminium needs far less energy than making one from raw material. At Sunrise School, the students started a recycling club last year. They put coloured bins in every corridor and made posters to explain what goes where. In six months, the school's rubbish was cut by almost half. The principal said, “We are small heroes for a big planet.” Even a ten-year-old can make a difference.

q.q: What happens to recycled glass and metal?
q.a: Factories melt them to make new products
w: They are sent to the ocean

q.q: What did the school club do?
q.a: Put coloured bins in corridors and made posters

q.q: What is the writer's main point?
q.a: Everyone, even children, can help the planet

6.t: The Mystery of the Missing Cookies
6.text: On Sunday afternoon, Mum baked twelve chocolate cookies and put them on the kitchen table to cool. When she came back after a phone call, there were only ten. “Who took the cookies?” she asked. My brother Max, who had chocolate on his chin, said, “It was not me.” My sister Lucy pointed at the dog. “Maybe Biscuit did it.” Mum looked at the dog, who was sleeping on the sofa. “Biscuit cannot reach the table,” she said. Then she looked at Max's chin. “And I think a detective does not need a magnifying glass today.” Max went red. “Okay, I took two,” he said quietly. “They smelled so good!” Mum could not stay angry. She laughed and gave everyone one more cookie. Then she made a new rule: next time, whoever takes cookies without asking must help to wash the dishes. Max agreed at once.

q.q: How did Mum know who took the cookies?
q.a: Max had chocolate on his chin

q.q: Why did Mum not blame the dog?
q.a: It could not reach the table

q.q: What is Mum's new rule?
q.a: Whoever takes cookies without asking helps with the dishes

6.text: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. It stands in the Himalayas, on the border between Nepal and China, and its top is about 8,849 metres above sea level. The Chinese call it Qomolangma, and the Nepalese call it Sagarmatha. Climbing it is a great challenge. Near the top, the air has so little oxygen that most climbers need extra bottles to breathe. The temperature can drop far below zero, and sudden storms are common. Climbers usually spend weeks getting used to the height, moving slowly up and down between camps. They are helped by Sherpas, local mountain guides who know the paths very well and often carry heavy loads. In 1953, Edmund Hillary from New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, became the first people known to reach the top. Today, many climbers try every spring, but the mountain still demands respect, patience and careful planning.

q.q: Why do climbers need extra oxygen?
q.a: There is very little oxygen near the top

q.q: Who are the Sherpas?
Who first reached the top, as far as we know?

6.text: Alice was sitting on a river bank next to her sister, feeling very bored. The sister was reading a book without pictures, and Alice thought, “What is the use of a book without pictures?” Suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran past her. It did not seem strange to Alice that the rabbit said, “Oh dear! I shall be late!” But when the rabbit took a watch out of his waistcoat pocket and hurried on, she jumped up. She had never seen a rabbit with a pocket or a watch, and she ran after him across the field. Just in time, she saw him jump into a large hole under a hedge. Alice followed without thinking about how she would get out again. The hole went straight down like a tunnel, and then she began to fall, slowly, down and down, past shelves full of jars and books.
6.src: adapted from Lewis Carroll, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (public domain)

q.q: Why did Alice run after the rabbit?
q.a: He had a pocket and a watch

q.q: Where did the rabbit go?
q.a: Into a hole under a hedge

q.q: What did Alice see as she fell?
q.a: Shelves full of jars and books

6.text: The internet is a wonderful place. You can learn new things, talk to friends and play games. But like a big city, it has some dangers, and you need to know how to be safe. First, protect your personal information. Never share your address, school or phone number with a stranger, even if he or she seems very friendly. Second, choose a strong password. A good password is long and mixes letters, numbers and symbols. Do not use your birthday, and do not give it to anyone except your parents. Third, think before you click. Some messages say that you have won a prize, but they are really tricks to steal information. If something looks too good to be true, it probably is. Finally, if anything online makes you feel worried or uncomfortable, tell an adult you trust at once. You are never in trouble for asking for help, and good habits keep everyone safe.

q.q: What makes a good password?
q.a: It is long and mixes letters, numbers and symbols

q.q: What should you do if a message says you won a prize?
q.a: Be careful, it may be a trick

q.q: What does “too good to be true” mean here?
w: It is a gift from a friend

6.text: Table tennis is very popular in China, and almost every school has a table in the playground. Last week, Yan played in the final of her school tournament against Jia, the champion of the last two years. Yan was not the stronger player, but she had a secret weapon: patience. In the first game, Jia hit the ball hard and won easily, eleven to four. In the second game, Yan stopped trying to hit winners. Instead, she sent every ball back with a gentle spin and waited for Jia to make mistakes. Slowly, the score became closer. In the last game, they were level at ten all, and everyone in the hall held their breath. Jia hit the ball too hard, and it flew off the table. Yan had won! She shook hands with her opponent. “You played well,” said Jia, smiling. “I will see you next year!” Yan laughed and said, “I will be ready.”

q.q: What was Yan's secret weapon?
How did Yan change her game in the second game?
q.a: She sent the ball back gently and waited for mistakes

q.q: How did the players behave at the end?

6.text: High above the city stood the statue of the Happy Prince. He was covered with thin gold, had two bright blue stones for eyes, and a red stone on his sword. One night, a little swallow, who was flying south for the winter, stopped to rest at the prince's feet. Suddenly a large drop of water fell on him. The statue was crying! “When I was alive,” said the prince, “I lived in a palace and knew no sorrow. Now I can see all the poverty of my city. Please, little swallow, take the red stone from my sword to a poor woman whose son is ill.” The swallow did so. Night after night he carried the prince's gold and jewels to people in need. Winter came, and the swallow grew very cold, but he stayed. In the end, he died at the prince's feet, and the statue's heart broke. Yet kindness had made both of them truly rich.
6.src: adapted from Oscar Wilde, The Happy Prince (public domain)

q.q: Why was the statue crying?
q.a: He saw the poverty of the city

q.q: What did the swallow carry to poor people?
What is the theme of the story?

6.text: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth. It can grow to about thirty metres, as long as three buses, and weigh as much as thirty elephants. Surprisingly, this giant eats some of the smallest creatures in the ocean. It feeds on krill, tiny animals like shrimps, and a single whale may eat millions of them in one day. A whale is not a fish. It is a mammal, which means that it breathes air with lungs, has warm blood and feeds its babies with milk. This is why whales must come up to the surface regularly to take a breath. They also sing, and their low songs can travel hundreds of kilometres under the water so that other whales can hear them. Long ago, people hunted whales for oil and meat, and the number of blue whales fell greatly. Today hunting is forbidden, and slowly the population is growing again.

q.q: What does the blue whale eat?
Why must whales come to the surface?
Why did the number of blue whales fall?

6.text: In 1405, the Ming emperor sent a huge fleet across the ocean. Its leader was Admiral Zheng He, a man born in Yunnan who had grown up at the royal court. The fleet had more than two hundred ships and about twenty-seven thousand people, including sailors, soldiers, doctors, translators and craftsmen. The largest ships, called treasure ships, were much longer than anything in Europe at that time. Over almost thirty years, Zheng He made seven voyages and visited places in Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and even the east coast of Africa. He carried silk, porcelain and tea, and brought back spices, medicine and unusual animals, such as giraffes. Importantly, the fleet did not conquer land. Zheng He's goal was to show China's friendship and to start trade. His journeys were a remarkable achievement, and in many harbours people still remember his visits with respect and wonder today.

q.q: How many voyages did Zheng He make?
What was the purpose of the fleet?
q.a: To show friendship and start trade

q.q: What did Zheng He bring back?

6.text: Saturday had come, and the summer morning was bright and full of life. But Tom Sawyer was not happy. His Aunt Polly had told him to paint a long fence, three metres high and thirty metres long. He looked at the fence, and the world seemed empty. Just then he saw his friend Ben coming along the road, eating an apple. Tom started to paint slowly, as if it were the most interesting job in the world. “Hello, Tom,” said Ben. “Working? I'm going swimming. Wouldn't you like to come?” Tom looked up. “Work? Is this work? A boy does not get a chance to paint a fence every day.” Ben became curious and asked to try. Tom refused at first, then he agreed, and Ben even gave him his apple! Soon other boys came, and each paid something for the honour of painting. By afternoon, Tom was rich, and the fence had three coats of paint.
6.src: adapted from Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (public domain)

q.q: What did Aunt Polly tell Tom to do?
How did Tom get Ben to paint?
q.a: He pretended that painting was great fun
w: He asked his aunt to order it

q.q: What happened by the afternoon?
q.a: Tom had gifts from other boys and the fence was finished

6.text: Every hour, the sun sends more energy to the Earth than all humans use in a whole year. The problem is how to catch it. Solar panels are one answer. A panel is made of many cells, usually of silicon, and when sunlight hits them, they produce a small electric current. Together, thousands of panels can power a school, a village or even a city. Solar energy has big advantages. It is clean, because it does not make smoke or carbon dioxide, and the sun will shine for billions of years. However, there are also challenges. Panels produce no power at night, and on cloudy days they give much less. To solve this, engineers store the extra energy in large batteries. China is now the biggest producer of solar panels in the world, and in some deserts, huge solar farms stretch to the horizon. Many scientists believe that sunshine will be one of the main sources of electricity in your lifetime.

q.q: What happens when sunlight hits solar cells?
q.a: They produce a small electric current

q.q: Why are batteries needed?
q.a: Panels give no power at night

q.q: What is one big advantage of solar energy?
q.a: It is clean and does not make carbon dioxide

6.t: The Night the Lights Went Out
6.text: It was a quiet Friday evening when, without warning, every light in our building went out. The television stopped, the fridge stopped humming, and the whole flat became dark. “Don't move,” said Dad. “I'll find a torch.” While he searched the drawers, my little sister Amy started to cry, so I took her hand and told her it was only a game. Mum found some candles and put them on the table, and the room filled with a warm, soft light. Without any screens, we did not know what to do at first. Then Dad suggested telling stories. Everyone had to say one sentence, and the next person added another. Our story was about a dragon who was afraid of the dark, and it became so silly that we laughed until our sides hurt. When the power came back two hours later, nobody wanted to turn on the television. It was the best evening of the month.

q.q: How did the narrator comfort Amy?
q.a: He took her hand and said it was a game

q.q: What did the family do in the dark?
q.a: They made up a story together

q.q: Why did nobody want the television afterwards?
q.a: They had enjoyed the evening so much

6.text: In the jungles of India, a tiger named Shere Khan once hunted a small human child. The baby crawled away and entered a cave where a family of wolves lived. Mother Wolf looked at the tiny boy and loved him at once. “I will keep him,” she said. “His name will be Mowgli, the Frog.” When Shere Khan came to the cave and demanded the child, Mother Wolf answered fiercely, “The man's cub is mine. He will live and run with the pack, and one day he will hunt you!” The tiger roared with anger, but the entrance was too narrow, and he had to leave. Mowgli grew up with the wolves. Baloo the bear taught him the Law of the Jungle, and Bagheera the black panther watched over him like a guardian. But Mowgli knew that, one day, he would have to face Shere Khan.
6.src: adapted from Rudyard Kipling, The Jungle Book (public domain)

q.q: Why could Shere Khan not enter the cave?
Who taught Mowgli the Law of the Jungle?
What does Mother Wolf's reaction show?
w: She is afraid of the tiger

6.text: Leonardo da Vinci was born in Italy in 1452, more than five hundred years ago. Today he is best known as a painter, because he made two of the most famous pictures in the world: the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. But Leonardo was much more than an artist. He was curious about everything. He studied the bodies of animals and humans and made very careful drawings of the bones and muscles. He watched birds for hours to understand how they fly, and then he drew machines with wings, a parachute and even a kind of helicopter. None of them was built in his lifetime, but his ideas were centuries ahead of their time. Leonardo wrote his notes in mirror writing, from right to left, so that you need a mirror to read them easily. He filled thousands of pages with his thoughts. People call him a genius, but he said that learning never tires the mind.

q.q: What is Leonardo best known as?
Why did Leonardo watch birds?
How did he write his notes?
q.a: In mirror writing from right to left

6.text: This winter, Zoe's class went on a three-day trip to a ski resort in the north. Most of the children had never seen so much snow, and they could not wait to start. On the first morning, an instructor named Mr Park showed them how to put on their boots and fix them to the skis. “Remember,” he said, “the most important thing is to learn how to stop.” They practised on a gentle slope. Zoe fell down five times in the first hour, and her trousers were wet with snow, but she got up each time. By the afternoon, she could make a slow turn by shifting her weight from one ski to the other. On the last day, the class skied down the beginners' hill together. At the bottom, Zoe took off her goggles and shouted, “Again!” Her teacher laughed. “This is just the beginning.” Skiing was now her new favourite sport.

q.q: What did Mr Park say was most important to learn first?
How did Zoe make a turn?
q.a: By shifting her weight from one ski to the other

q.q: How did Zoe feel at the end of the trip?
q.a: Excited and eager to ski again

6.text: Della and Jim were a young married couple who were very poor, but they loved each other deeply. They each owned one treasure. Jim had a gold watch that belonged to his father and grandfather. Della had long, beautiful brown hair. It was Christmas Eve, and Della had only one dollar and eighty-seven cents to buy Jim a present. She stood in front of the mirror and made a sad decision. She sold her hair for twenty dollars, and with the money she bought a platinum chain for Jim's watch. When Jim came home, he stopped at the door and stared at her short hair. Then he gave her a package. Inside were a set of beautiful combs for her hair, which she had admired for months. He had sold his watch to buy them! The two gifts were now useless, but the two young people understood that love is the greatest gift of all.
6.src: adapted from O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi (public domain)

q.q: What did Della sell?
What did Jim sell?
What is the main message?

6.text: The International Space Station circles the Earth about sixteen times every day, at a height of roughly four hundred kilometres. It was built by several countries working together, and astronauts from many nations have lived there. Life in space is very different from life on the ground. Because everything is weightless, astronauts float through the rooms and sleep in bags fixed to the wall, so they do not drift away. Water does not pour into a glass but forms little balls in the air, so astronauts drink from special bags with straws. Without gravity, the muscles and bones become weaker, so every astronaut must exercise for about two hours a day. The crew also does many science experiments, for example growing plants and studying how the human body changes. When they look out of the window, they see wonderful views of oceans, clouds and thin glowing air. Many of them say it changes how they think about our planet.

q.q: Why do astronauts sleep in bags fixed to the wall?
q.a: So they do not drift away

q.q: Why must astronauts exercise two hours a day?
q.a: Muscles and bones become weaker without gravity

q.q: How does the view from the window affect many astronauts?
q.a: It changes how they think about the Earth

6.t: A Letter to a Pen Friend
6.text:
Dear Emma,
Thank you very much for your letter and the lovely photo of your dog. I was really happy to get it. My name is Wei, and I live in Hangzhou, a city famous for its beautiful West Lake. I am twelve years old and I am in Grade Six. I have a younger sister, and we share a room. At the weekends, I usually play badminton with my father in the park, or I read adventure stories. My favourite subjects are science and English, though maths can be difficult for me sometimes. You asked about our food. My mother cooks many dishes, but my favourite is fish with sweet and sour sauce, which is a speciality of Hangzhou. What do children in your country like to eat? Also, how do you celebrate your birthday? Please write back soon and tell me about your school, your friends and your hobbies. I look forward to your reply.
Your friend,
Wei

q.q: Where does Wei live?
What does Wei do at weekends?
q.a: Plays badminton with his father or reads

q.q: What does Wei want Emma to do?
q.a: Write back and tell him about her life

6.text: Many years ago, there lived an emperor who cared about nothing except his clothes. He had a different coat for every hour of the day. One day, two clever tricksters arrived in the city. They said they could weave a cloth with the most beautiful colours, and that this cloth had a magic power: it was invisible to anyone who was stupid or unfit for his job. The emperor gave them gold and silk, and they pretended to work at empty looms day and night. Several times the emperor sent his minister to look. The old man saw nothing, but he was afraid to say so, and he praised the cloth. At last the tricksters said the suit was ready and helped the emperor put it on. He walked in the grand parade, and everyone cried, “How wonderful!” Then a small child said, “But the emperor has nothing on!” The crowd began to laugh, and the emperor knew the child was right.
6.src: adapted from Hans Christian Andersen, The Emperor's New Clothes (public domain)

q.q: What did the tricksters say about the cloth?
q.a: Stupid people could not see it

q.q: Why did the minister praise the cloth?
q.a: He was afraid to say he saw nothing

q.q: What does the child's sentence teach us?
q.a: It is important to tell the truth

6.text: It is the last week of the year, and I am sitting at my desk thinking about everything that has happened. In January, I could hardly understand the English songs on the radio, but now I can sing most of them. In spring, I joined the school science club, and we built a small model of a volcano that really made smoke. Summer was my favourite season because we went on a long trip to the seaside, where I learned to swim without a ring. I also read twelve books this year, and I wrote a short story that my teacher put on the classroom wall. I failed a maths test in October, and I felt terrible. But my mother said, “One bad mark is not the end of the world,” and I studied harder. Next year, I want to learn to play the guitar and to help my younger cousin with her homework. I am thankful for the year, and ready for the next one.

q.q: What did the narrator make in the science club?
How did the narrator react to the failed maths test?
What does the narrator want to do next year?
q.a: Learn the guitar and help a cousin

7.text:
On the first day of the new term, Lin Hua sat at her desk and opened a clean notebook. She wanted to make a plan for the year. Last year she had often forgotten her homework, and she had never finished the books on her reading list.
She wrote three goals. First, she would read one English book every month. Second, she would go to bed before ten o'clock. Third, she would learn to play a simple song on the guitar.
Her deskmate Tom looked at the list and smiled. "These are good goals," he said, "but have you thought about how to reach them?" Lin Hua had not. So they sat together and added small steps: twenty minutes of reading after dinner, a phone alarm at nine thirty, and ten minutes of guitar practice every Saturday.
By the end of January, Lin Hua had finished her first book. She felt proud. A plan, she realised, is only a dream until you break it into small, easy steps.

q.q: Why did Lin Hua make a plan?
q.a: She had forgotten homework and not finished books last year
w: She had to give it to her teacher
Tom asked her to do it
She wanted to win a prize

q.q: What did Tom help her to do?
q.a: Add small steps to reach her goals
w: Choose a new book to buy

q.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
q.a: Small steps help us turn plans into real results
w: Friends should make our plans for us
It is better not to make plans

7.text:
One hot summer afternoon, a hungry fox was walking through a farm. Suddenly he saw a bunch of ripe, purple grapes hanging high on a vine. They looked sweet and juicy, and his mouth began to water.
"What a fine lunch!" he said. He jumped as high as he could, but the grapes were too far away. He tried again and again. He ran back, took a deep breath and leapt once more, but his teeth only closed on the air.
After an hour, the fox was tired and thirsty. He sat down and looked up at the grapes. Then he turned his nose up and said, "I am sure those grapes are sour. Only a foolish fox would want them!"
And he walked away, pretending that he did not care at all.
People say that we sometimes speak badly of things we cannot have. It is easier to blame the grapes than to say, "I failed."

q.q: Why could the fox not eat the grapes?
q.a: They were too high for him to reach

q.q: Why did the fox say the grapes were sour?
q.a: He wanted to hide that he had failed
w: He really did not like grapes

q.q: What does the story teach us?
q.a: People may speak badly of what they cannot get

7.text:
Have you ever caught a snowflake on your glove and looked at it closely? Every flake is a tiny work of art, and scientists say that it is very hard to find two that are exactly the same.
Snow begins high in the sky, in clouds where the air is far below freezing. Tiny drops of water in the cloud freeze around specks of dust. These small pieces of ice are called crystals. As more water vapour touches a crystal, it grows and forms six arms, because water molecules join together in a six-sided pattern.
When the crystals become heavy, they fall. If the air near the ground is cold enough, they reach us as snow. If the air is a little warmer, they melt and turn into rain.
Snow is useful, too. It covers the ground like a blanket and protects plants and small animals from the worst of the winter cold. In spring, the melting snow gives rivers the water they need.

q.q: Around what do water drops freeze in a cloud?
Why do snow crystals have six arms?
q.a: Water molecules join in a six-sided pattern
w: The wind cuts them that way
They are made in a factory

q.q: How does snow help plants and small animals?
q.a: It protects them from the worst of the cold
w: It makes the air warmer than summer

7.text:
Mei had always loved machines. When her school started a robot club, she was the first to join. On the first day, the teacher, Mr Chen, gave each group a box of plastic parts, a small motor and a tiny computer.
"Your job," he said, "is to build a robot that can follow a black line on the floor."
Mei's group worked for three weeks. At first, their robot spun in circles. Then it drove straight off the line and hit the wall. Everyone laughed, but Mei did not give up. She checked the program and found a mistake: the sensor was looking at the wrong side of the line.
On the day of the contest, their little robot rolled smoothly around the whole track. It did not win first prize, but it finished without a single error.
"What did you learn?" Mr Chen asked.
"That technology is not magic," Mei answered. "It is patient work, and mistakes are part of the way."

q.q: What was the robot supposed to do?
q.a: Follow a black line on the floor

q.q: What was wrong with the robot at first?
q.a: The sensor looked at the wrong side of the line

q.q: What did Mei learn?
q.a: Technology needs patient work and mistakes are normal

7.text:
The Spring Festival is the most important holiday in China, and its heart is the reunion dinner on New Year's Eve. Families who live far apart travel for hours, or even days, to sit at the same table.
In the north, many families make dumplings together. Grandmother mixes the dough, father prepares the filling, and the children help to fold. Sometimes a clean coin is hidden in one dumpling, and whoever finds it is said to have good luck for the year. In the south, people often eat fish, because the Chinese word for fish sounds like the word for "extra". It means that there will be more than enough in the coming year.
After dinner, children receive red envelopes with money inside. The colour red stands for happiness and is thought to keep bad luck away.
At midnight, fireworks light up the sky. Although customs differ from place to place, the feeling is the same everywhere: love, thanks and hope for a better year.

q.q: What is at the heart of the Spring Festival?
q.a: The reunion dinner on New Year's Eve

q.q: Why do people in the south often eat fish?
q.a: The word for fish sounds like the word for extra
w: Fish is red like lucky envelopes

q.q: What do customs at the festival have in common?
q.a: They all show love, thanks and hope
w: They all use coins in food
They all take place in the north

7.text:
The Great Wall of China is not one single wall. It is a long chain of walls, towers and forts that were built by different rulers over more than two thousand years. Some parts are made of stone and brick, while others are only packed earth.
The walls were built mainly to protect the northern borders from attack. Watchtowers stood along the top, and soldiers sent messages by lighting fires so that smoke could be seen from tower to tower. In this way, news could travel much faster than a rider on a horse.
Today, millions of visitors walk on the Wall each year. The most famous parts, near Beijing, are well repaired and have steps and handrails. Other parts are wild and broken, and are covered with grass and small trees.
If you visit, bring comfortable shoes and plenty of water. The steps are steep, and the view from the top is worth every tired step. You will understand why people call it one of the great wonders of the world.

q.q: How was the Great Wall built?
q.a: By different rulers over more than two thousand years
w: By one emperor in ten years

q.q: How did soldiers send messages?
q.a: By lighting fires so smoke could be seen
w: By ringing bells in the valley

q.q: What advice does the writer give visitors?
q.a: Bring comfortable shoes and plenty of water

7.t: Marie Curie, a Woman of Science
7.text:
Marie Curie was born in Poland in 1867. Her family was not rich, and in those days girls were not allowed to study at university in her country. But Marie loved learning, and she saved money for years so that she could go to Paris.
In Paris she studied physics and mathematics. She often had little to eat and lived in a cold room, but she worked harder than almost anyone. There she met a young scientist, Pierre Curie, and they married.
Together they studied a strange kind of energy that came from certain rocks. Marie called it radioactivity. After years of difficult work, they discovered two new elements, polonium and radium.
Marie won the Nobel Prize twice, once in physics and once in chemistry. She was the first person to do so. During the First World War she also helped doctors by driving X-ray machines close to the soldiers.
Marie Curie showed that curiosity, courage and hard work can open doors that society tries to close.

q.q: Why did Marie save money for years?
q.a: To go to Paris and study
w: To visit her family in Poland

q.q: What did Marie and Pierre discover?
What is special about her Nobel Prizes?
q.a: She was the first person to win two
w: She won them in one year
She won them with Pierre in Paris

7.text:
It was raining hard when Ben left the library. He reached into his bag, but his umbrella was gone.
"That's strange," he said. "I'm sure I brought it this morning."
He went back to the desk. "Excuse me," he asked the librarian, "has anyone found a blue umbrella?"
"What does it look like?" she said.
"It's blue, with a small yellow duck on the handle."
The librarian smiled and pointed behind him. A small girl was standing by the door, holding a blue umbrella with a yellow duck.
"Hey, that's mine!" said Ben.
"No, it's mine," said the girl. "My grandma gave it to me."
Ben looked more carefully. The duck on her umbrella had a red hat. His duck had no hat at all.
"Oh dear," he laughed. "I think I've made a mistake. I'm sorry!"
Just then his friend Anna walked in. "Ben! Why did you leave your umbrella in the cinema yesterday?" she said, holding up a blue umbrella with a duck.
Everyone burst out laughing, and Ben's face turned as red as the duck's little hat.

q.q: What did Ben's umbrella look like?
q.a: Blue with a yellow duck on the handle

q.q: Why was the girl's umbrella not Ben's?
q.a: Her duck wore a red hat
w: It was found in the cinema

q.q: Where had Ben left his umbrella?
q.a: In the cinema the day before

7.t: Life at the Bottom of the World
7.text:
Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent on Earth. Almost no plants grow there, and no people live there permanently. Yet emperor penguins have lived on its ice for thousands of years.
These birds cannot fly, but they are excellent swimmers. Their bodies are covered with thick layers of fat and short, tight feathers that keep out the freezing water. In winter, when temperatures fall to minus forty degrees, the females lay a single egg and then go to the sea to feed.
The males stay behind. For about two months they carry the egg on their feet, covered by a warm fold of skin. They eat nothing and huddle together in huge groups, taking turns to stand on the outside where the wind is strongest.
When the mothers return with food, the chicks are hatching. Now it is the fathers' turn to walk to the sea. Scientists are worried because melting ice makes life harder for these remarkable birds.

q.q: How do male penguins keep the egg warm?
q.a: They carry it on their feet under a fold of skin
w: They bury it in warm snow
They sit on it in the sea
They keep it inside a cave

q.q: Why do the penguins take turns on the outside of the group?
w: The food is on the outside
The chicks live on the outside

q.q: Why are scientists worried?
q.a: Melting ice makes life harder for penguins

7.text:
Many students stay up late to study or play games, but doctors say that sleep is just as important as food and exercise. At your age, you need between nine and eleven hours every night.
While you sleep, your body is not simply switched off. Your brain is busy sorting the things you learned during the day and storing the important ones in your long-term memory. This is why a student who sleeps well before an exam often does better than one who studies all night.
Sleep also helps your body to grow and to fight illness. Children who do not sleep enough catch colds more easily, and they often feel angry or sad without a clear reason.
Here are some tips for better sleep. Go to bed at the same time every day. Turn off screens an hour before bed, because their bright light tells your brain that it is still daytime. Keep your room dark and quiet. If you follow these simple rules, you will wake up fresh and ready to learn.

q.q: What does the brain do during sleep?
q.a: It sorts and stores what you learned
w: It forgets all the day's lessons

q.q: Why should you turn off screens before bed?
q.a: Their bright light makes the brain think it is day

q.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
q.a: Enough good sleep is important for learning and health
w: Sleep is only needed in winter

7.text:
A mighty lion was sleeping in the shade of a tree when a little mouse ran across his nose. The lion woke up with a roar and caught the mouse in his huge paw.
"Please let me go, great King," cried the mouse. "If you are kind to me, I will help you one day."
The lion laughed. "How could a tiny mouse ever help a lion?" But he was in a good mood, and he lifted his paw and let the mouse go.
Some weeks later, hunters caught the lion in a strong net of ropes. He pulled and roared, but he could not break free. The mouse heard his cry and hurried to the spot. With her sharp little teeth, she bit through the ropes one by one until the lion was free.
"You laughed at me once," said the mouse, "but now you see that even a small friend can be a great help."
The lion bowed his head. He never forgot the lesson: kindness is never wasted.

q.q: Why did the lion let the mouse go?
q.a: He was in a good mood
w: The mouse was too big to eat

q.q: How did the mouse save the lion?
q.a: She bit through the ropes of the net
w: She dug a hole under the net

q.q: What lesson did the lion learn?
q.a: Even small friends can be a great help

7.text:
Every Friday, the students of Class 7B hold a recycling day. They bring empty bottles, old newspapers and used batteries from home, and sort them into big coloured boxes in the schoolyard.
It began last autumn, when their teacher showed them a photograph of a beach covered in plastic. "This is what happens when we throw things away without thinking," she said. Nobody spoke for a long time.
Since then, the class has learned many surprising facts. A glass bottle can be recycled again and again without losing quality. Recycling one aluminium can saves enough energy to run a television for three hours. Paper can be turned into new paper, but the fibres get shorter each time, so it can only be reused a few times.
The students do not only sort rubbish. They also try to reduce it. Many of them now carry water bottles and cloth bags. "Recycling is good," says Jing, the class monitor, "but using less is even better."

q.q: What made the class start recycling?
q.a: A photograph of a beach covered in plastic

q.q: What happens to paper when it is recycled?
q.a: Its fibres get shorter each time

q.q: What does Jing think is even better than recycling?
q.a: Using less in the first place

7.text:
The sky was grey on Saturday morning, and by ten o'clock the rain was pouring down. Coach Wang looked at the muddy pitch and asked the boys, "Do you still want to play?"
"Yes!" they shouted together.
The match against Green Hill School began on time. At first, nobody could run properly, and the ball stopped dead in every puddle. Daniel, the best player in the team, slipped three times in the first ten minutes. Green Hill scored first.
At half time, the boys were wet and cold, and some of them wanted to give up. Coach Wang gave each of them a hot drink. "Look at the other team," he said. "They are just as wet as we are. The difference will be teamwork."
In the second half, the boys passed the ball short and quickly instead of kicking it far. It worked! They scored twice and won two to one.
After the match, everyone was covered in mud, but nobody cared. They had learned that a team that works together can win in any weather.

q.q: What was the weather like on the day of the match?
What did the team change in the second half?
q.a: They passed the ball short and quickly
w: They played in a new place

q.q: What was the final score?
q.a: Two to one for the writer's team
w: One to two for Green Hill
Three to one for Green Hill

7.t: The Man Who Wanted to Hear
7.text:
Alexander Graham Bell was born in Scotland in 1847. His mother was almost deaf, and his father taught people how to speak clearly. From an early age, Alexander was interested in sound and in the ways in which people communicate.
When he grew up, he moved to America and became a teacher of deaf children. In the evenings he worked on a different idea: could the human voice travel along a wire? Many people laughed at him. Even his friends thought that the idea was impossible.
Bell worked with a young helper named Thomas Watson. They spent many months building strange machines in a small room. Then, in March 1876, something wonderful happened. Bell spilled some acid on his clothes and called out, "Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you." Watson, in another room, heard the words through the machine.
That was the first successful telephone call. Within a few years, thousands of telephones had been installed. Bell, however, never stopped teaching, and he always said that his work with deaf children was the most important of his life.

q.q: What was Bell's job before he made the telephone?
w: He was a doctor in Scotland

q.q: How did Watson hear Bell's words?
q.a: Through the machine, from another room

q.q: What did Bell think was the most important work of his life?

7.src: adapted from Hans Christian Andersen (public domain)
7.text:
On a sunny farm, a mother duck sat on her eggs. One by one the shells broke, and little yellow ducklings came out. But the last egg was bigger than the others, and the bird that came out of it was grey and clumsy.
"What an ugly duckling!" said the other animals. The ducks bit him, the hens pecked him, and even his brothers and sisters laughed at him. Sad and lonely, the duckling ran away.
He spent a long, cold winter alone beside a frozen lake. He was hungry and often afraid, but he did not give up. When spring finally came, he saw three white swans swimming on the water. They were the most beautiful birds he had ever seen.
"I will go to them," he thought. "They may kill me, but I would rather be killed by them than bitten by ducks."
He bent his head and looked down into the water. Looking back at him was not a grey duckling, but a graceful white swan. He had changed during the winter, and now he was happy.

q.q: Why did the others laugh at the duckling?
q.a: He looked different and was grey and clumsy

q.q: What did the duckling do when spring came?
q.a: He went to the white swans on the water
w: He flew away from the lake

q.q: What did he see in the water?
q.a: A beautiful white swan was his own reflection
w: A frozen lake with no birds

7.text:
Deep under our feet, the Earth is so hot that rock melts. This liquid rock is called magma. Sometimes it finds a weak place in the Earth's crust and pushes its way up. When it reaches the surface, we call it lava, and the mountain that forms around the opening is a volcano.
Eruptions can be very different. Some volcanoes, such as those in Hawaii, let lava flow slowly in glowing red rivers that people can watch from a safe distance. Others explode with great force, throwing ash and stones high into the sky. In 79 AD, the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in Italy buried the Roman town of Pompeii under ash. Today, visitors can walk through its streets and see houses just as they were.
Volcanoes are dangerous, but they also bring benefits. Volcanic soil is rich and helps farmers to grow good crops. Hot rocks underground can warm water, which is used to heat homes and make electricity in countries like Iceland.
Scientists now use machines to measure small earthquakes and gases, so that they can warn people before a volcano wakes up.

q.q: What is lava?
q.a: Magma that has reached the surface

q.q: What happened to Pompeii?
q.a: It was buried under ash from Vesuvius
w: It was washed away by a flood
It was destroyed by Hawaii lava

q.q: How do volcanoes help people?
q.a: They make soil rich and give heat and electricity
w: They supply fresh water to cities

7.text:
Every year, on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, many Chinese families celebrate the Dragon Boat Festival. It is a day of colourful races, sweet smells and old stories.
The festival remembers Qu Yuan, a poet and minister who lived more than two thousand years ago. He loved his country and gave honest advice to his king, but the king did not listen. In great sadness, Qu Yuan threw himself into a river. According to the legend, local people rushed out in their boats to look for him. They beat drums to scare the fish away, and they threw rice into the water so that the fish would not eat his body.
Today, teams paddle long boats shaped like dragons. A drummer sits at the front and sets the rhythm, and everyone must paddle at the same moment, or the boat will not move fast.
After the race, families eat zongzi, sticky rice wrapped in leaves. Some are sweet, with red beans or dates, and others are salty, with meat or egg yolk. Children also wear small bags of herbs, which are believed to keep them safe and healthy.

q.q: Whom does the Dragon Boat Festival remember?
q.a: Qu Yuan, a poet who loved his country
w: A fisherman who lost his net

q.q: Why did people beat drums in the legend?
w: To make music for Qu Yuan

q.q: Why must all the paddlers move at the same moment?
q.a: Otherwise the boat will not go fast

7.text:
Nowadays, many students spend several hours a day looking at screens, and more and more of them need glasses. Doctors say that we cannot always avoid screens, but we can protect our eyes with a few simple habits.
The first is the twenty-twenty-twenty rule. Every twenty minutes, look at something about twenty feet, or six metres, away for twenty seconds. This lets the muscles inside your eyes relax. When we stare at something close for a long time, we also blink less, and our eyes become dry and tired.
The second habit is to spend time outdoors. Research suggests that children who play outside for two hours a day are less likely to become short-sighted. Natural light seems to help the eyes to grow in a healthy way.
Finally, keep a good distance. Books and screens should be about thirty centimetres from your face, and you should never read in the dark or while lying down.
Healthy eyes do not just happen. We have to look after them every day.

q.q: What does the twenty-twenty-twenty rule ask you to do?
q.a: Look at something far away for twenty seconds every twenty minutes

q.q: Why do our eyes get dry when we stare at screens?
What is the writer's main message?
q.a: Simple daily habits can protect our eyes
w: Glasses are better than outdoor play

7.t: The River That Shaped a Nation
7.text:
The Yellow River is the second longest river in China, flowing for more than five thousand kilometres from the high mountains in the west to the sea in the east. It is often called the cradle of Chinese civilisation, because some of the earliest farming villages and cities grew up along its banks.
The river gets its name from the yellow mud it carries. Water flows across a huge area of soft, yellow soil called loess, and washes tonnes of it into the river every year. When the river reaches the flat land in the east, it slows down and drops the mud on its bed. Over centuries, the bed rose higher than the land around it, and floods became a terrible danger.
For thousands of years, people fought the floods by building walls of earth beside the river. Today, large dams and reservoirs help to control the water, and millions of trees have been planted on the hills to hold the soil in place.
The Yellow River still gives water to farms and cities, so protecting it means protecting millions of lives.

q.q: Why is the Yellow River called the cradle of Chinese civilisation?
q.a: Early farming villages and cities grew along its banks
w: It is the longest river in China
It has no mud in it

q.q: Why did floods become a danger?
q.a: The mud raised the river bed above the land

q.q: How do trees on the hills help?
q.a: They hold the soil in place
w: They bring water from the sea

7.text:
"I can't do it," whispered Hannah. She stood behind the curtain with her violin, and her hands were shaking. Through a small gap she could see two hundred people waiting in the school hall.
"Of course you can," said her friend Zoe. "You've practised every day for two months."
"But what if I forget the notes?"
"Then you play something else and smile. Nobody will know."
Hannah laughed in spite of her fear. The headmaster announced her name, and she walked slowly to the middle of the stage. For a moment the hall was completely silent. She raised the violin, took a deep breath and began.
The first notes were a little shaky, but soon the music flowed and she forgot about the people. When the last note faded away, there was a second of silence, and then the whole hall exploded into applause.
Behind the curtain, Zoe was jumping up and down. "You see?" she said. "You were wonderful!"
"Thank you for believing in me," Hannah said. "Next time, I might even enjoy the nervous part."

q.q: How did Hannah feel before the show?
q.a: Afraid that she would forget the notes

q.q: What advice did Zoe give her?
q.a: Play something else and smile if she forgot

q.q: What happened when the music ended?

7.text:
In the early fifteenth century, the Ming emperor sent out the largest fleet the world had ever seen. Its leader was Zheng He, an admiral who was born in Yunnan and had grown up in the emperor's court.
Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He made seven long voyages. His fleet included hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of men. The biggest ships, called treasure ships, were much larger than anything built in Europe at that time. They carried silk, porcelain and tea, and they returned with exotic goods such as spices, medicine and even a giraffe.
The fleet visited places in Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and the east coast of Africa. Zheng He was not a conqueror. He wished to show China's strength and to make friends, and he gave valuable gifts to local rulers wherever he went.
After his death, the new emperors decided that such expensive voyages should stop, and the great ships were left to rot. However, the memory of Zheng He lives on, and in many countries people still tell stories about his visits.

q.q: How many voyages did Zheng He make?
What was the purpose of the voyages?
q.a: To show China's strength and make friends

q.q: Why did the voyages stop?
q.a: The new emperors thought they were too expensive

7.text:
A honeybee lives for only a few weeks in summer, yet in that short time it can do something that amazes scientists. It can tell its sisters exactly where to find flowers, using a dance.
When a worker bee discovers a good patch of flowers, she flies back to the hive and begins to move on the honeycomb. If the flowers are close, she dances in a circle. If they are far away, she dances a figure of eight and shakes her body in the middle. The angle of that straight middle line shows the direction of the flowers compared with the sun, and the longer she shakes, the greater the distance.
The other bees follow her closely and touch her with their feelers. Then they fly out and, in a short time, find the exact place.
Bees are very important to people, too. They carry pollen from flower to flower, and without them many of our fruits and vegetables would not grow. This is why it is so worrying that bee numbers are falling in many parts of the world.

q.q: What does a bee do after finding good flowers?
q.a: She flies back and dances to tell the others
w: She stays and guards the flowers

q.q: What does the length of the shaking show?
q.a: How far away the flowers are

q.q: Why are bees important to people?
q.a: They carry pollen so fruits and vegetables can grow

7.src: adapted from Hans Christian Andersen (public domain)
7.text:
Long ago, there lived an emperor who cared about nothing but fine clothes. One day, two clever cheats came to his city. They said that they could weave the most beautiful cloth in the world, and that it was invisible to anyone who was stupid or unfit for his job.
"Wonderful!" thought the emperor. "With this cloth, I can find out which of my ministers are foolish." He gave the men a lot of gold, and they sat at empty looms, pretending to work.
One by one, the old minister, the officers and finally the emperor himself went to see the cloth. They saw nothing, but each was afraid to say so. "It is magnificent!" they all cried.
At last the cheats dressed the emperor in his "new clothes", and he walked through the city in a grand procession. The crowd cheered, afraid to seem foolish too.
Then a small child said loudly, "But he has nothing on!"
The words ran from one person to another, until everyone was shouting. The emperor shivered, but he walked on proudly to the end.

q.q: What did the cheats say about the cloth?
q.a: Stupid people could not see it
w: It could only be worn in winter

q.q: Why did everybody say the cloth was beautiful?
q.a: They were afraid to seem foolish

q.q: Who told the truth?

7.text:
Twenty years ago, electric cars were rare, slow and expensive. Today they are quiet and fast, and in some cities they are everywhere. Why have they become so popular?
The main reason is that they do not burn petrol. An electric car has a large battery and a motor, and it produces no smoke from its exhaust pipe. In cities with heavy traffic, this makes the air cleaner and the streets quieter.
However, electric cars are not perfect. A battery can take from thirty minutes to several hours to charge, and in some places there are not enough charging stations. Making the battery also needs metals that must be mined, and if the electricity comes from coal, the car is not really clean.
Engineers are working hard on these problems. New batteries last longer and charge faster, and more and more electricity comes from the sun and wind. Many experts believe that in the future most of the cars on our roads will run on electricity, and that our cities will be a little healthier because of it.

q.q: Why do electric cars make cities cleaner?
q.a: They do not give out smoke from an exhaust pipe
w: They are made of recycled paper

q.q: What is one problem with electric cars?
q.a: Charging can take a long time and stations are few

q.q: What do experts think about the future?
q.a: Most cars will probably run on electricity
w: Cars will be banned in cities

7.text:
Dear Mum and Dad,
I have been at summer camp for five days, and I want to tell you everything. The camp is in the mountains beside a clear lake, and the air smells of pine trees.
On the first day I was very homesick. I shared a tent with three boys I did not know, and the food was strange. But on the second day we went canoeing, and my partner, a boy named Carlos, turned our canoe over in the middle of the lake. We were both soaked, and we laughed so much that we could hardly swim back. After that, we were friends.
Every morning we learn something new. Yesterday a ranger taught us how to read a map and a compass, and today we found our way through the forest without any help. In the evening we sit around the fire, sing songs and look at the stars. I never knew there were so many!
I have eaten all the biscuits you packed, so please do not worry about me. I miss you, but I think I will be sad on the last day.
Love, Peter

q.q: How did Peter feel on the first day?
How did Peter and Carlos become friends?
q.a: They fell into the lake and laughed together
w: They won a race on the lake

q.q: Why will Peter be sad on the last day?
q.a: He will have to leave the camp

7.text:
Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and Tibet, is the highest mountain on Earth. Its top is almost nine thousand metres above sea level, higher than the flight path of many small aircraft. In Tibetan it is called Qomolangma, which means "Goddess Mother of the World".
For a long time, people thought that nobody could reach the top. The air there is so thin that every breath contains only about a third of the oxygen we breathe at sea level. The temperature can fall to minus forty degrees, and winds can blow stronger than a storm.
In 1953, a beekeeper from New Zealand, Edmund Hillary, and a Sherpa guide from Nepal, Tenzing Norgay, became the first people known to stand on the summit. They said that they had succeeded because they had helped each other all the way.
Today hundreds of climbers reach the top each year, but the mountain is still dangerous. Many Sherpa guides risk their lives to carry heavy loads, and the slopes are covered with rubbish. Climbers are now asked to bring all their waste back down.

q.q: Why is it hard to climb Everest?
q.a: The air is thin and it is very cold and windy

q.q: Who were the first people known to reach the top?
What are climbers asked to do now?
q.a: Bring all their waste back down

7.src: adapted from Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (public domain)
7.text:
On a bright Saturday morning, Tom Sawyer's Aunt Polly gave him a punishment. He had to paint the long wooden fence in front of the house, and he could not go swimming until it was finished. Tom looked at the fence and sighed. It was thirty metres long and nearly three metres high.
Then his friend Ben came along, eating a juicy apple. "Hello, Tom! Working? I'm going swimming. Wouldn't you like to come? But I suppose you'd rather work, wouldn't you?"
Tom turned and looked at him carefully. "What do you call work?" he said. "Is painting a fence work? It seems to me that it is a rare chance. How many boys get to paint a fence every day?"
Ben stopped eating his apple. "Let me try, Tom," he said. "Just a little!"
"I'm afraid I can't," said Tom. "Aunt Polly wants it done very well."
Ben begged, and at last Tom gave him the brush, but only after Ben had paid with his apple. By afternoon, other boys had joined in, and every one of them had paid something. Tom sat in the shade, rich and happy, while the fence received three coats of paint.

q.q: Why did Tom have to paint the fence?
q.a: It was a punishment from his aunt

q.q: How did Tom make Ben want to paint?
q.a: He made the work seem like a rare chance
w: He told him it was easy
He said Aunt Polly was away

q.q: What happened in the end?
q.a: The other boys paid Tom for the chance to paint

7.text:
If you spend a day at the seaside, you will notice that the water does not stay in the same place. Twice a day, the sea rises up the beach and then slowly goes out again. These movements are called tides, and they are mainly caused by the Moon.
The Moon pulls on everything on Earth with the force of gravity. Solid land hardly moves, but water is free to flow. On the side of the Earth that faces the Moon, the sea is pulled towards it and makes a bulge, called a high tide. A second bulge appears on the opposite side of the planet. As the Earth turns once a day, each place passes through both bulges, so there are two high tides and two low tides every day.
The Sun also pulls the oceans, but it is much farther away, so its effect is weaker. When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a line, at new moon and full moon, the tides are the strongest.
Fishermen, sailors and children building sandcastles all need to know when the tide will come in. Tide tables are published for every port, and they are very accurate.

q.q: What mainly causes the tides?
q.a: The pull of the Moon's gravity

q.q: Why are there two high tides every day?
q.a: There is a bulge on each side of the Earth
w: The Moon goes round twice a day
The sea is pulled by two moons

q.q: When are the tides the strongest?
q.a: When the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line
w: When the sea is very cold
When the Moon cannot be seen at night

7.text:
The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, when the moon is at its roundest and brightest. For many Chinese people, a round moon is a symbol of a family that stays together, so this festival is a time for reunion.
On that evening, families gather outdoors, put fruit and moon cakes on a table and look up at the sky. Moon cakes are round pastries with thick fillings, such as lotus seed paste, red bean paste or salted egg yolk. They are usually cut into small pieces and shared, so that everyone can have a taste.
Children love the legends told on this night. The most famous is the story of Chang'e, a woman who drank a magic medicine and floated up to the moon, where she lives with a white rabbit. Some say that, if you look carefully at the dark patches on the moon, you can see the rabbit pounding medicine.
People who are far from home cannot always be with their families. They look at the same moon and think of one another, and perhaps that makes the distance seem a little smaller.

q.q: What does a round moon stand for?
What happens to moon cakes at the table?
q.a: They are cut up and shared
w: They are thrown to the rabbit
They are kept for a week
They are given to the moon

q.q: How can people far from home feel closer to their families?
q.a: By looking at the same moon

7.text:
Imagine a city where there are no cars, no buses and no bicycles. In Venice, in northern Italy, this is not a dream. The city is built on more than a hundred small islands in a shallow lagoon, and instead of streets it has about a hundred and fifty canals.
People in Venice travel by boat. Water buses, called vaporetti, carry passengers along the main canal, and elegant black boats called gondolas take tourists through the narrow waterways. Even the police, the ambulances and the rubbish collectors have boats. On land, people walk across more than four hundred bridges.
The city is famous for its beautiful old buildings, many of which were built hundreds of years ago on wooden poles pushed deep into the mud.
Unfortunately, Venice is sinking slowly, and the sea level is rising. In autumn and winter, high water sometimes floods the main square. Engineers have built a system of gates to keep the sea out, but many people believe that more must be done to save this unique place.

q.q: How do people mostly travel in Venice?
How were many old buildings in Venice supported?
q.a: On wooden poles pushed into the mud

q.q: What problem does Venice have today?
q.a: It is sinking slowly while the sea rises

7.src: adapted from the Brothers Grimm, The Town Musicians of Bremen (public domain)
7.text:
A donkey had worked for his master for many years, but now he was old and weak, and the farmer wanted to get rid of him. "I will go to the town of Bremen," the donkey thought, "and become a musician."
On the road he met an old dog who could no longer hunt, then a cat who was no longer able to catch mice, and finally a rooster who was going to be cooked for Sunday dinner. All of them had been thrown out by their owners. "Come with us to Bremen," said the donkey. "We will make beautiful music!"
By night they had not reached the town, so they stopped in a forest. Through the trees the rooster saw a light, and the animals found a house where robbers were eating a large meal. The donkey stood at the window, the dog climbed on his back, the cat on the dog and the rooster on the cat. Then they all sang at the same time.
The terrible noise frightened the robbers, who ran into the forest. The four friends sat down to the feast and stayed in the house for the rest of their lives.

q.q: Why did the animals leave their owners?
q.a: They were old and no longer useful to them
w: They wanted to see the sea
They were looking for work as thieves

q.q: How did the animals frighten the robbers?
q.a: They stood on each other and sang loudly
w: They threw stones at the window

q.q: Where did the animals finally stay?
q.a: In the robbers' house in the forest

7.text:
The giant panda, one of China's most famous animals, lives in the misty bamboo forests of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu. Although it belongs to the group of meat-eating animals, a panda eats almost nothing but bamboo.
Bamboo does not give much energy, so pandas have to eat between twelve and fourteen hours every day, and they can eat about ten kilograms of it. They hold the stems with a special part of the paw that works like a thumb. When they are not eating, they usually sleep or rest, which saves energy.
Pandas are shy and live alone. A mother normally has one cub at a time. A newborn cub is tiny, pink and blind, and it weighs only about a hundred grams, no more than a large apple. It stays with its mother for one or two years.
For decades, pandas were in great danger because forests were being cut down. Reserves have since been created, bamboo corridors have been built to connect them, and the number of wild pandas has slowly increased. This shows what can be done when people decide to care.

q.q: Why do pandas eat for so many hours?
w: They are afraid of other animals
They want to grow bigger tusks

q.q: What is special about a newborn cub?
q.a: It is tiny, pink and blind

q.q: What has helped the number of wild pandas to increase?
w: Moving them to zoos in cities

7.text:
"I will cook dinner tonight," Dad announced on Sunday. Mum, my sister Lucy and I looked at one another with fear. Dad is a great engineer, but he has never been a great cook.
"Don't worry," he said. "I have watched a video, and it looks easy. If you follow the recipe, nothing can go wrong."
An hour later, the kitchen looked like a battlefield. There was flour on the floor, tomato sauce on the wall and a strange black smoke over the stove. The smoke alarm began to scream, and Lucy ran around opening every window.
"It is only a little burnt," said Dad bravely, lifting the lid of the pot. Inside was something grey and sticky. Nobody could say what it had been.
"What was it supposed to be?" asked Mum.
"Spaghetti," said Dad quietly.
In the end, we ordered pizza, and we all laughed so hard that tears ran down our faces. Dad has promised that he will never cook again unless he practises first. We have promised to help him, but only if he keeps the kitchen windows open.

q.q: Why were the others afraid when Dad said he would cook?
q.a: He is not a good cook
w: They had no food at home

q.q: What was the grey, sticky food meant to be?
What did the family do in the end?

7.text:
Artificial intelligence, or AI for short, is a kind of computer program that can learn from large amounts of data. We have probably met it already, even if we did not notice. When a phone suggests the next word in a message, when a map finds the fastest road or when a video app recommends a film, AI is at work.
Such programs do not think like people. A language program, for example, has read millions of texts, and it predicts which words are likely to follow others. It can answer questions or translate sentences quickly, but it sometimes makes mistakes and states them with great confidence. For this reason, we should always check important facts in a book or with a teacher.
AI can be a good helper for students. It can explain a difficult idea in simple words, give examples or help you practise a language. However, if you let it do all your homework, you will not learn anything yourself, because the brain, like a muscle, becomes stronger only when it is used.
The best way to use AI is as a partner, not as a replacement for your own thinking.

q.q: What is one example of AI in daily life?
q.a: A map that finds the fastest road

q.q: Why should we check important facts?
q.a: AI programs sometimes make mistakes with confidence

q.q: What happens if a student lets AI do all the homework?
q.a: The student will not learn anything
w: The student will become a muscle

7.text:
Leonardo da Vinci was born in 1452 in a small Italian town. As a boy, he loved to draw animals and plants, and when he was about fourteen, his father sent him to work with a famous artist in Florence. There he learned painting, but also sculpture and how to make machines.
Leonardo is best known for two paintings: the Mona Lisa, which hangs in the Louvre in Paris, and The Last Supper, which is painted on a wall in Milan. But he was much more than a painter. He filled thousands of pages of notebooks with drawings of the human body, water, birds and flying machines. He wrote many of his notes backwards, so that they could be read in a mirror.
He was always asking questions. Why does the sky look blue? How does a bird stay in the air? How does blood move around the body? Many of his ideas were far ahead of his time. Although his flying machines never left the ground, they were based on careful study of birds.
Leonardo showed that art and science are not enemies. Both begin with looking closely and asking why.

q.q: What did young Leonardo learn in Florence?
q.a: Painting, sculpture and how to make machines

q.q: Why did Leonardo write many notes backwards?
q.a: So they could be read in a mirror
w: Because he was left-handed and tired

q.q: What does the writer say about art and science?
q.a: Both begin with looking closely and asking why
w: Science is more useful than art

7.text:
Every afternoon, the children of the village played in a beautiful garden belonging to a Giant. It had soft green grass, sweet flowers and peach trees that were covered with pink blossoms in spring.
One day the Giant returned from a long visit to a friend. When he saw the children in his garden, he shouted angrily, "My own garden is my own garden! Nobody is allowed to play in it except myself." He built a high wall and put up a notice: TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED.
After that, the poor children had nowhere to play. Strangely, spring did not come to the Giant's garden. Snow and frost stayed all year, and the North Wind and Hail were the only visitors.
One morning the Giant heard lovely birdsong. Through a hole in the wall, the children had crept in, and wherever they sat, the trees had burst into flower. Only one corner was still wintry, where a small boy was too little to climb into a tree.
The Giant's heart melted. He lifted the boy into the branches, knocked down the wall and said, "It is your garden now, children." From that day on, spring never left.

q.q: Why did the Giant build a wall?
q.a: He did not want anybody else in his garden
w: He wanted to keep out the wind
He was afraid of the snow
He was building a new house

q.q: What happened when the children crept in?
Why did the Giant change his mind?
q.a: He felt sorry for a small boy and understood his mistake

7.text:
Last month, twelve students from a school in Lyon, France, visited our school for two weeks. Each of them stayed with a Chinese family, and I was lucky to host a girl named Camille.
On the first evening, we were both shy. Camille had studied Chinese for only a year, and my French is limited to "bonjour" and "merci". We solved the problem with gestures, a translation app and a lot of laughing.
During the visit, we showed our guests how to write characters with a brush and how to make dumplings. In return, they taught us a French song and some easy card games. Camille was surprised that we have lessons at 7:30 in the morning and that our lunch is eaten at school. She said that in France, students often have a two-hour break in the middle of the day.
When the two weeks were over, we cried at the airport. We have promised to write to each other every month. I have realised that, although our countries are far apart, young people everywhere share the same hopes, jokes and worries.

q.q: How did the writer and Camille solve their language problem?
q.a: With gestures, an app and laughing

q.q: What surprised Camille about Chinese schools?
q.a: Lessons start at 7:30 and lunch is eaten at school

q.q: What did the writer learn from the visit?
q.a: Young people everywhere share the same hopes and worries

7.text:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all sea creatures live in or around them. Because of this, scientists sometimes call them the rainforests of the sea.
A reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Each polyp makes a hard skeleton of limestone around its soft body, and when it dies, the skeleton stays behind. Over thousands of years, millions of these skeletons pile up and form huge structures. The Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Australia, is so large that it can be seen from space.
Polyps live together with tiny plants that give them food and bright colours. But corals are very sensitive. If the water becomes too warm, the plants leave, and the coral turns white. This is known as bleaching, and it may kill the reef.
Other dangers are pollution, careless fishing and chemicals in sunscreen. If we want healthy reefs for our grandchildren, we must cut pollution, protect fish and control climate change. Reefs have survived for millions of years, but they may not survive us.

q.q: Why are reefs called the rainforests of the sea?
q.a: A great number of sea creatures live in or near them
w: Rain falls on them every day
They are found only in warm forests

q.q: What happens when the water becomes too warm?
q.a: The tiny plants leave and the coral turns white
w: The reef moves to deeper water

q.q: What is one thing we can do to protect reefs?

7.text:
Many students leave home in the morning without eating anything. They say that they are in a hurry, or that they are not hungry, or that they want to lose weight. But nutrition experts agree that breakfast is one of the most important meals of the day.
During the night, your body uses up the energy from your last meal. By morning, your blood sugar is low, and your brain, which uses about a fifth of your energy, does not have enough fuel. Students who skip breakfast often find it hard to concentrate, and they may feel tired before the second lesson.
A good breakfast should include a few different kinds of food. Whole grains, such as oats or wholemeal bread, give energy that lasts. Eggs, milk or beans provide protein, and a piece of fruit adds vitamins. Sugary cereals and fried snacks taste good, but they give a quick burst of energy that soon disappears.
If you really cannot manage a full meal, take something small with you, such as a banana or a boiled egg. Your morning classes will thank you.

q.q: Why is the brain short of fuel in the morning?
q.a: The body has used up the energy from the last meal
w: The blood sugar is very high

q.q: Which food gives energy that lasts?
What is the writer's advice for students in a hurry?
q.a: Take something small like a banana or an egg

7.text:
More than two thousand years ago, a Chinese envoy named Zhang Qian travelled west from the Han capital. His mission was to find allies against the enemies of the empire. He was captured, spent years as a prisoner and finally returned with news of unknown lands and peoples.
His journeys opened the way for what we now call the Silk Road. It was not a single road but a network of routes that crossed deserts, mountains and grasslands, and joined China with Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean.
