Few merchants travelled the whole way. Goods were passed from trader to trader, rising in price at every stage.
Chinese silk was the most famous product, but camels also carried tea, paper and porcelain westward. In the other direction came grapes, walnuts, glass and horses, as well as new musical instruments and ideas.
The Silk Road carried more than goods. Religions, stories and inventions travelled along it, too. Paper-making and printing, for example, reached the West this way. The routes taught people that contact with strangers, though risky, can make every nation richer.

q.q: What was Zhang Qian's mission?
q.a: To find allies against the empire's enemies

q.q: Why did goods become more expensive along the Silk Road?
q.a: They were passed from trader to trader

q.q: What travelled along the Silk Road besides goods?

7.t: The Old Man Who Moved Mountains
7.src: adapted from a Chinese folk tale (Yu Gong Yi Shan, public domain)
7.text:
Long ago, an old man called Yu Gong lived in a small village. He was nearly ninety years old. In front of his house stood two huge mountains that blocked the way, so that every trip to the town meant a long walk around them.
One day Yu Gong called his family together. "Let us dig away these mountains," he said. "Then we will be able to walk straight to the town." His sons and grandsons agreed, and the next morning they began to carry stones and earth to the sea, and each trip to the sea took a whole year.
A wise man in the neighbouring village laughed. "You are too old," he said. "You cannot even remove a small hill."
Yu Gong answered calmly, "When I die, my sons will continue. They will have children, and those children will have more. But the mountains cannot grow any higher. Why can't we move them one day?"
The gods in heaven heard these words and were moved. They sent two heavenly beings to carry the mountains away. The way was clear, and people still tell this story to show that perseverance can achieve great things.

q.q: Why did Yu Gong want to move the mountains?
q.a: They blocked the way to the town

q.q: What was Yu Gong's reply to the wise man?
q.a: His family would continue the work for generations
w: He would ask the gods for money
He would stop when he was ninety

q.q: What does the story teach?

7.text:
A tropical rainforest is like a tall building with four floors, and each one has its own residents. Scientists believe that more than half of all the plant and animal species on land live in rainforests, even though these forests cover only a small part of Earth.
At the top is the emergent layer, where the tallest trees rise above the rest, sometimes as high as a fifteen-storey building. Eagles and butterflies live here, enjoying the sun and the wind. Below it is the canopy, a thick green roof of leaves and branches. It blocks most of the sunlight and is home to monkeys, parrots and snakes.
The third floor, the understory, is dark and still. Small trees and big-leafed plants grow here, and jaguars and tree frogs hide among them. Finally, on the forest floor, it is so dark that very few plants can grow. Fallen leaves are broken down by insects and fungi within weeks, and the nutrients go back into the soil.
Sadly, rainforests are disappearing fast. Trees are cut down for farms, wood and roads, and every lost tree is a home destroyed.

q.q: Which layer is a thick green roof?
Why can few plants grow on the forest floor?
Why are rainforests disappearing?
q.a: Trees are cut down for farms, wood and roads

7.text:
When Helen Keller was nineteen months old, a serious illness left her blind and deaf. She grew into a wild and angry child, because she could not understand the world around her or explain what she wanted. Her parents were desperate, but they did not give up.
When Helen was almost seven, a young teacher named Anne Sullivan came to live with the family. She began to spell words into Helen's hand, using her fingers. At first, Helen thought it was only a game. Then, one day at a water pump, Anne held Helen's hand under the cool water and spelled the word "water" into her palm again and again. Suddenly, Helen understood that everything has a name.
From that moment, she learned with great speed. She learned to read in Braille, to write and even to speak. In 1904 she graduated from a famous university with honours, the first deaf and blind person to do so.
Helen Keller spent her life writing books and giving speeches to help people with disabilities. She proved that a person's limits are often smaller than we think.

q.q: Why was Helen an angry child?
q.a: She could not understand the world or say what she wanted

q.q: What happened at the water pump?
q.a: Helen understood that everything has a name
w: Anne took Helen to the doctor

q.q: What did Helen do for the rest of her life?
q.a: She wrote books and gave speeches to help disabled people
w: She taught Braille in a school only
She worked in a water factory

7.text:
Wei had been swimming since he was six, and at fourteen he was the fastest boy in his club. So when the regional championship came, everyone expected him to win the two hundred metres.
He did not. In the final, he started badly, was overtaken at the turn and finished fourth. When he climbed out of the pool, he could hardly look at his coach. "I have ruined everything," he said.
Coach Liu did not shout. "Tell me what happened," she said, and together they watched a video of the race. Wei saw that he had been looking at the other swimmers instead of concentrating on his own strokes. He had also gone out too fast, and by the last fifty metres he had no strength left.
"Losing is a teacher," said the coach. "If you learn from it, it is worth more than an easy win."
Three months later, in a new race, Wei held back at the start, kept his rhythm and sprinted at the end. He won by half a second, but what he remembered most was the lesson that had made it possible.

q.q: Where did Wei finish in the final?
What did Wei learn from the video?
q.a: He had looked at others and started too fast
w: His coach had made an error

q.q: What did Coach Liu mean by "Losing is a teacher"?

7.text:
It was Christmas Eve, and Della had only one dollar and eighty-seven cents. She had counted it three times. Tomorrow was Christmas, and she wanted to buy a present for her husband Jim, whom she loved more than anything.
The young couple was poor, and they had two treasures. One was Jim's gold watch, a gift from his grandfather. The other was Della's long, shining brown hair, which fell below her knees.
Della stood by the window for a minute, and then she hurried out. She sold her hair to a shop for twenty dollars, and with the money she bought a beautiful chain for Jim's watch. At seven o'clock, she waited for him with her short hair and a nervous heart.
Jim came in and stopped, staring at her. "Don't be sad," she said. "My hair will grow again." Slowly, he took a package out of his pocket. Inside were beautiful combs for her hair. But Jim had sold his watch to buy them.
They smiled, hugging each other. They had both given up their greatest treasure for love, and that made them the wisest of all gift-givers.

q.q: What did Della sell?
What did she buy for Jim?
Why was Jim's present now useless?
q.a: Della had cut off her hair, and he had sold his watch
w: He had lost it on the way

7.text:
For thousands of years, people have used the wind. Ancient sailors crossed seas with sails, and farmers in many countries built windmills to grind corn and pump water. Today, we use the same energy in a new way: giant machines called wind turbines make electricity.
A modern turbine can be as tall as a seventy-storey building. The wind turns its long blades, and the blades spin a generator. A single large turbine can supply enough electricity for hundreds of homes. When many turbines are built together, they form a wind farm, often in open land or out at sea, where the wind is stronger and steadier.
Wind power has important advantages. It produces no smoke and uses no fuel, and the wind will never run out. However, wind farms are not perfect. They make a little noise, they can harm birds if they are built in the wrong place, and, of course, the wind does not blow all the time.
That is why engineers combine wind with other sources, such as solar panels and batteries. China now has more wind power than any other country, and many experts think this will keep growing.

q.q: How does a wind turbine make electricity?
q.a: The wind turns the blades, which spin a generator
w: The blades burn small amounts of fuel

q.q: Why are wind farms often built at sea?
q.a: The wind is stronger and steadier there
w: There is no noise at sea

q.q: Why do engineers combine wind with other sources?
q.a: The wind does not blow all the time
w: Turbines cannot be built on land

7.text:
Last week, my grandfather bought a smart speaker. He had read that it could play music, tell the weather and even answer questions, and he was very excited. Unfortunately, he does not speak to machines the way young people do.
On the first evening, he stood in front of the speaker and said politely, "Good evening, would you be so kind as to play some old opera?" The speaker replied, "Sorry, I did not understand." Grandfather tried again, louder and slower. Again, the speaker did not understand. Finally he shouted, and the speaker started to play a loud pop song.
"That is not opera!" he roared. "Stop at once!" The speaker stopped, and then it said: "Now playing: Stop at Once, by a band you have never heard of."
My sister and I were laughing so much that we had to leave the room. When we returned, Grandfather was sitting in his chair, and the speaker was playing a quiet opera. "I asked nicely," he said, "and I added the word 'please'." We never found out whether it was the "please" or luck.

q.q: Why was Grandfather excited about the speaker?
q.a: He had read it could play music and answer questions
w: His grandchildren gave it to him

q.q: What happened when Grandfather shouted?
q.a: The speaker played a loud pop song

q.q: Why did the children laugh?
q.a: The speaker took his words as a song title

7.text:
Every culture has special days to celebrate, and although the customs differ, many festivals share the same ideas: thanks, hope, family and light.
In India, Diwali is the festival of lights. In autumn, families clean their homes, put small oil lamps along the windows and light fireworks. The lamps are a symbol of the victory of light over darkness. In the United States, people celebrate Thanksgiving on the fourth Thursday of November. Families travel long distances to share a big meal with turkey and pumpkin pie, and to say thank you for the year's harvest.
In Mexico, the Day of the Dead is not a sad day at all. Families build colourful altars with photographs, flowers and favourite foods of relatives who have died. They believe that the spirits come back to visit, and they remember them with love and laughter.
In many countries, Christmas is celebrated on the twenty-fifth of December, with gifts, songs and family meals. The Chinese Lantern Festival, with its glowing lanterns and sweet rice balls, closes the Spring Festival.
When we learn about other festivals, we discover that the world is different in its customs, but alike in its heart.

q.q: What do the lamps of Diwali stand for?
q.a: The victory of light over darkness

q.q: What is special about the Day of the Dead in Mexico?
q.a: People remember dead relatives with love and laughter
w: It is a sad and silent day

q.q: What is the writer's main idea?
q.a: Festivals differ in customs but share similar hearts

7.src: adapted from Rudyard Kipling, The Jungle Book (public domain)
7.text:
A young mongoose called Rikki-Tikki was carried away from his home by a flood and found lying in a garden in India. A kind English family took him in. The little boy, Teddy, put him in his bed, and Rikki-Tikki soon became part of the family.
But the garden had a terrible danger. Two cobras, Nag and Nagaina, lived in it, and they wanted the family to leave. Rikki-Tikki was born to fight snakes, and he was not afraid. "I will protect this house," he told himself.
One morning he attacked Nag in the bathroom, and after a long fight, he killed him. Nagaina was furious. She decided to bite Teddy at breakfast, while the family sat on the veranda.
Rikki-Tikki heard her plan from the little bird Darzee. He ran to the snake's nest, found her eggs and took one in his mouth. When Nagaina saw him, she forgot everything else. "Give it back!" she hissed.
The mongoose led her away from the house, and in a last fierce fight in a hole in the ground, he defeated her. From then on, the garden was safe, and the birds sang again in the trees.

q.q: How did Rikki-Tikki come to the garden?
w: He was bought at a shop

q.q: How did Rikki-Tikki lure Nagaina away from the house?
q.a: He took one of her eggs
w: He set fire to the nest

q.q: What happened at the end?

7.text:
The internet has changed the way we learn, play and talk to our friends. It gives us instant answers and brings people together from all over the world. But, like a busy street, it has dangers, and it is wise to learn the rules before we go out alone.
The first rule is to protect your private information. Never share your home address, your school or your passwords with people you only know online. A stranger may pretend to be a child, but he could be an adult with bad intentions. If someone asks you to keep a secret from your parents, tell a trusted adult immediately.
The second rule is to think before you post. Photos and messages can be copied and shared within seconds, and it is almost impossible to take them back. Ask yourself, "Would I be happy if my teacher, my grandmother or a future employer saw this?"
Finally, be kind. Words on a screen can hurt as much as words said face to face. If you see cruel behaviour, do not join in; support the person who is being hurt and report it. A good online citizen makes the internet a better place for everyone.

q.q: Why is the internet compared to a busy street?
q.a: It is useful but has dangers

q.q: What should you do if someone online asks you to keep a secret from your parents?
w: Keep the secret to be polite

q.q: Why should you think before you post?
q.a: Posts can be copied and are hard to take back

7.text:
On a clear night, far from city lights, you can see about two thousand stars with your own eyes. Long before telescopes were invented, people looked at them, imagined pictures in the groups they formed and gave them names. We call such groups constellations.
In China, ancient astronomers divided the sky into many small areas and named them after officials, animals and everyday things. One of the best known is the Northern Dipper, seven bright stars shaped like a spoon. In Western tradition, the same stars are part of the Great Bear. By following two stars at the end of the spoon, one can find the Pole Star, which stays almost still in the northern sky. For centuries, travellers used it to find their way at night.
The stars look as if they are all at the same distance, but they are not. Many are enormous suns, and the light we see tonight may have left them hundreds of years ago. Looking at the night sky is therefore also a look into the past.
Next time the sky is clear, put your phone away, lie down on the grass and let your eyes get used to the dark.

q.q: What is a constellation?
q.a: A group of stars that people have given a name

q.q: Why was the Pole Star useful to travellers?
q.a: It stays almost still in the northern sky
w: It moves in the shape of a spoon

q.q: Why is looking at the night sky also a look into the past?
q.a: The light may have left the stars hundreds of years ago
w: The stars are very old men
The sky is darker than before

7.text:
It was the last week of the year, and Mr Zhang asked his class to write a short letter to themselves. "Think about the past twelve months," he said. "What have you achieved, and what would you like to do better?"
Xiao Yu chewed her pencil for a while. At the beginning of the year, she had been afraid to speak English in front of others. This autumn, she had given a talk about pandas, and everybody had listened. She wrote: "I was brave. I will be braver next year."
Liang wrote about football. He had not become the best player, but he had practised every week and made the school team. Then he wrote with a smile that he had also failed his maths test in October. "I did not give up," he wrote. "I asked for help, and in December I got eighty-five."
After the class, the students put their letters in an envelope, and Mr Zhang promised to give them back next year.
Later, Xiao Yu thought about her letter. The year had been difficult at times, but looking back, she realised that she had grown, and she was looking forward to the new one.

q.q: What did Mr Zhang ask the class to do?
w: Make a plan for the school

q.q: How did Liang improve his maths?
q.a: He asked for help and kept trying

q.q: How did Xiao Yu feel at the end?
q.a: She felt that she had grown and looked forward to the new year
w: She was ashamed of her talk
She wanted to leave the school

8.text:
Long ago, a young shepherd looked after his village's sheep on a green hill. The work was lonely, and he often felt bored. One afternoon he had a cruel idea. 'If I shouted that a wolf was coming, the villagers would run up the hill,' he thought. 'That would be funny.'
So he shouted, 'Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is attacking the sheep!' The villagers dropped their tools and hurried up the hill with sticks. But they found only the boy, laughing at them. They were angry and went home.
A few days later he played the same trick again. Again the villagers ran to help, and again they were laughed at. The old farmer who led them said that the boy should be ashamed of himself.
Then, one evening, a real wolf crept out of the forest. The boy screamed, 'Wolf! Please help! The wolf is really here!' This time nobody came. The villagers believed that he was joking once more. By the time the sun went down, many of the sheep had been eaten, and the boy was sitting on the grass in tears.
That night an old man told him a sad truth: a liar is not believed, even when he tells the truth.

q.q: Why did the boy shout 'Wolf!' the first time?
q.a: He thought it would be funny
w: He wanted to sell his sheep
He was afraid of the dark

q.q: What happened when the real wolf came?
q.a: Nobody believed the boy and came to help
w: The villagers killed the wolf quickly
The boy ran away with the sheep
The farmer took the boy home

q.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
q.a: People do not trust a liar, even when he is honest
w: Wolves are always dangerous to sheep
Villagers should be kinder to children

8.t: Spring Festival in a Modern City
8.text:
For many Chinese families, the Spring Festival is the most important holiday of the year. Every winter, hundreds of millions of people travel home to be with their relatives. Trains and airports are crowded, but nobody seems to mind, because the reunion dinner on New Year's Eve is worth the journey.
Lin Mei, who lives in Shanghai, remembers how different the holiday was when her grandmother was young. In those days, children waited all year for new clothes and a few sweets. Today, the family still makes dumplings together, and the children still receive red envelopes, but some traditions have changed. Many people now send greetings by phone, and some families even give their money in a digital red envelope.
In big cities, fireworks are limited because of air pollution and safety, so people enjoy lantern shows and temple fairs instead. Lin Mei says that the noise she misses most is the sound of firecrackers, but she admits that the cleaner air is a good trade.
If you asked her what makes the festival special, she would not mention the gifts or the food. She would tell you that it is the feeling of being together, which no technology can replace.

q.q: Why do people not mind the crowded trains?
q.a: The family dinner is worth the journey
w: They have to go to work

q.q: Why are fireworks limited in big cities?
q.a: Because of air pollution and safety
w: Because children are afraid of them
Because people no longer like them

q.q: What does Lin Mei think makes the festival special?

8.text:
In the 1840s, a young Englishwoman named Ada Lovelace did something that nobody had done before. She wrote instructions for a machine that did not yet exist.
Ada was born in 1815. Her father was the famous poet Lord Byron, but she hardly knew him. Her mother, who wanted her to be sensible, made sure that she studied mathematics and science instead of poetry. Ada turned out to be brilliant at both.
When she was a teenager, she met Charles Babbage, an inventor who was designing a huge mechanical calculator called the Analytical Engine. Babbage never finished building it, but Ada understood its possibilities better than almost anyone. She translated an article about the machine and added her own long notes. In them, she explained how it could be given a series of steps to follow. Many historians call this the first computer program.
Ada also had a remarkable vision. She believed that a machine like this could do more than calculate numbers. If it were given the right rules, she wrote, it might even create music.
Ada died young, at the age of thirty-six. Her ideas were forgotten for a long time, but today she is remembered as a pioneer, and a programming language has been named after her.

q.q: Why did Ada's mother make her study mathematics?
q.a: She wanted her daughter to be sensible
w: She wanted her to build machines
She did not like poetry at all
She wanted her to meet Babbage

q.q: What did Ada add to the article she translated?
q.a: Her own long notes about how the machine could follow steps
w: A drawing of the finished machine
The money to build the engine

q.q: What does 'pioneer' mean in the last paragraph?

8.text:
'What would you do if you were invisible for one day?' Tom asked his sister Anna at breakfast.
'That's easy,' said Anna. 'I would go into the school and read the maths test before the exam. Then I would get full marks.'
'That's cheating!' Tom laughed. 'I would never do that. If I could turn invisible, I would walk into the best football stadium in the country and watch the match from the pitch.'
'You would be run over by the players,' said Anna.
Their father, who was reading the newspaper, put it down. 'Do you know what I would do?' he asked. 'I would visit the boss of my company and listen to what he really thinks about me.'
'And if he said something terrible?' asked Anna.
'Then I would quietly go home and look for a new job,' said Dad with a smile.
Mum came in with the tea. She said that she had been listening from the kitchen. 'If I were invisible,' she said, 'I would stay at home. For once, I could sit in my chair in peace and nobody would ask me where their socks were.'
Everyone laughed. Then Tom added that being invisible might not be so wonderful after all. 'If nobody could see you,' he said, 'nobody would say hello to you either.'
'That's true,' Anna agreed. 'Let's eat our breakfast. I prefer being seen.'

q.q: What would Anna do if she were invisible?
q.a: Read the maths test before the exam

q.q: Why would Mum like to be invisible?
q.a: She could sit in peace without being asked questions
w: She could find a new job

q.q: What does Tom think is a problem with being invisible?

8.text:
Most teenagers know the feeling of being too tired to think in the morning. Scientists say that this is not just laziness. Young people between thirteen and eighteen need about eight to ten hours of sleep every night, but many get much less.
During sleep, the body is not simply switched off. Your brain is busy sorting the information it has received during the day. Memories are stored, and unimportant details are thrown away. This is why students who sleep well after studying often remember more than those who stay up all night. Sleep is also the time when muscles are repaired and the body grows.
Teenagers have another problem. Their body clocks change, so they feel sleepy later in the evening and want to wake up later in the morning. Unfortunately, school often starts early. Some schools in other countries have moved their first lesson to a later time, and they report that students are healthier and happier.
How can you sleep better? Doctors recommend going to bed at the same time every day and keeping the bedroom dark and quiet. Screens should be avoided for an hour before bed, because the bright light tells the brain that it is still daytime. A good night's sleep is not a luxury. It is as important as food and water.

q.q: How much sleep do teenagers need?
What does the brain do during sleep?
q.a: It sorts information and stores memories

q.q: Why should we avoid screens before bed?
q.a: Bright light makes the brain think it is still daytime
w: They make the room too noisy
They make the body grow too fast

8.text:
The Great Wall of China is not one single wall, and it was not built at one time. It is a series of walls and towers that were constructed by different rulers over more than two thousand years. The earliest walls were built by small kingdoms to defend themselves from their neighbours. Later, the first emperor of China joined several of them together around 220 BC.
Most of the Great Wall that tourists visit today was built much later, during the Ming dynasty. The Ming builders used bricks and stone, which made the wall stronger than the earlier ones of packed earth. Soldiers lived in the watchtowers, and they sent messages along the wall by lighting fires. A column of smoke could warn the next tower that enemies were approaching, and the news travelled hundreds of kilometres in a short time.
All together, the walls and their branches stretch for more than twenty thousand kilometres. Contrary to a popular story, the Great Wall cannot be seen from the Moon. Astronauts have said that it is hard to see even from a low orbit, because the wall is long but very narrow.
Building it was hard and dangerous, and many workers lost their lives. Today the wall is no longer a defence. It is a symbol of Chinese history and a place visited by millions of people every year.

q.q: Who built the part of the wall that most tourists visit today?
q.a: The builders of the Ming dynasty

q.q: How did soldiers send messages along the wall?
q.a: By lighting fires that made smoke
w: By shouting from tower to tower

q.q: What does the writer say about seeing the wall from the Moon?
q.a: It is a popular story that is not true
w: It can be seen with a telescope only
Only the towers can be seen

8.text:
Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the ocean. Bottles, bags and fishing nets are carried by rivers and wind from the land to the sea, and once they are there, they can stay for hundreds of years. Plastic does not rot like food or paper. Instead, it breaks into smaller and smaller pieces, which are called microplastics.
The effects on wildlife are serious. Sea turtles often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and eat them, and seabirds feed pieces of plastic to their chicks. Scientists have even found microplastics in the stomachs of tiny fish, which means that the problem reaches the food chain, and perhaps even our own dinner plates.
However, the situation is not hopeless. Many countries have banned thin plastic bags, and some cities have begun to charge for them. Volunteers clean beaches at weekends, and inventors are designing machines that collect rubbish from rivers before it reaches the sea.
What can ordinary people do? If everybody carried a cloth bag and a reusable bottle, millions of items would never be thrown away. Choosing products with less packaging also helps. Small decisions are not enough on their own, but if enough people make them, the ocean will have a better chance to recover.

q.q: What are microplastics?
q.a: Very small pieces that come from larger plastic
w: A new kind of fish food

q.q: Why do sea turtles eat plastic bags?
q.a: They think the bags are jellyfish
w: They like the taste of plastic
They want to clean the sea

q.q: What is the writer's main message?
q.a: Small everyday choices can help the ocean
w: Only governments can solve the problem
The ocean can never be cleaned
Plastic should never be used again

8.text:
Every afternoon, when school was over, the children went to play in the Giant's garden. It was a large, lovely garden with soft grass and beautiful flowers, and the birds sang in the trees. The children were very happy there.
One day the Giant came home. He had been away for seven years, visiting a friend. When he saw the children playing, he shouted, 'My garden is my own garden! Nobody may play in it but myself.' He built a high wall around it and put up a notice: TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED.
The poor children had nowhere to play. Then spring came to the country, but in the Giant's garden it was still winter. The birds did not sing, the trees forgot to blossom, and snow and frost covered everything. 'I cannot understand why the spring is so late,' said the Giant, looking out of his window.
One morning he heard lovely music. The children had crept in through a hole in the wall, and wherever they sat, the trees were covered with flowers. Only in one corner was it still winter, where a tiny boy was standing, too small to climb into the tree.
The Giant's heart melted. 'How selfish I have been!' he said. He lifted the little boy into the tree and knocked down the wall. From that day, the children played in the garden, and the Giant played with them.
8.src: adapted from Oscar Wilde, The Selfish Giant (public domain)

q.q: Why did the Giant build a wall?
q.a: He did not want anyone to play in his garden
w: He wanted to keep the birds inside
He was afraid of the snow

q.q: Why was it still winter in the garden?
q.a: Spring did not come because the children were kept out
w: The wall kept the sun away
The birds had flown to another country

q.q: Why did the Giant change his mind?
q.a: He saw a small boy who could not climb the tree

8.text:
Every year in May, Hanwen's school holds a ten-kilometre race through the park next to the river. Hanwen had never been a good runner. In fact, in the sports lessons he was usually the last to finish. But this year, after his grandfather became ill, he decided to take part. His grandfather had always said that the most important thing in any race is to finish.
For three months, Hanwen trained before breakfast. At first he could only run for five minutes without stopping, and his legs hurt so much that he almost gave up. His coach advised him not to compare himself with others, but to try to be a little better than he had been the day before.
On the day of the race, the weather was warm, and hundreds of students stood at the starting line. At the sound of the whistle, the fastest runners rushed ahead. Hanwen started slowly and kept a steady speed. At the eighth kilometre, he felt dizzy and wanted to stop, but he remembered his grandfather's words.
He crossed the finish line in more than seventy minutes, far behind the winners. Yet when he saw his grandfather waiting there in a wheelchair, he felt like a champion. 'I knew you could do it,' the old man said, and he smiled with pride.

q.q: Why did Hanwen decide to take part in the race?
w: He wanted to win a prize

q.q: What did the coach advise him to do?
q.a: Try to be better than he had been the day before
w: Stop running if his legs hurt
Start at the front of the race

q.q: Why did Hanwen feel like a champion at the end?
q.a: His grandfather was proud of him
w: He came first in the race

8.text:
'Have you decided which club you're going to join?' Mia asked her friend Jack in the school corridor.
'Not yet,' Jack replied. 'My mother says that I should join the chess club, because it would help me to think more carefully. My father told me that the football team is much better for my health.'
'And what do you want?' asked Mia.
Jack scratched his head. 'To be honest, I'd like to join the drama club. But I would be too nervous to speak in front of people.'
'You are not nervous when you talk to me,' said Mia. 'Besides, the teacher said that nobody in the drama club has to be a star. Some people work on the lights, and others design the costumes.'
'Really? I didn't know that,' said Jack. 'What are you going to do?'
Mia smiled. 'I'm joining the science club. Last week, they made a small rocket from a plastic bottle, and it flew over the roof of the school!'
'That sounds fun. But if I joined your club, who would play the hero in our class play?'
'You could do both,' said Mia. 'Drama club is on Tuesdays, and science club is on Thursdays. If you want to try everything, you can. The school says that students may change clubs at the end of each term.'
Jack thought for a moment. 'All right,' he said. 'I'll start with drama. If I hate it, I'll come and build rockets with you.'

q.q: What does Jack's mother want him to join?
Why is Jack worried about the drama club?
q.a: He would be nervous speaking in front of people
w: It is on the wrong day

q.q: What will Jack do first?

8.text:
Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in 1867, at a time when women in Poland were not allowed to study at university. Her family was not rich, but she loved learning, and she worked as a teacher for several years to save money. In 1891 she moved to Paris, where she studied physics and mathematics. She often had very little to eat, and in winter she wore all the clothes she owned to keep warm.
In Paris she married a scientist, Pierre Curie, and together they investigated a new kind of energy that certain materials give off. Marie called this property radioactivity. After years of difficult work in a poorly equipped shed, the couple discovered two new elements, polonium and radium. The first was named after her native country.
In 1903 the Curies shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with another scientist. Pierre died in an accident in 1906, but Marie carried on, and in 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry. She remains the only person who has been awarded Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
During the First World War, she helped doctors by organising mobile X-ray machines that were used near the battlefield. Her work saved many lives, though it also harmed her health, because the dangers of radiation were not understood at that time.

q.q: Why did Marie work as a teacher before going to Paris?
q.a: To save money for her studies
w: Because she wanted to be a teacher forever

8.text:
A bee colony is like a small city where each insect has a job. In summer, a single hive can contain more than fifty thousand bees, but only one of them is the queen. Her task is to lay eggs. The workers, which are all female, clean the hive, feed the young and guard the entrance, and when they are older, they fly out to find food.
To make honey, workers visit flowers and collect a sweet liquid called nectar. They store it in a special stomach and carry it back to the hive. There, other bees take it and pass it from mouth to mouth. During this process, natural substances change the nectar chemically. Then the bees spread it into the wax cells and fan it with their wings until most of the water has evaporated. When the honey is thick enough, they cover the cell with a thin layer of wax to keep it fresh.
Bees do not only make honey. As they move from flower to flower, pollen sticks to their legs and bodies, which helps plants produce fruit and seeds. Scientists estimate that bees help to pollinate about one third of the food we eat.
Sadly, bee numbers have fallen in many places because of pesticides and the loss of wild flowers. Planting flowers in gardens and balconies is a simple way to help these hard-working insects.

q.q: What is the queen bee's main job?
Why do the bees fan the honey with their wings?
q.a: To make the water in it disappear

q.q: How can ordinary people help bees?

8.text:
On Friday afternoon, Leo realised that his phone was missing. He had used it on the bus, he remembered, and he had been sure that he put it back in his bag. Now the bag was empty, except for two pencils and a half-eaten sandwich.
His sister Chloe, who enjoyed detective stories, offered to help. 'First,' she said, 'tell me exactly what you did after you got off the bus.'
'I walked to the bakery and bought some bread,' said Leo. 'Then I went home.'
'Did you pay with your phone?' asked Chloe.
Leo's face went red. 'Yes, I did. The woman at the bakery held it while I looked for the bread.'
Chloe grinned. 'That is where we should look first. If she is a sensible person, she will have kept it safe.'
They hurried to the bakery, which was just closing. The woman behind the counter smiled when she saw Leo. 'I was hoping that you would come back,' she said. 'Your phone is on the shelf behind me. It rang twice, and a very worried lady asked who I was.'
'That was my mother,' groaned Leo.
When they got home, their mother wanted to know why her son had lost his phone for the third time that year. Leo promised that he would be more careful. 'If I forget it again,' he said, 'I'll buy you a cake from that bakery.'
Chloe laughed. 'You will be buying a lot of cakes, then.'

q.q: Where was Leo's phone?
Why did Leo's face go red?
q.a: He remembered that he had left the phone with the woman
w: He was angry with his sister
He had run to the bakery

q.q: What does 'sensible' mean in the story?

8.text:
Every year at the Mid-Autumn Festival, Chinese families gather to eat mooncakes and look at the full moon. Many parents also tell their children the old story of Chang'e, which has been told for thousands of years.
In ancient times, ten suns rose in the sky together, and the heat burned the crops and dried the rivers. A brave archer called Hou Yi shot down nine of them and saved the people. As a reward, a goddess gave him a magic pill. Whoever swallowed it would live for ever and fly up to heaven. Hou Yi did not want to leave his wife, Chang'e, so he hid the pill safely at home.
One day, while he was out hunting, an evil man called Feng Meng broke into the house. He forced Chang'e to hand over the pill. To stop him from taking it, she swallowed it herself. At once her body became light, and she floated out of the window and up into the sky until she reached the moon.
When Hou Yi came home and learned what had happened, he was heartbroken. He looked up and saw a shape on the bright moon that looked like his wife. Since then, people say, she has lived there with a white rabbit, and families on earth think of those who are far away from them whenever the moon is round.
8.src: adapted from a Chinese folk tale (public domain)

q.a: He shot down nine of the ten suns
w: He flew up to the moon

q.q: Why did Chang'e swallow the pill?
q.a: She did not want the evil man to have it
w: She was ill and needed medicine

q.q: What do families think of when the moon is round?
q.a: People who are far away from them

8.text:
A volcano is a place where hot melted rock, called magma, finds a way out of the Earth. Deep underground, the temperature is so high that rock turns into a thick liquid. Because magma is lighter than the rock around it, it slowly rises. When enough pressure builds up, it bursts out through an opening in the surface, and we call it lava.
Most volcanoes are found along the edges of the huge plates that make up the Earth's crust. The best-known example is the 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific Ocean, where about three quarters of the world's active volcanoes are located. Japan, Indonesia and Chile all lie on this ring, and their people have learned to live with the danger.
Eruptions are not all the same. Some volcanoes pour out slow rivers of lava that give people time to escape. Others explode violently and throw ash high into the air. In 1883, the eruption of Krakatoa in Indonesia was heard thousands of kilometres away, and the ash even changed the colour of sunsets around the world.
Volcanoes are not only destructive, however. The ash makes soil rich and fertile, which is why farmers often live close to them. Scientists now use instruments to measure small earthquakes and gas, and they can often warn villages before an eruption begins. That knowledge has saved countless lives.

q.q: Why does magma rise?
q.a: It is lighter than the rock around it
w: It is pushed by the wind
It is attracted by the Moon
It is colder than the rock

q.q: What is the 'Ring of Fire'?
q.a: An area around the Pacific with many active volcanoes

q.q: Why do farmers often live near volcanoes?
q.a: The ash makes the soil rich

8.text:
Ask a group of teenagers how many hours they spend online every day, and you will probably hear different answers. Some say two hours, others four or five. In several surveys, young people have admitted that they check their phones more than fifty times a day.
Social media has clear advantages. It allows friends to stay in touch when they live in different cities, and it helps shy people to find others who share their interests. During the pandemic, many students would have felt completely alone if they had not been able to talk to their classmates on screen.
But there are risks as well. People often show only the best parts of their lives, so it is easy to feel that everyone else is more successful or more beautiful. Experts have warned that this comparison can make teenagers anxious. Another problem is time itself. Apps are designed to be difficult to put down, and an evening of 'just checking' can easily disappear.
How can young people use the internet in a healthy way? Many schools recommend simple rules. Turn off notifications during homework. Keep phones out of the bedroom at night. Remember that a photograph is not the same as real life. Most importantly, spend time with friends face to face.
If you could live without your phone for a week, what would you miss most? And what, perhaps, would you discover instead?

q.q: What is one advantage of social media?
q.a: Friends can stay in touch over long distances

q.q: Why can social media make teenagers anxious?
q.a: People compare themselves with others' best moments
w: Phones are too heavy to carry

q.q: Which rule do schools recommend?
q.a: Keep phones out of the bedroom at night
w: Never use a phone at all
Check the phone fifty times a day

8.text:
A farmer had a donkey that had worked for him for many years. Now the donkey was old and weak, and the farmer decided to get rid of him. The donkey guessed what was going to happen and ran away. 'I shall go to the city of Bremen,' he thought. 'I can become a town musician there.'
On the road he met a hound that lay panting by the side of the path. 'My master wanted to kill me because I am too old to hunt,' said the dog. 'Come with me,' said the donkey. 'I will play the lute, and you can beat the drum.' Soon they met a cat with a sad face, and then a rooster that was about to be cooked for Sunday dinner. All of them agreed to go to Bremen.
But the city was far, and that evening they stopped in a forest. The rooster, from the top of a tree, saw a light in the distance. It was a house where a gang of robbers were eating a huge meal. The four animals climbed on top of each other at the window and made a terrible noise together. The robbers, thinking that a monster had come, ran into the woods.
The animals sat down to the feast and then went to sleep. They liked the house so much that they never went to Bremen at all.

q.a: The farmer wanted to get rid of him

8.text:
The Silk Road was not a single road. It was a network of trade routes that connected China with the Mediterranean world for more than a thousand years. The name was invented by a German geographer in the nineteenth century, because silk was the most famous product that travelled along it.
The journey began in the Han dynasty. In the second century BC, an official named Zhang Qian was sent to the west to look for allies. He was captured, spent about ten years as a prisoner, and eventually returned with valuable information about the countries beyond the deserts. Soon afterwards, merchants began to follow his route.
Very few traders travelled the whole way. Instead, goods were passed from one merchant to the next across deserts, mountains and rivers. Camels, which can survive for days without water, carried heavy loads through the Taklamakan Desert. Besides silk, traders exchanged tea, spices, glass, paper and precious stones.
Ideas moved along the roads as well. Buddhism travelled from India to China, and techniques such as papermaking slowly spread westward. Artists, musicians and cooks also learned from each other, and some of today's foods, such as noodles and grapes, may have crossed the routes in both directions.
Today, China has launched a modern plan to build new railways and ports, which it calls the Belt and Road Initiative. Whatever you think of this plan, it shows that the old idea of connecting distant places still inspires people.

q.q: Why was the Silk Road given that name?
q.a: Silk was its most famous product
w: It was built by silk traders
The roads were soft and smooth

q.q: What did Zhang Qian bring back after his journey?
q.a: Valuable information about lands beyond the deserts
w: A map of the Great Wall

q.q: Why did camels carry goods through the desert?
q.a: They can survive many days without water

8.text:
Rainforests cover only about six per cent of the Earth's land, yet they are home to more than half of all the plant and animal species in the world. The biggest one is in the Amazon basin in South America. Others can be found in Central Africa, Southeast Asia and parts of Australia.
The forest is organised in layers. At the top, the 'emergent layer' consists of a few giant trees that rise above everything else. Below them is the canopy, a thick roof of leaves where most of the animals live. Monkeys, parrots and snakes hardly ever come down to the ground. The forest floor, in contrast, is dark and damp, because only a little light gets through. There, fallen leaves are quickly broken down by insects and fungi, and the nutrients are used again.
Rainforests are important for all of us. Their trees take in huge amounts of carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and they also help to control rainfall. Many medicines, including some used to treat cancer, were discovered from rainforest plants.
Unfortunately, forests are being cut down for farmland, wood and roads. Every year, an area larger than many countries is lost. If this continues, countless species could disappear before scientists have even given them names. Supporting companies that use wood responsibly is one way in which ordinary people can protect these precious places.

q.q: Where do most rainforest animals live?
Why is the forest floor dark?
q.a: Very little light passes through the leaves

q.q: What is mentioned as a reason for losing forests?

8.text:
Tom Sawyer woke up on Saturday morning and looked out at a beautiful summer day. Unfortunately, his Aunt Polly had a different plan. She handed him a brush and a bucket of whitewash and told him to paint the long wooden fence in front of the house. Tom's heart sank.
He began slowly. Soon his friend Ben Rogers came walking along, eating an apple. 'Hello, old fellow, you're working, are you?' Ben said, laughing.
Tom looked at the fence like an artist. 'Why, it's you, Ben! I didn't notice you. What do you call work?'
'Why, isn't that work?'
Tom went on painting. 'Well, maybe it is, and maybe it isn't. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?'
That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped eating his apple. 'Say, Tom, let me paint a little.' Tom pretended to hesitate. 'No, Ben, Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence. I don't think that one boy in a thousand could do it well enough.'
'Oh, please! I'll give you my apple.'
Tom handed over the brush with a reluctant face, but with joy in his heart. By the afternoon, the fence had three coats of paint, and Tom had collected a pocket full of treasures from the boys who had paid to work. He had learned something important: to make a person want something, you only have to make it hard to get.
8.src: adapted from Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (public domain)

How did Tom make Ben want to paint?
q.a: He pretended that painting was a special chance
w: He told him it was an order

q.a: People want what seems hard to get

8.text:
'Have you seen the rubbish bins in the canteen?' Yuki asked her classmates at the student council meeting. 'Yesterday I counted forty plastic bottles in the general waste bin. Not one of them was recycled.'
'That is terrible,' said Daniel. 'But the bins are all the same colour. How would anyone know where to put things?'
'Exactly,' said Yuki. 'If we had different bins for paper, plastic and food waste, students would find it much easier. I asked the headmaster whether the school could buy some, and he said that the money was not available.'
Daniel thought about it. 'We could make them ourselves. The art club has plenty of paint, and the cleaner told me that there are several old boxes in the storeroom.'
'Good idea!' said Yuki. 'And we could put up posters that explain what goes in each bin. Many people think that greasy pizza boxes can be recycled, but they cannot.'
Another student, Hui, asked what would happen to the food waste. Yuki explained that the school garden could use it as compost. 'If the vegetables grow better, we can even eat them in the canteen,' she said.
The council voted, and everybody agreed. The following Monday, three colourful bins stood in the canteen. Within a month, the amount of general waste had dropped by half, and the headmaster, who had been so worried about the money, proudly wrote about the project in the school newsletter.

q.a: Plastic bottles were not being recycled

8.t: Zhang Heng and the Earthquake Detector
8.text:
About 1,900 years ago, in the Han dynasty, there lived a remarkable man named Zhang Heng. He was a scientist, an astronomer, a mathematician, a poet and an official at the imperial court. He studied the movement of the stars and built a water-powered model of the sky. But he is most famous for an invention that is often considered the world's first earthquake detector.
In the year 132, Zhang Heng completed his instrument, which was made of bronze. It looked like a big wine jar, about two metres across. Around the top, eight dragons faced in different directions, and each held a bronze ball in its mouth. Below them sat eight toads with their mouths open.
Inside the jar, an inner mechanism, perhaps a kind of pendulum, reacted to vibrations that arrived from far away. When an earthquake occurred, a ball dropped from the mouth of the dragon that pointed towards the quake, and it fell into a toad with a loud clang. In this way, the court knew in which direction to send help.
According to historical records, the device once detected an earthquake that nobody in the capital had felt. Some days later, a messenger arrived with news of the disaster in a faraway region, and the officials were amazed. Scientists today are still discussing exactly how the original machine worked, but they agree that it was a very clever idea.

q.q: What did the eight dragons hold in their mouths?
How did the court know the direction of an earthquake?
q.a: A ball fell from the dragon pointing that way
w: A bell rang in the capital
A messenger told them at once
The toads moved to the right place

q.q: Why were the officials amazed?
q.a: The device detected a quake that nobody in the capital had felt
w: The machine was made of gold

8.t: Where Does Our Tap Water Come From?
8.text:
When you turn on the tap, clean water flows out in an instant. We do this so often that we rarely wonder how the water got there. In fact, the journey is long and requires a great deal of work.
Most cities take their water from rivers, lakes or underground sources. First, the water is pumped into a treatment plant. There it passes through several stages. In the first stage, chemicals are added so that small pieces of dirt stick together and sink to the bottom. Then the water is filtered through layers of sand and gravel, which remove even smaller particles. Finally, a little chlorine is added to kill harmful bacteria. The treated water is checked many times before it is allowed to enter the pipes.
From the plant, the water is sent to huge towers or reservoirs, which are built high above the city. Gravity then pushes it through a network of underground pipes to homes, schools and factories. If the pipes are old, a lot of water can be lost through leaks, which is a serious problem in many places.
After we have used the water, it is not simply thrown away. It flows through the sewers to another treatment plant, where it is cleaned before it is returned to a river.
Fresh water is limited, and only about one per cent of the world's water is easily available for people. Closing the tap while brushing our teeth is a small habit that makes a real difference.

q.q: What happens in the first stage of treatment?
q.a: Chemicals make small pieces of dirt stick together
w: The water is filtered through sand

q.q: What moves the water from the towers to homes?
What is the main idea of the last paragraph?
q.a: Fresh water is limited, so small habits matter
w: Water should be sold at a higher price
The world has too much water

8.t: How the Camel Got His Hump
8.text:
In the beginning of years, when the world was so new, the Camel lived in the middle of a Howling Desert because he did not want to work. He ate sticks and thorns and prickles, and when anybody spoke to him he said 'Humph!' and nothing else.
Presently the Horse came to him on Monday morning, with a saddle on his back. 'Camel, O Camel, come out and trot like the rest of us.'
'Humph!' said the Camel, and the Horse went away to tell the Man.
Presently the Ox came to him, with the yoke on his neck. 'Camel, O Camel, come and plough like the rest of us.'
'Humph!' said the Camel, and the Ox went away to tell the Man.
At the end of the day the Man called the Horse and the Ox together. 'Two, O Two, I'm very sorry for you, but that Camel in the desert cannot work, so I shall leave him alone, and you must work double time to make up for it.'
Then the Djinn, who was in charge of All Deserts, rolled by in a cloud of dust. 'Camel, O Camel,' he said, 'why do you not work?'
'Humph!' said the Camel.
'Well,' said the Djinn, 'since you refuse to work, you will have a Humph of your own to carry. And you will be able to work for three days without eating, because you will live on the Humph!'
8.src: adapted from Rudyard Kipling, Just So Stories (public domain)

q.q: Why did the Camel live in the desert?
q.a: He did not want to work
w: He was afraid of the Man
He liked eating sticks and thorns more than grass

q.q: What happened because the Camel did not work?
q.a: The other animals had to work double time
w: The Dog went to the desert

q.q: What did the Djinn give the Camel?

8.text:
The first Olympic Games were held in Olympia, in Greece, more than two and a half thousand years ago. According to tradition, the first competition took place in 776 BC. The games were held to honour Zeus, the king of the Greek gods, and they happened every four years. At the beginning, there was only one event, a running race of about two hundred metres. Later, wrestling, boxing and chariot races were added.
Only free Greek men were allowed to compete, and women could not even watch. The winners did not receive gold medals. Their prize was a simple crown made of olive leaves, but they came home as heroes. Even wars were stopped for the period of the games, so that people could travel safely to Olympia.
The ancient games continued for about twelve hundred years until a Roman emperor banned them. They were revived in 1896 in Athens, thanks to a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin. He believed that sport could help to bring nations closer together. Only fourteen countries and about two hundred and forty athletes took part in the first modern Games.
Today, the Summer Olympics attract more than ten thousand athletes from over two hundred countries. Women compete in every sport, and a Winter Games takes place in between. The Olympic motto, 'Faster, Higher, Stronger', reminds us to do our best, whether we win or not.

q.q: What was the prize for winners in ancient Olympia?
Who made the modern Games happen in 1896?
q.a: A French educator named Pierre de Coubertin

q.q: What does the writer say about the motto?
q.a: It reminds people to do their best
w: It means that only winners matter
It was invented by the Greeks
It is used only in winter

8.text:
It had been raining since Friday evening, and by Sunday morning, the Parker family was going mad indoors. The children had played every board game in the house. Their father had read the same newspaper twice, and their mother had started to clean the kitchen cupboards, which was always a bad sign.
'I have an idea,' said Dad suddenly. 'Let's go to the park.'
'In this weather?' said Mum. 'We would get soaked.'
'If we took our umbrellas, we would be fine,' said Dad cheerfully. He went to the hall and came back holding a large black umbrella. Unfortunately, it was broken. When he opened it, three of its metal arms bent backwards, and it looked like a giant crow with a damaged wing.
'Perhaps I should mend it,' he said. He fetched his toolbox, and for half an hour, the family watched while he tried to fix it with tape and string. When he finished, the umbrella looked even worse.
'That is the ugliest umbrella that I have ever seen,' said the youngest child, Sam.
In the end, they decided to walk to the park under the ugly umbrella, with everybody squeezed tightly together. A strong gust of wind caught it in the street, and it flew away over a garden wall. They were completely wet when they arrived.
But they splashed in puddles and laughed so much that, afterwards, everybody agreed it was the best Sunday of the year.

q.a: They had been indoors for two days because of the rain
w: They did not have any food

What happened to the umbrella in the street?
q.a: The wind blew it over a garden wall
w: It was left in the park

8.text:
Many years ago there lived an emperor who cared so much about fine new clothes that he spent all his money on them. He had a different coat for every hour of the day.
One day two swindlers came to the city. They said that they were weavers who could make the most beautiful cloth in the world. 'The colours and patterns are wonderful,' they said, 'and the clothes made from it have a strange power. They are invisible to anyone who is unfit for his position or who is hopelessly stupid.'
The emperor was delighted. 'If I wore such clothes, I could find out which of my officials are not clever,' he thought. They set up two looms and pretended to work, though there was nothing on them at all.
The emperor sent his old minister to check the progress. The minister saw nothing, but he did not dare to say so. 'It is marvellous,' he reported. Everyone in the city had heard about the cloth, and nobody wanted to be called stupid.
At last the emperor put on his new suit and walked in a grand procession through the streets. 'How splendid the emperor's clothes are!' the people shouted. Then a small child said, 'But he has nothing on!' The whisper spread through the crowd until everyone was crying out the same thing. The emperor shivered, because he knew they were right, but he walked on proudly to the end.
8.src: adapted from Hans Christian Andersen (public domain)

q.q: What power did the swindlers say the cloth had?
q.a: It was invisible to stupid people or people unfit for their jobs
w: It could keep the emperor warm in winter

q.a: He did not dare to admit he saw nothing
