8.text:
They say that breakfast is the most important meal of the day, but the definition of a good breakfast depends on where you live. In China, a typical morning might begin with a bowl of rice porridge, called congee, together with pickled vegetables, or steamed buns filled with meat.
In Britain, the traditional 'full English breakfast' includes eggs, bacon, sausages, tomatoes and toast. It is delicious, but very heavy, so most British people eat it only at weekends or when they are on holiday. During the week they usually prefer cereal or toast with jam.
French people, on the other hand, tend to have a light breakfast. A croissant or a slice of bread, a cup of coffee and perhaps some fruit are enough for most of them. In Japan, breakfast can look like a small dinner, with grilled fish, rice, miso soup and pickles. In Mexico, a popular morning dish is chilaquiles, which are made of fried tortillas covered in sauce.
Nutrition experts say that, whatever the food is, a good breakfast should contain protein, which keeps you full for longer, and some fruit or vegetables. Sugary drinks and sweet pastries give energy quickly, but it disappears just as fast, and you may feel hungry again before lunch.
So what is your ideal start to the day? It does not matter where it comes from, as long as it is healthy.

q.q: Why do most British people eat the full English breakfast only at weekends?
w: They do not know how to cook it

q.q: How is a French breakfast described?
Why is protein recommended at breakfast?
q.a: It keeps you full for longer

8.text:
On the morning of 17 December 1903, a cold wind blew across the sand dunes at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, stood next to a strange wooden machine with two wings.
The Wrights were not scientists or soldiers. They owned a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and they had learned about mechanics by repairing wheels and chains. Since boyhood, they had been fascinated by flight. They studied the way that birds twist their wings to turn, and they built a small wind tunnel to test different wing shapes. Many of the numbers in the books that they read turned out to be wrong, so they had to produce their own.
Their main problem was control. Other inventors had built machines that could rise into the air but then crashed. The brothers realised that a pilot had to be able to steer in three directions, and they developed a system of controls that is still used in aeroplanes today.
On that cold morning, Orville lay on the lower wing, and the engine started. The machine left the ground and flew for twelve seconds, covering about thirty-seven metres. It was not much, but it was the first time in history that a powered, controlled aeroplane had carried a person. By the end of the day, Wilbur flew almost a minute. Within a few decades, the world was connected by air.

q.q: What was the brothers' job?
What was the main problem for the early inventors?
q.a: Controlling the machine in the air

q.q: What was special about the flight on 17 December 1903?
q.a: It was the first powered, controlled flight with a person

8.text:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all marine species depend on them at some time in their lives. For this reason, reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. The largest, the Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Australia, is so big that it can be seen from space.
Many people think that corals are plants or even rocks, but they are in fact animals. A coral is a tiny creature called a polyp, which builds itself a hard skeleton of limestone. Thousands of polyps live together in colonies, and over hundreds or thousands of years, their skeletons form the enormous structures we call reefs.
Corals have a clever partnership with microscopic algae that live inside their tissues. The algae produce food from sunlight and share it with the coral, and in exchange, they receive a safe home. The bright colours of a reef come from these algae.
Unfortunately, this partnership is fragile. When the sea becomes too warm, the corals push the algae out, and they turn white. This is called bleaching. If the water cools down quickly enough, the corals can recover, but if it stays hot, they die.
Scientists around the world are working on solutions, from growing new corals in laboratories to protecting areas of the sea. They agree, however, that the most important step is to slow down climate change, which is warming our oceans.

q.q: Why are reefs called the rainforests of the sea?
q.a: Many sea species depend on them
w: They grow only in warm rain

q.q: What is a coral?
q.a: A tiny animal that builds a hard skeleton

q.q: What causes bleaching?

8.text:
'Grandpa, is it true that you had no television when you were a boy?' asked Lily one evening.
Her grandfather laughed. 'Of course. We had a radio, and it was as big as a suitcase. The whole family sat around it to listen to the news and music.'
Lily said that she could not imagine life without a phone. Grandpa replied that he had never missed one. 'If I wanted to talk to a friend, I walked to his house,' he said.
'And what did you do at school?' Lily asked.
'We learned by heart,' he said. 'The teacher wrote on a blackboard with chalk, and if we made a mistake, we had to copy the sentence twenty times. There were fifty children in my class.'
Grandpa told her that he had walked six kilometres to school every day, and in winter, the road was covered with snow. Lily looked doubtful. 'Is that really true, or are you exaggerating?' she asked.
'Perhaps a little,' Grandpa admitted with a wink. 'It was five kilometres, not six.'
Lily giggled, and then she asked the question she had been thinking about. 'Were you happier then?'
Grandpa thought for a long time. 'I was different,' he said at last. 'We had less, so we valued things more. But I would not give up the doctor's medicine we have today. Every age has good things and bad things.'

q.q: What did Grandpa's family do with the radio?
q.a: They sat around it to hear the news and music
w: They used it to speak to friends
They sold it to buy a television

q.q: Why did Lily ask if Grandpa was exaggerating?
q.a: The story of the walk to school sounded too hard to believe
w: He told her the radio was big
He forgot the name of his teacher

q.q: What is Grandpa's final opinion?
q.a: Every age has good and bad things

8.t: Qu Yuan and the Dragon Boat Festival
8.text:
The Dragon Boat Festival is celebrated on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month. People eat sticky rice dumplings, called zongzi, and watch exciting boat races in which teams of paddlers row long, narrow boats decorated with dragon heads. Behind these customs lies the story of a famous poet, Qu Yuan.
Qu Yuan lived more than two thousand years ago, in the state of Chu. He was an honest and intelligent minister who loved his country. He advised the king to fight against the powerful state of Qin and to choose capable officials. But jealous courtiers spread lies about him, and the king, who believed them, sent him away from the court.
During his years of exile, Qu Yuan wandered through the countryside and wrote beautiful poems about his love for his homeland and his sadness about its future. When he heard that Qin soldiers had captured the capital of Chu, he was so full of grief that he walked into the Miluo River and drowned.
According to the legend, the local people were deeply moved. They rowed out in their boats to look for him and beat drums to frighten the fish away from his body. They also threw rice wrapped in leaves into the water, so that the fish would eat it instead of him. Over the centuries, these actions became the traditions that we know today. In 2009, UNESCO added the Dragon Boat Festival to its list of intangible cultural heritage.

q.q: Why was Qu Yuan sent away from the court?
q.a: Jealous courtiers told lies about him
w: He wrote poems against the king

q.q: Why did he walk into the river?
q.a: He was full of grief after Chu's capital was captured
w: He was trying to cross it

q.q: Why did people throw rice into the water?
q.a: So that the fish would not eat his body

8.text:
Della counted her money three times. It came to one dollar and eighty-seven cents. She wanted to buy a present for her husband, Jim, whom she loved more than anyone. They were poor, and they had only two treasures. One was Jim's gold watch, which had belonged to his father and his grandfather. The other was Della's beautiful long brown hair, which fell below her knees like a waterfall.
Della stood for a minute in front of the mirror. Then she put on her old jacket and hurried to a shop with a sign that said, 'Hair goods of all kinds'. She sold her hair for twenty dollars. With the money, she searched the stores until she found the perfect gift: a simple platinum chain for Jim's watch, which had no chain at all.
That evening Jim came home, stopped at the door and stared at her short hair. 'Don't be upset,' said Della. 'I sold it to buy you a Christmas present. It will grow again.'
Slowly, Jim took a package from his pocket. Inside were the beautiful combs she had admired in a shop window for months, but now she had no hair to wear them in. Jim smiled. 'Let's put the presents away for a while,' he said. 'I sold the watch to buy the combs.'
They were foolish, yet they were also the wisest of all who give gifts, because they gave up their greatest treasures for each other.
8.src: adapted from O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi (public domain)

q.q: What were the couple's two treasures?
q.a: Jim's gold watch and Della's hair

q.q: What did Della buy with the money?
What is the message of the story?
q.a: Real love means giving up what you value most

8.text:
Look at any busy street today, and you will notice more quiet cars than you would have seen ten years ago. Electric vehicles, which are powered by batteries instead of petrol, are becoming common. In some countries, more than half of all new cars sold are already electric.
The advantages are clear. An electric car produces no exhaust gas, so the air in cities becomes cleaner. It is also much quieter, and driving it costs less, because electricity is cheaper than fuel and the engine has fewer moving parts that can break. When the brakes are used, some of the energy is even recovered and stored in the battery.
However, there are also difficulties. Batteries are expensive and heavy, and they need materials such as lithium and cobalt, which must be mined, sometimes under bad conditions. Charging takes longer than filling a tank, and in many places, there are not enough charging stations.
Another question is where the electricity comes from. If the power station burns coal, the car is only moving the pollution from the city to somewhere else. The real benefit appears when electricity is produced from wind, sun or water.
Engineers are now developing batteries that charge faster and last longer, and some companies are also recycling old batteries. Perhaps within a generation, petrol cars will be as unusual as horse carts are today. Whether that happens quickly depends on the decisions of governments, companies and ordinary buyers.

q.q: Why does an electric car cost less to drive?
q.a: Electricity is cheaper and the engine has fewer parts that break
w: It uses the same fuel as petrol cars
It is lighter than other cars

q.q: What is one problem with electric cars?
q.a: There are not enough charging stations in many places
w: They produce a lot of exhaust

q.q: When is an electric car really clean?
q.a: When the electricity comes from wind, sun or water

8.text:
There was a table set out under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at it. A Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep, and the other two were using it as a cushion. The table was a large one, but the three were all crowded together at one corner.
'No room! No room!' they cried out when they saw Alice coming. 'There's plenty of room!' said Alice indignantly, and she sat down in a large armchair at one end.
'Have some wine,' the March Hare said in an encouraging tone. Alice looked all round the table, but there was nothing on it except tea. 'I don't see any wine,' she remarked.
'There isn't any,' said the March Hare.
'Then it wasn't very civil of you to offer it,' said Alice angrily.
The Hatter opened his eyes. 'Why is a raven like a writing desk?' he asked.
Alice thought for a moment. 'I think I can guess that,' she said.
'Then you should say what you mean,' said the March Hare.
Alice sighed. 'I think you might do something better with the time than waste it in asking riddles that have no answers.'
8.src: adapted from Lewis Carroll, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (public domain)

q.q: Why was Alice angry about the wine?
q.a: They offered wine when there was none

q.q: How is the Dormouse used?
q.a: As a cushion by the other two

q.q: What is Alice's final opinion of the riddles?
q.a: They waste time because they have no answers

8.text:
The Great Pyramid of Giza, near modern Cairo, was built about 4,500 years ago as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu. For almost four thousand years, it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth. Today, it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still stands.
The pyramid was made of more than two million blocks of stone, and each block weighs, on average, as much as a small car. For a long time, many people believed that slaves had been forced to build it. However, archaeologists have found the remains of the workers' village near the site. The skeletons and the food leftovers suggest that the builders were paid labourers who were given bread, beer and meat, and that they were buried with honour near the pyramid they had built.
How did they move such heavy stones without modern machines? Historians believe that the blocks were dragged on wooden sleds over wet sand, which reduces friction. Thousands of men also used ramps and ropes, and they worked in organised teams. Papyrus found in 2013 even includes the diary of an official who transported limestone to Giza by boat.
The pyramids were designed to protect the pharaoh's body and treasures for the afterlife. Sadly, robbers found their way inside long ago, and almost nothing remained. Yet the buildings themselves, which stand calmly in the desert, remain the most impressive treasure that ancient Egypt left to us.

q.q: What did archaeologists discover near the pyramid?
q.a: The remains of the workers' village
w: A list of the builders' names

q.q: Why were wet sand and sleds useful?
q.a: They reduced friction when dragging the stones

q.q: What happened to the treasures inside the pyramids?
q.a: Robbers took almost everything long ago
w: They are in a museum in Cairo
They were sold by the pharaoh

8.text:
A week before the exams, Chen's stomach hurt every morning. He could not eat breakfast, he slept badly, and his thoughts kept returning to the same question: 'What if I fail?' He did not tell anyone, because he thought that the others were calm.
In fact, almost every student feels nervous before important exams, and a little stress is even useful. It makes the body produce adrenaline, which helps you concentrate. The trouble starts when the stress becomes too big. Then it can cause headaches, tiredness and a feeling that you cannot cope.
Chen's older cousin, who is a doctor, gave him some advice. First, she told him to make a realistic study plan with short breaks, because the brain cannot work well for hours without a rest. Second, she said that he should sleep at least eight hours and avoid studying late at night. Third, regular exercise, even a walk of twenty minutes, would reduce his tension. She also reminded him that exams measure only a small part of a person's abilities.
Most importantly, she encouraged him to talk. When Chen finally told his parents how he felt, they were surprised and relieved. His mother admitted that she had been very nervous before her own exams, and his father promised not to compare him with other students.
Chen did not become a different person overnight. But when exam day arrived, he felt prepared, and he knew that he had people who supported him.

q.q: Why is a little stress useful?
What did the cousin say about studying?
q.a: He should take short breaks and not study late at night
w: He should avoid talking to anyone

q.q: What happened when Chen talked to his parents?
q.a: They were surprised and relieved and promised to support him
w: They told him to see a doctor at once

8.text:
Leonardo da Vinci was born in 1452 in a small town near Florence, in Italy. He is best known as the painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, but he was much more than an artist. He was also a scientist, an engineer, an inventor and a student of nature, and he is often described as the greatest example of the 'Renaissance man'.
As a young man, Leonardo trained in the workshop of a famous painter, where he learned to mix colours and to draw. He soon became so skilful that the master allowed him to paint part of a picture, and the master's work was said to look dull beside his. Throughout his life, Leonardo filled thousands of pages of notebooks with drawings and thoughts. He wrote them from right to left in mirror writing, which can be read only with a mirror.
He was curious about everything. He studied the flight of birds and designed flying machines, though none of them was built in his lifetime. He drew careful pictures of the human body after he had examined bodies to understand how muscles and bones work. He also planned bridges, weapons and canals for the rulers who paid him.
Surprisingly, Leonardo left only about fifteen finished paintings, because he often lost interest or was never satisfied. He died in France in 1519. His notebooks remind us that curiosity is the beginning of every discovery.

q.q: What is unusual about Leonardo's notebooks?
q.a: They were written from right to left
w: They were all about the Mona Lisa

q.q: Why did he leave so few finished paintings?
q.a: He often lost interest or was not satisfied
w: He died when he was very young

q.q: What does 'curious' mean?
q.a: Wanting to find out about things

8.text:
The whole of Class 8B was waiting in front of the City Museum when it started to drizzle. Their teacher, Mr Wang, counted the students twice. 'Thirty-one, thirty-two... one is missing,' he muttered. 'Where is Peter?'
'He said he was going to buy a bottle of water,' said Sara.
Mr Wang sighed. Peter had been late for the last three school trips. Just as he was about to call his mother, Peter came running round the corner with a huge ice cream in each hand. 'Sorry, sir!' he said. 'The shop was very busy.'
'You cannot take ice cream into the museum,' said Mr Wang. Peter looked at his two ice creams sadly and ate them both in about four minutes, with his eyes closed from the cold.
Inside, the guide led them to a giant skeleton of a dinosaur. She explained that it was almost seventy million years old. 'If it were alive today, it would be taller than this building,' she said. Peter, whose head still hurt from the ice cream, asked whether it was a vegetarian. The guide replied that it had eaten meat, and Peter took two steps back.
In the gift shop afterwards, the students bought postcards and pencils. Peter bought a rubber dinosaur for his little sister. On the bus home, Mr Wang asked them to write a report about their favourite object. Peter's report began, 'The best thing in the museum was my ice cream, but the dinosaur was also quite good.'

q.q: Why was Mr Wang worried at the beginning?
What did the guide say about the dinosaur?
What did Peter write in his report?
q.a: That the ice cream was the best thing but the dinosaur was good too
w: That Mr Wang was too strict
That he wanted to be a guide

8.t: Polar Bears and a Warming Arctic
8.text:
The polar bear is the largest land predator on Earth. An adult male can weigh as much as ten grown men, and its thick white fur and layer of fat keep it warm in temperatures far below freezing. Yet this powerful animal is now in trouble.
Polar bears depend on sea ice. They use it as a platform for hunting seals, which are their main food. In spring, a bear waits patiently beside a hole in the ice until a seal comes up to breathe. If there is no ice, the bear cannot reach its prey. Over the last forty years, the area of Arctic sea ice in summer has become much smaller, and the ice also forms later in the autumn. As a result, bears have to fast for longer periods, and in some regions, mothers are now thinner and have fewer cubs that survive.
Some people suggest that polar bears can simply adapt by eating other food, such as birds' eggs or berries. Scientists, however, have shown that these foods provide far too little energy for such a huge animal.
The main cause of the melting is global warming, which is produced by burning coal, oil and gas. If countries reduced their emissions quickly, the ice could stabilise, and the bears would have a better chance. The polar bear has become a symbol of climate change, reminding us that our decisions affect even the most distant corners of the planet.

q.q: Why do polar bears need sea ice?
w: They sleep on it in summer

q.q: Why can the bears not simply eat birds' eggs and berries?
q.a: These foods do not give enough energy
w: The bears do not like them
Birds do not lay eggs in the Arctic

q.q: What is the main cause of the melting ice?
q.a: Global warming from burning coal, oil and gas

8.text:
Many cultures celebrate the coming of light at the darkest time of the year, or at other important moments. Although the festivals are different, they share the same hope, which is that brightness will defeat darkness.
In India, Hindus celebrate Diwali in October or November. Families clean their houses, wear new clothes and place small oil lamps outside their doors. The festival is dedicated to the victory of good over evil.
Hanukkah is a Jewish holiday that lasts eight nights in December. It remembers a time more than two thousand years ago when the Jews took back their temple in Jerusalem. According to tradition, there was oil for only one day, but it kept the lamp burning for eight. Today, families light one more candle of a special candleholder each evening.
China also has its own festival of lights. The Lantern Festival takes place on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, and it brings the New Year celebrations to an end. People hang colourful lanterns in streets and parks, solve riddles written on them and eat tangyuan, round sweet dumplings that symbolise family unity.
In Sweden, the Feast of Saint Lucia is celebrated on 13 December. A girl wearing a white dress and a crown of candles leads a procession, bringing light to the long, dark winter.
Whether they use candles, lamps or lanterns, people everywhere seem to feel that light is a promise that better days are coming.

q.q: What do the festivals have in common?
q.a: They share the hope that light will defeat darkness

q.q: What happens at the Lantern Festival?
q.a: People solve riddles and eat tangyuan
w: A girl wears a crown of candles

q.q: How many nights does Hanukkah last?

8.text:
There was once a shoemaker who, through no fault of his own, had become so poor that at last he had leather for only one pair of shoes. In the evening he cut out the shoes, planning to sew them the next morning, and since he had a good conscience, he lay down quietly in his bed, said his prayers and fell asleep.
In the morning he found the pair of shoes already made, standing on his table. The shoes were so beautifully finished that a rich customer soon came in and paid a high price for them. With the money, the shoemaker bought leather for two pairs of shoes. He cut them out in the evening, and the next morning they were finished again.
This went on for weeks, until the shoemaker was a prosperous man. One evening before Christmas, he said to his wife, 'Let us stay up tonight to see who is helping us.' They hid behind a curtain.
At midnight, two tiny elves came in, sat down at the table and began to work with their small fingers,. When all was finished, they ran away.
The next day his wife said, 'The little men have made us rich, and we must thank them. They have no clothes and must be freezing.' So they made two small shirts, coats and trousers, and left them on the table. The elves put them on with great joy and danced away, never to return.
8.src: adapted from the Brothers Grimm, The Elves and the Shoemaker (public domain)

q.q: What did the shoemaker find on his table in the morning?
Why did the shoemaker and his wife make clothes for the elves?
q.a: To thank them and keep them warm
w: To sell them in the market
Because the elves asked for them

q.q: What happened after the elves received the clothes?
q.a: They danced away and never came back

8.text:
Today, almost everyone carries a phone in their pocket, but the first telephone call was made less than one hundred and fifty years ago. The man usually credited with the invention is Alexander Graham Bell, who was born in Scotland in 1847.
Bell's mother was almost deaf, and his father was an expert in the way that people produce speech. From childhood, Bell was fascinated by sound, and as an adult, he became a teacher of deaf students in Boston. In his spare time, he experimented with devices that could send sounds through wires. He was helped by a young assistant named Thomas Watson, who built the equipment.
In 1876, in their workshop, Bell spilled some acid on his clothes and called out to Watson, who was in the next room. 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.' Watson, who heard the words clearly through the device, ran in, very excited. It was the first sentence ever to be spoken over a telephone.
Within a few years, telephone lines connected the main cities of America, and soon the invention reached Europe and Asia. At first, people had to ask an operator to connect them, but by the twentieth century, automatic exchanges let users dial the number themselves.
Bell himself never put a phone in his study, because he thought that the ringing was a distraction from his work. It is said that he would not have liked today's smartphones, which interrupt us dozens of times a day.

q.q: What was Bell's job before his famous invention?
Who helped Bell build the equipment?
Why did Bell not keep a phone in his study?

8.t: Yuan Longping, Father of Hybrid Rice
8.text:
Rice is the main food for more than half of the world's population. For centuries, China suffered from famines in which millions of people died. One scientist who helped to change this situation was Yuan Longping, who is often called the 'father of hybrid rice'.
Yuan was born in 1930 and became a teacher of agriculture in Hunan province. During the early 1960s, he saw hunger with his own eyes, and he decided to devote his life to growing more food. At that time, many experts believed that rice could not produce stronger offspring by crossing different plants, because rice flowers pollinate themselves. Yuan did not accept this idea.
He searched the rice fields for years, looking for a natural plant with male sterility, which would be necessary for crossbreeding. In 1970, his team found one on Hainan Island, in a patch of wild rice. This discovery opened the door to a new kind of rice. In the following decade, the new hybrid varieties produced significantly higher yields than ordinary rice, and they were gradually planted in millions of hectares across China.
Yuan also shared his knowledge with other countries, training thousands of agricultural experts from Asia and Africa. He remained modest and was often seen working in the fields, even when he was very old. When he died in 2021, many people mourned him as a hero who had helped to feed the world.

q.q: Why did many experts think hybrid rice was impossible?
w: Rice is a kind of grass that dies

q.q: What did Yuan's team find on Hainan Island?
q.a: A wild rice plant with male sterility

q.q: How did Yuan help other countries?
q.a: He trained thousands of agricultural experts
w: He sold seeds at high prices

8.text:
Dorothy and her little dog Toto were walking along the yellow brick road to see the Wizard of Oz, who lived in the Emerald City. Dorothy hoped that he would send her home to Kansas. On the way, they passed a field of corn, and in the middle of it stood a scarecrow on a pole.
To her great surprise, the Scarecrow winked at her. 'Good day,' he said in a rather husky voice. 'How do you do?'
'I'm pretty well, thank you,' said Dorothy politely. 'How do you do?'
'I'm not feeling well,' said the Scarecrow with a smile, 'for it is very tedious being perched up here night and day to scare away crows.'
Dorothy lifted him off the pole, and he thanked her.
He told her that he wanted a brain. 'My head is stuffed with straw,' he said, 'so I do not know anything. If I had a brain, I would be able to think, and I could stop the crows from eating the corn.'
'Come with us,' said Dorothy. 'The Wizard might help you.' The Scarecrow thanked her and joined them.
As they walked together, Dorothy noticed that the Scarecrow was cleverer than he believed. When they reached a ditch, it was he who suggested that they should find a log to cross it. 'Perhaps you already have a brain,' she told him. He only shook his head, which made the straw inside rustle.
8.src: adapted from L. Frank Baum, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (public domain)

q.q: Why was the Scarecrow not feeling well?
q.a: It was boring to sit on a pole all day and night

q.q: What did the Scarecrow want from the Wizard?
What does the example of the ditch show?
q.a: The Scarecrow could already think well
w: The Scarecrow was afraid of water

8.t: A Visit to the Care Home
8.text:
'I'm not sure about this,' said Kai, as the minibus stopped in front of the Sunshine Care Home. 'What if I have nothing to say to them?'
His classmate Rose laughed. 'Our teacher said that older people love to talk, so you will just need to listen.'
The students, who had volunteered for a project called 'Friends at Any Age', were welcomed by a cheerful nurse. She told them that most of the residents did not have visitors very often. 'A single conversation can make their whole week brighter,' she said.
Kai was introduced to Mr Zhou, who was ninety years old and sat in a wheelchair by the window. At first, there was an awkward silence. Then Kai noticed an old photograph on the table. 'Who is that?' he asked. Mr Zhou's eyes lit up. 'That is my first bicycle,' he said, and he spoke for almost an hour about the city where he had grown up, about the teacher who had punished him for being late and about the day he met his wife.
When it was time to leave, Mr Zhou held Kai's hand. 'You are a good listener,' he said. 'Will you come back?'
On the bus home, Kai was surprised at how fast the afternoon had passed. 'I thought that I would be the one helping them,' he said to Rose. 'But I think I received much more than I gave.'
The following month, he signed up for the visits every week.

q.q: Why was Kai worried at the start?
q.a: He thought he would have nothing to say
w: He was afraid of the nurse
He did not like old photographs
He was late for the bus

q.q: How did Kai start the conversation with Mr Zhou?
q.a: He asked about an old photograph

q.q: What did Kai learn from the visit?
q.a: He received as much as he gave

8.text:
Chocolate is one of the most popular foods in the world, yet few people know where it comes from. It is made from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows only in warm, wet regions near the equator. The seeds were first used by peoples of Central and South America thousands of years ago.
The Aztecs and the Maya did not eat chocolate as a sweet. They ground the roasted seeds into a paste, mixed it with water, chilli and spices, and drank it as a bitter, foamy drink. In the sixteenth century, Spanish explorers took the beans to Europe, where people began to add sugar and honey, and the drink became a fashionable luxury for the rich.
The invention of a machine that pressed the fat out of the beans, in the nineteenth century, made it possible to produce solid chocolate. Soon afterwards, makers in Switzerland and Britain began to mix cocoa with milk, and the sweet bars that we know today were born.
Today, about two thirds of the world's cocoa is grown in West Africa, usually by small farmers. Many of them earn very little, and some farms have been criticised for using child labour. For this reason, more and more shoppers look for chocolate with a fair-trade label, which promises that farmers receive a fair price. The next time that you eat a piece, you might think about the long journey it has made.

q.q: How did the Aztecs and Maya use chocolate?
What did Europeans change in the drink?
Why do some shoppers choose fair-trade chocolate?
q.a: The farmers receive a fair price

8.text:
I remember as if it were yesterday the day the old sailor came to our inn, the Admiral Benbow. He walked slowly down the road, followed by a man who pushed a hand-barrow with his sea-chest. He was a tall, strong, heavy man with a nut-brown face, black broken nails and a white scar across one cheek.
'This is a handy cove,' he said, looking round, 'and a pleasant sittyation for a grog-shop. Much company, mate?' My father told him that very little company was the rule, and the man said, 'Well, then, this is the berth for me.' He gave us the name of Captain, and he asked for a room that looked out on the sea.
He stayed for weeks, and he never paid, though he gave my father a few gold coins at first. All day, he wandered along the cliffs with a brass telescope, and at night he sat by the fire drinking rum and singing wild songs about dead men's chests. Sometimes he made the guests so frightened that they hurried away.
The captain had only one fear. He asked me to watch the road for 'a seafaring man with one leg', and he promised me a silver fourpenny on the first of every month if I would keep my eye open. In my dreams, that one-legged man often visited me on stormy nights.
8.src: adapted from Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island (public domain)

q.q: What did the captain look like?
q.a: Tall and strong with a scar on his cheek
w: Short and thin with a beard
Old and weak with a stick

q.q: What did the captain do during the days?
q.a: He walked along the cliffs with a telescope
w: He taught the boy to sail

q.q: What was the captain afraid of?
q.a: A seafaring man with one leg

8.text:
The International Space Station, or ISS, circles the Earth at a height of about four hundred kilometres. It travels at such a high speed that it goes round the planet roughly every ninety minutes, which means that the astronauts on board see about sixteen sunrises and sunsets every day. The station was built by several countries working together, and it has been continuously occupied since the year 2000.
Life in space is very different from life on Earth. Because everything floats in microgravity, astronauts must fasten themselves to a wall or the floor when they sleep. Otherwise, they would drift around the cabin and bump into the equipment. Food is eaten from sealed packages, and drinks are sipped through straws, since liquid would form floating balls in the air. Even brushing teeth is a challenge, because the water cannot be poured down a sink.
Without the weight of the body to work against, muscles and bones become weaker. For this reason, the crew must exercise for about two hours every day, using special machines. Astronauts also grow slightly taller in space because the spine is no longer compressed, but they return to their normal height after a few days at home.
Most importantly, the station is a laboratory. Experiments carried out there help scientists to understand diseases, new materials and the long-term effects of space on the human body, which will be vital if humans one day travel to Mars.

q.q: Why must astronauts fasten themselves when they sleep?
q.a: Otherwise they would float around the cabin
w: The station moves too fast to sleep

q.q: Why do astronauts exercise for two hours a day?
q.a: Their muscles and bones become weaker in space

q.q: What is one purpose of experiments on the station?
q.a: To understand the effects of space on the human body
w: To grow food for sale on Earth

8.t: A Letter from a Pen Friend
8.text:
Dear Wei,
Thank you for your last letter. I was very happy to hear that you passed your music exam. My mother said that she would send you a recording of my school choir, if you promised not to laugh at it.
You asked me what winter holidays are like in Canada. Well, it has been snowing for a week, and the whole town looks like a postcard. Every morning, my brother and I shovel the path in front of our house, and in the afternoon, we go skating on the frozen lake near our school. Last Saturday, my father taught me how to make a snow sculpture, but my fox looked more like a potato.
On the twenty-fifth of December, we celebrate Christmas. The family gets together, and we eat a big dinner with turkey, potatoes and a dessert that my grandmother makes every year. It is a tradition to open the presents in the morning. I told my cousin that I would be happy with just a book, and she laughed because I always say the same thing.
You told me that you will celebrate the Spring Festival with your relatives. I would love to see it one day! My teacher said that if I studied hard, I might be able to visit China as part of a school exchange. If that really happened, I would try to learn how to make dumplings.
Please write soon and tell me everything.
Your friend,
Emma

q.q: What does Emma do on the frozen lake?
How did Emma's snow fox turn out?
w: It was bigger than her father

q.q: What would Emma do if she visited China?
q.a: Try to learn how to make dumplings

8.text:
We often think of mistakes as failures, but the history of science shows that they can lead to wonderful discoveries. Many inventions that we use every day began with an accident or an experiment that went wrong.
In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday and found that one of his dishes of bacteria was covered in mould. To his surprise, the bacteria close to the mould had died. He realised that the mould produced a substance that kills bacteria. This substance, penicillin, became the first widely used antibiotic and has saved millions of lives.
Another famous accident involved sticky notes. In the late 1960s, a scientist at the American company 3M was trying to make a very strong glue, but he produced one that was weak and could be peeled off easily. For years, nobody knew what to do with it. Then a colleague, who used pieces of paper as bookmarks in his hymn book, realised that a weak glue would keep them in place without damaging the pages. The product became a worldwide success.
These stories teach an important lesson. Discoveries often come to people who are curious and who pay attention when something unexpected happens. Perhaps the next time you make a mistake, you should ask yourself what you can learn from it.

q.q: What did Fleming notice about the mould?
What was the scientist at 3M trying to make?
What is the main message of the passage?
q.a: Mistakes can lead to useful discoveries
w: Glue is a very important invention

8.text:
On the last evening of December, the Lin family sat around the table, writing their New Year's resolutions on small pieces of paper. It was a family tradition. The rule was that each person had to read his resolution aloud, and everybody would check at the end of the next year whether it had been kept.
'I will exercise every day,' read Dad confidently. His wife looked at the large pile of books beside his chair and smiled. 'I will not eat sweets before dinner,' said Mum.
The turn of fourteen-year-old Jun came next. 'My resolution is to be more organised,' he read. His sister, Hua, laughed. 'You? You lost your school bag last week!' Jun blushed, and Grandma told them that it was kind to encourage each other rather than to make fun.
When it was Hua's turn, she stood up and took a deep breath. 'I will learn to play the piano properly,' she said. 'I know I always give up after a month. But this year, if I fail, I will start again instead of stopping.'
The room became quiet, and then Grandpa clapped. 'That is the best resolution of the evening,' he said. 'The real secret is not that you never fail. It is that you do not stop trying.'
The clock struck twelve, and the family hugged each other. Outside, fireworks lit up the sky, and a new year began.

q.q: What was the rule of the family tradition?
q.a: Everyone read his resolution aloud and checked it a year later
w: The resolutions were sent to friends

q.q: What is Hua's resolution?
q.a: To learn the piano and to start again after failing
w: To keep her school bag safe

q.q: Why did Grandpa say it was the best resolution?
q.a: Success comes from not stopping to try
w: Hua had the most difficult task
Hua had practised for a year

9.text:
Mr. Lin repaired clocks in a narrow street near the old market. His shop was small, but it was full of sound: hundreds of clocks ticked together, and every hour they all chimed at slightly different moments, like a choir that could never agree.
On the last day of the year, a girl named Mei came in holding a broken pocket watch. “It belonged to my grandfather,” she said quietly. “He passed away last spring. Can you make it work again?”
Mr. Lin opened the back of the watch and frowned. The tiny springs were rusty, and one gear had snapped in two. “This will take time,” he warned. “Perhaps weeks. Some parts do not exist any more, so I may have to make them by hand.”
“I can wait,” said Mei.
She came back every Saturday. While Mr. Lin worked, she watched through a magnifying glass, and slowly she learned the names of the parts: the balance wheel, the mainspring, the escapement. Mr. Lin never hurried. “A clock is patient,” he told her. “It does its work one second at a time. If we rush it, it breaks.”
On the fifth Saturday, the watch began to tick. Mei held it against her ear and smiled, because the sound reminded her of her grandfather’s heartbeat, which she had once listened to with her head on his chest.
She tried to pay, but Mr. Lin shook his head. “Come and be my apprentice instead,” he said. “This shop needs someone who knows how to listen.”
Years later, Mei took over the little shop. Every New Year’s Eve she wound all the clocks by hand and waited, with a cup of tea, for the one minute of the year when they chimed together.

q.q: Why did Mei bring the pocket watch to the shop?
q.a: It had belonged to her late grandfather
w: It was a present for Mr. Lin
She had found it in the street

q.q: What does Mr. Lin mean by “A clock is patient”?
q.a: Careful work should not be rushed
w: Old clocks work better than new ones

q.q: Why did Mr. Lin refuse Mei’s money?
q.a: He wanted her to become his apprentice
w: The watch was too cheap to charge for
He planned to keep the watch himself

9.text:
Everybody yawns. Babies yawn before they are born, dogs yawn, even fish and snakes do it. Yet nobody is completely sure why. Scientists have several ideas, and each of them may be partly right.
The oldest idea says that yawning brings extra oxygen into the body. When we are tired, we breathe more slowly, so, the theory goes, a deep breath wakes us up. But experiments have shown that people who breathe pure oxygen still yawn just as often, so this explanation is now doubted.
A newer idea is about temperature. The brain works best when it is slightly cool. A big yawn pulls in cool air and increases the flow of blood around the head, which may act like a tiny fan. Researchers noticed that people yawn less in very hot weather, when the air no longer cools them, and also less in freezing weather, perhaps because a cold breath would be a shock. This supports the cooling theory.
Then there is the mystery of contagious yawning. Watching someone yawn, or even reading about it, often makes you yawn too. Some experts believe this is connected to empathy, our ability to share the feelings of others. Children under four rarely catch yawns from others, and the habit appears more strongly between close friends than between strangers.
The same effect has been seen in dogs, which sometimes yawn when their owners do.
So the next time you yawn in class, do not feel guilty. Your brain may simply be cooling itself, or you may be showing that you care about the person next to you. And if you have yawned at least once while reading this passage, you have just proved one of the theories.

q.q: Why is the oxygen explanation now doubted?
q.a: People breathing pure oxygen still yawn as often

q.q: What does the cooling theory say about yawning?
q.a: A yawn helps keep the brain cool
w: A yawn warms up the lungs
A yawn shows the body is hungry
A yawn makes the heart beat slower

q.q: What is said about contagious yawning?
q.a: It may be linked to empathy and is stronger between friends
w: It is strongest in small children
It is caused by hot weather

9.t: The Miller, His Son and the Donkey
9.text:
A miller and his son were walking to market, leading their donkey behind them. They hoped to sell it for a good price. Soon they passed some girls drawing water at a well. “Look at those fools!” one girl laughed. “They have a donkey but they walk in the dust!”
The miller felt embarrassed, so he told his son to climb up. A little later they met an old man, who shook his head. “Shameful! A strong boy rides while his poor father trudges along on foot!” The miller quickly swapped places with his son.
They had gone only a short way when they met a group of women. “How selfish!” they cried. “That lazy man rides, and the poor child can hardly keep up!” Not wanting to be criticised again, the miller pulled his son up behind him, and both of them rode on the donkey.
By now they had almost reached the town. A shopkeeper stared at them. “Is that animal yours?” he asked. “Yes,” said the miller. “Then you treat it very badly. Two big people on one small donkey! You should carry it yourselves.”
The miller thought, “Perhaps he is right.” They climbed down, tied the donkey’s legs to a long pole, and lifted it onto their shoulders. They staggered across the bridge into the town.
People crowded round to laugh at the strange sight. The donkey, frightened by the noise and the crowd, kicked free, fell off the pole and tumbled into the river. It was never seen again.
The miller went home with nothing. “I tried to please everyone,” he sighed, “and in the end I pleased no one, and lost my donkey as well.”

q.a: He felt embarrassed by the girls’ laughter
w: The boy was tired and ill
The donkey could not carry a man
The old man had asked him to

q.q: What is the main lesson of the story?
q.a: Trying to please everybody can leave you with nothing

q.q: What finally happened to the donkey?
q.a: It fell into the river and was lost
w: It was sold at the market
It was carried safely into town

9.t: A Phone Call About the Trip
9.text:
Ms. Zhang: Hello, is that Mr. Wang? This is Ms. Zhang, your daughter Yu’s class teacher.
Mr. Wang: Oh, hello! Is something wrong?
Ms. Zhang: Not at all. I am calling about next Friday’s trip to the science museum. We still need a signed permission form from every family, and I haven’t received Yu’s yet.
Mr. Wang: I’m so sorry. She told me about it, but I forgot to sign it. Is it too late?
Ms. Zhang: No, you can send it on Monday. But I have a few more things to explain. The bus leaves at 8:30 sharp, so the children should arrive by 8:15. Please remind her to wear comfortable shoes, because we will be walking a lot.
Mr. Wang: Of course. What about lunch?
Ms. Zhang: The museum has a cafeteria, but it is expensive and often crowded, so I suggest a packed lunch. Please avoid anything with nuts, because one of the children is seriously allergic.
Mr. Wang: That’s very sensible. Should she bring any money?
Ms. Zhang: A little, if she wants a souvenir from the gift shop, but no more than thirty yuan. We don’t want anyone to feel left out.
Mr. Wang: I agree. By the way, Yu is very excited. She has been reading about the planetarium for weeks.
Ms. Zhang: That’s lovely to hear. The show is at eleven, and I think it will be the highlight of the day. Oh, and one last thing: could you tell her to bring a notebook? I want each student to write a short report afterwards.
Mr. Wang: A report? She will enjoy that. Thank you for calling, Ms. Zhang.
Ms. Zhang: My pleasure. See you on Friday, Mr. Wang. Goodbye!

q.q: Why does Ms. Zhang phone Mr. Wang?
q.a: Yu’s permission form has not arrived

q.q: Why does she suggest a packed lunch without nuts?
q.a: The cafeteria is crowded and one child is allergic

q.q: What will the students do after the trip?
w: Draw a picture of the planetarium

9.text:
The Lantern Festival falls on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, when the first full moon of the new year appears. It marks the end of the Spring Festival celebrations, and for many families it is the last chance to enjoy the holiday together.
The festival has a history of more than two thousand years. According to one popular explanation, it began in the Han dynasty, when emperors ordered lamps to be lit in the palace to honour Buddha on that night. Over time, ordinary people joined in, and the custom spread across the country.
Today, the most striking sight is the lanterns themselves. Some are simple red paper globes, while others are enormous works of art shaped like dragons, flowers or famous cartoon characters, lit by thousands of tiny bulbs. In some cities the lanterns are arranged along rivers or around ancient walls, and visitors walk for hours in the glow.
Another beloved tradition is solving lantern riddles. Riddles are written on slips of paper and hung from the lanterns. Anyone who guesses an answer can pull the slip down and, if they are right, receive a small prize. A typical riddle might ask, “What has a mouth but never eats, and a bed but never sleeps?” The answer, of course, is a river.
No celebration would be complete without food. Families eat tangyuan, sweet round dumplings filled with sesame or peanut paste. Their round shape, like the full moon, stands for unity and togetherness. In northern China, people often call the same food yuanxiao, and people still enjoy discussing which name is correct.
Whatever the name, the message is the same: warmth, light and family.

q.q: When is the Lantern Festival celebrated?
q.a: On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month
w: On the first day of the new year
On the last day of the year
At the start of the autumn harvest

q.q: What do people do with lantern riddles?
q.a: Guess the answer and may win a small prize

q.q: Why are tangyuan round?
q.a: Their shape stands for the full moon and family unity
w: They are easier to fill with sesame
They copy the shape of lanterns only

9.t: Tu Youyou and the Ancient Recipe
9.text:
In 2015, a Chinese scientist named Tu Youyou travelled to Stockholm to receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. She was the first woman from China to win a Nobel Prize in science, and her discovery has saved millions of lives.
Tu was born in 1930 in the city of Ningbo. As a young woman she fell seriously ill with tuberculosis, which made her curious about medicine. She later studied pharmacology at university in Beijing and became a researcher at a traditional medicine institute.
In the 1960s, malaria was killing huge numbers of people in Asia and Africa, and the parasite that caused it had become resistant to the usual drugs. In 1969 Tu was asked to lead a team to find a new treatment. She began by reading ancient medical books, searching for any plant that had been used against fever.
She tested hundreds of plants, but the results were disappointing. Then she remembered a short line in a fourth-century book by Ge Hong, which suggested soaking sweet wormwood in cold water, rather than boiling it. Tu realised that heat might be destroying the active ingredient. She changed her method and extracted the substance at a low temperature. This time the result was striking: the extract killed the parasites in animals almost completely.
Tu and her colleagues even tested the medicine on themselves before trying it on patients. The drug, artemisinin, became the foundation of modern malaria treatment.
When reporters praised her, Tu insisted that the honour belonged to her whole team, and to the wisdom of Chinese medicine. “This is a gift from traditional medicine to the world,” she said. Her story shows how patient reading of the past can solve problems of the present.

q.q: Why did Tu Youyou start by reading ancient medical books?
q.a: She was looking for plants once used against fever
w: She wanted to write a history book
She had no laboratory to use

q.q: What change in method led to success?
q.a: Extracting the substance at a low temperature
w: Using a different kind of animal
Adding more plants to the mixture

q.q: How did Tu feel about the honour of the prize?
q.a: She said it belonged to her team and traditional medicine
w: She believed she alone deserved it
She felt it came too late
She did not think the discovery mattered

9.text:
The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world, flowing about 6,300 kilometres from the glaciers of the Tibetan Plateau to the East China Sea. Along the way it changes character so often that people say it has many faces.
In its upper reaches, the river is young and wild. It rushes through deep valleys, cutting steep canyons in the mountains of Qinghai, Tibet, Sichuan and Yunnan. Few people live here, but rare animals such as the snow leopard and the Tibetan antelope are at home on the high grasslands nearby.
The middle section is the most famous. At the Three Gorges, cliffs rise on both sides of a narrow channel, and for centuries poets have written about the misty peaks. In 2006, the enormous Three Gorges Dam was completed here. It produces a great deal of electricity and helps to control floods, though it also forced more than a million people to move and changed the habitats of many creatures.
Below the gorges, the river slows and widens, winding across a fertile plain where rice, cotton and vegetables have been grown for thousands of years. Large cities such as Wuhan and Nanjing grew up along its banks, and boats still carry coal, grain and cars between them.
Finally the Yangtze reaches Shanghai, where it spreads into a vast delta before entering the sea. The Yangtze finless porpoise, a smiling grey animal found only in this river, is now endangered, and the government has banned fishing in the main river for ten years to give wildlife a chance to recover.
From glacier to ocean, the Yangtze connects mountains, farms, cities and the sea. It is not only a river but the backbone of a whole region.

q.q: What is the river like in its upper reaches?
q.a: Young and wild, with few people nearby
w: Slow and wide with many cities
Dry and almost empty of water

q.q: What is one effect of the Three Gorges Dam?
q.a: It produces electricity and helps control floods
w: It stopped boats from using the river
It created the snow leopard’s home

q.q: Why has fishing in the main river been banned?
q.a: To give endangered wildlife time to recover
w: To protect the dam from damage
Because the water is too deep
Because there are no fish left to catch

9.t: The Parrot Who Answered the Door
9.text:
My aunt Lucy owns a parrot called Pepper, and he is, without doubt, the cleverest and most embarrassing bird in the world. Pepper can copy almost any sound he hears, and unfortunately he hears everything.
Last summer, my aunt invited her new neighbours for tea. She had cleaned the house for two days, baked a lemon cake, and put on her best dress. When the doorbell rang, she hurried to answer it. But before she reached the door, a deep voice from the living room shouted, “Come in, it’s open!”
The guests walked in, looking puzzled, while my aunt turned red. “That was only the parrot,” she explained. Pepper, sitting proudly on his perch, said, “Who’s that? Not him again!”
The neighbours laughed politely. My aunt quickly offered cake, hoping that the little disaster was over. It was not. Pepper imitated the sound of a phone, then the microwave, then my aunt’s voice saying, “I hope they don’t stay too long.”
There was a terrible silence. My aunt wanted to disappear under the table. But the old gentleman next door burst out laughing. “My wife says exactly the same thing about our guests,” he said, wiping his eyes. “Your parrot is an honest fellow!”
After that, everyone relaxed. The neighbours stayed for three hours, ate the whole cake, and taught Pepper a new phrase, which he repeated for the rest of the afternoon: “More cake, please!”
Now the neighbours visit every month, and my aunt has stopped trying to hide anything from Pepper. “Honesty,” she says with a sigh, “is the best policy, especially when you own a parrot.”

q.q: Why was the aunt embarrassed at the door?
q.a: The parrot shouted to the guests before she arrived
w: She had forgotten to invite them

q.q: How did the old neighbour react to the parrot’s remark?
q.a: He laughed because his wife says the same
w: He asked the aunt to sell the parrot
He pretended not to hear it

q.q: What does “Honesty is the best policy” mean in this story?
q.a: It is pointless to hide things from such a parrot

9.text:
Many students believe that sleeping less is a clever way to gain extra study time. Scientists disagree strongly. During sleep the brain is far from idle: it organises the day’s learning, strengthens memories and clears away chemical waste that builds up while we are awake.
Teenagers need about eight to ten hours of sleep a night, more than most adults. Yet surveys show that a large number of students get far less, partly because of homework and partly because of late-night phone use. The bright light of a screen tells the brain that it is still daytime and delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy.
There is also a biological reason for late nights. During puberty the body clock shifts, so teenagers naturally feel awake later in the evening and find it hard to rise early. This is not laziness; it is biology. Some schools that have started lessons a little later have reported better attendance, higher marks and fewer accidents among students.
What happens when we do not sleep enough? Concentration drops, mistakes increase, and mood becomes unstable. Over a longer period, poor sleep may weaken the immune system and increase the risk of weight gain.
Fortunately, a few simple habits help. Go to bed and get up at roughly the same time every day, even at weekends. Stop using screens at least an hour before sleeping. Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and avoid strong tea or cola in the afternoon. If worries keep you awake, writing them down on paper can calm the mind.
So before your next all-night study session, remember this: sleep is not time wasted. It is when much of the learning actually becomes permanent.

q.q: What does the brain do during sleep?
q.a: It organises learning and strengthens memories
w: It forgets everything from the day

q.q: Why do teenagers often feel awake late at night?
q.a: Their body clock shifts during puberty
w: They are too lazy to sleep
They need less sleep than adults

q.q: Which habit does the passage recommend?
q.a: Going to bed at about the same time every day

9.t: The Little Ball That Opened a Door
9.text:
In April 1971, a small white ball helped to change the world. At that time, China and the United States had had almost no contact for more than twenty years. Then, during a table tennis tournament in Japan, something unexpected happened.
An American player, Glenn Cowan, missed his team’s bus and accidentally stepped onto the Chinese team’s bus instead. Nobody spoke at first. Then the Chinese champion Zhuang Zedong, who had won the world title several times, walked over and greeted him in a friendly way. He gave Cowan a silk painting as a present. The next day, Cowan gave Zhuang a T-shirt in return. Photographers noticed, and the story appeared in newspapers across the world.
Soon afterwards, China surprised everybody by inviting the American team to visit. The young players, along with a few journalists, crossed the border and became some of the first Americans to enter China in decades. They toured the Great Wall, watched a ballet, and played friendly matches in Beijing, where the hosts famously stressed the slogan “friendship first, competition second.”
The trip, later nicknamed “ping-pong diplomacy”, showed that ordinary people could build bridges when governments could not. Within a year, the American president Richard Nixon visited Beijing, and the two countries began to rebuild their relationship.
Of course, a game of table tennis did not solve every problem. Historians point out that political leaders were already preparing for change, and the sport simply gave them a gentle, friendly way to begin.
Still, the story reminds us that sport can speak a language everyone understands, and that a small gesture of kindness may be remembered for a lifetime.

q.q: How did Glenn Cowan meet the Chinese players?
q.a: He got onto their bus by mistake
w: He played against them in the final

q.q: What does “ping-pong diplomacy” mean?
q.a: Sport helped two countries start to build friendship
w: A war fought with table tennis
A law about sports in schools
A trade contract for sports goods

q.q: What do historians add about the story?
q.a: Leaders were already preparing for change
w: Nobody noticed the event at the time

9.t: How Does GPS Know Where You Are?
9.text:
Today we take it for granted that a phone can show our exact position on a map. Yet the technology behind it, the Global Positioning System, or GPS, is one of the most remarkable inventions of the twentieth century.
GPS depends on a group of about thirty satellites that circle the Earth at a height of around twenty thousand kilometres. Each satellite carries an extremely accurate atomic clock and constantly broadcasts a simple message: its own position and the exact time at which the message was sent.
Your phone does not send anything to the satellites. It only listens. When it receives a signal, it compares the time of sending with the time of arrival. Because radio waves travel at the speed of light, the difference, only a fraction of a second, reveals how far away the satellite is. One satellite alone is not enough, because it would only say that you are somewhere on a huge sphere. With three satellites, the phone can calculate a point on the surface of the Earth, and a fourth corrects the small error in the phone’s own cheap clock.
Surprisingly, Einstein’s theories also matter. The satellites move fast and sit in weaker gravity, so their clocks run at slightly different speeds from clocks on the ground. If engineers ignored this effect, positions would drift by several kilometres every day.
GPS was first built for the military, but today it guides ships, helps farmers plant seeds precisely, and allows delivery drivers to find narrow lanes. Its signals can be blocked by tall buildings, tunnels and thick forests, which is why your map sometimes loses you in the city.
The next time you follow a blue dot, remember that it began with a clock in space.

q.q: What does a phone do to use GPS?
q.a: It listens to signals from satellites
w: It sends its position to satellites

q.q: Why is a fourth satellite needed?
q.a: To correct the error in the phone’s own clock
w: To make the signal travel faster
To count how many phones are nearby

q.q: Why does GPS sometimes fail in cities?
q.a: Tall buildings can block the signals
w: There is too much radio music
The clocks in cities run slowly

9.t: The Fisherman and the Golden Fish
9.text:
Long ago a poor fisherman lived with his wife in a tiny hut beside the sea. One morning he caught a large fish whose scales shone like gold. To his amazement, the fish spoke. “Please let me go,” it said. “I am an enchanted prince. I am no use to you as a meal.” The kind fisherman put it back in the water without asking for anything.
When he told his wife, she scolded him. “You should have asked for a wish! Go back and ask for a cottage. This hut is horrible.” Unwillingly, the man returned and called to the fish, which granted the wish at once. When he went home, a pretty cottage stood where the hut had been.
But a few weeks later the wife grew tired of it. “I want a stone house,” she said, and the fish gave her one. Then she demanded a palace, then to be queen, and finally the fish granted that too. Each time the sea looked darker and the wind blew harder.
Yet even a queen can be unhappy. “I want to rule the sun and the moon,” she announced at last. The frightened fisherman hurried to the shore, where the waves were as black as ink and a storm roared overhead. He repeated her words.
“Go home,” said the fish quietly. “She is back in her hut.”
And when the fisherman reached the place where the palace had been, he found only the old hut, and his wife sitting in the doorway, still dreaming of things she did not have.
The tale warns us that greed has no end: those who always want more can lose even the happiness they already own.
9.src: adapted from the Brothers Grimm, “The Fisherman and His Wife” (public domain)

q.q: Why did the fisherman free the fish?
q.a: It was an enchanted prince and asked him to
w: It was too small to eat

q.q: What did the wife want at the end?
q.a: To rule the sun and the moon

q.q: What does the story teach?
q.a: Greed can make us lose what we already have

9.text:
When Class 9B started a project on pollution, they expected to read a few articles and make a poster. Instead, their teacher Mr. Ortiz handed each group a pair of rubber gloves and a bag. “Today,” he said, “you are detectives. Your mission is to investigate the beach.”
The school was ten minutes from the coast, so the class walked there in the morning. At first the sand looked clean, but when they began to search carefully, the evidence appeared everywhere: bottle caps, fragments of fishing net, straws, old toothbrushes and countless tiny coloured pieces smaller than a grain of rice. “Those are microplastics,” explained Mr. Ortiz. “Big plastic never really disappears. The sun and the waves just break it into smaller and smaller pieces, which fish and birds may swallow.”
In two hours the students filled eleven bags. Back in the classroom they sorted, counted and weighed everything. The largest group, to their surprise, was not bottles but tiny pieces of foam used in packaging. One student, Amir, discovered that a plastic cup had a date printed on the bottom, from a company that had closed years earlier. “This one has been floating for a long time,” he whispered.
The class then moved from investigation to action. They wrote letters to local shops asking them to reduce packaging, organised a monthly beach clean-up and designed a campaign for the school canteen, encouraging everyone to bring a refillable bottle.
Within three months, the canteen sold nearly sixty per cent fewer plastic bottles. “It is only a small step,” said Mr. Ortiz proudly, “but every big change starts as someone’s small step.”

q.q: What did the students do on their first day of the project?
q.a: They searched a beach for rubbish

q.q: According to Mr. Ortiz, what happens to big plastic?
q.a: It breaks into smaller and smaller pieces

q.q: What was the result of the canteen campaign?
q.a: Far fewer plastic bottles were sold

9.text:
Many years ago there lived an emperor who loved beautiful clothes more than anything else. He spent all his money on them and changed his outfit for every hour of the day. Other kings might say, “The king is in his council room,” but of this emperor people always said, “The emperor is in his wardrobe.”
One day two swindlers arrived in the city. They claimed to be weavers who could make the most magnificent cloth in the world. “It has a wonderful quality,” they said. “It is invisible to anyone who is stupid or unfit for his position.”
The emperor was delighted. “With such cloth I could find out which of my ministers are fools!” He paid them a large sum of gold. The swindlers set up two looms and pretended to work day and night, though there was nothing on the machines at all.
Curious but nervous, the emperor sent his oldest minister to check the progress. The minister saw nothing, but he was afraid to say so. “It is marvellous,” he reported. A second official did the same. At last the emperor himself visited. He saw nothing, too, and thought, “Am I a fool?” So he declared, “Excellent! I am very pleased.”
The swindlers helped him put on the “clothes” for a great procession. Everyone in the crowd cheered and praised the splendid new outfit, because nobody dared to admit that they could see nothing.
Then a little child shouted, “But he has nothing on!” The whisper spread. “He has nothing on!” cried the whole crowd.
The emperor shivered. He knew they were right, but he held his head high and marched on to the end of the procession, while the swindlers had already escaped with the gold.
9.src: adapted from Hans Christian Andersen, “The Emperor’s New Clothes” (public domain)

q.q: What did the swindlers say about the cloth?
q.a: Stupid people could not see it
w: It was made of pure gold
It could only be worn at night
It was too heavy for a king

q.q: Why did the minister say the cloth was marvellous?
q.a: He was afraid of looking foolish

q.q: Who finally told the truth?
q.a: A small child in the crowd

9.text:
On Monday morning, a tall boy with a nervous smile stood at the front of our classroom. “This is Lukas,” said Mrs. Brown. “He has come all the way from Germany and will study with us for a term.” Some students whispered, some waved, and Lukas gave a small bow, which made everyone smile.
His English was excellent, but he was surprised by many small things at our school. In Germany, he explained at lunch, students did not wear uniforms, and classes finished at one o’clock. “Here you stay until four,” he said, shaking his head. “Then you do homework for three more hours! When do you play?”
We did not know what to answer. Then, on Wednesday, he discovered the school cafeteria. He stared at the plastic tray and said, “Rice, chicken, vegetables and soup, all in one meal? In my school we had a sandwich.” By Friday, he had tried every dish, and he declared that the sweet and sour pork was the best food he had ever eaten.
The real difficulty came in the third week. Lukas was homesick. He stopped talking in class and sat alone at lunch, looking at photographs on his phone. My friend Hao noticed this and invited him to play basketball after school. Lukas was not a good player at all, and he missed nearly every shot, yet everyone laughed together and the awkward silence disappeared.
After that, Lukas taught us German words, such as “Schadenfreude”, while we taught him how to use chopsticks, and he became really quite skilled.
When the term ended, he gave each of us a postcard of his town. On mine he wrote, “Thank you for making a stranger feel at home.” I still keep it above my desk, and I hope I will visit him one day.

q.q: What surprised Lukas about the school day?
q.a: Classes finished much later than in Germany
w: Students did not do any homework

q.q: How did Hao help Lukas when he felt homesick?
q.a: He invited him to play basketball
w: He took him to the cafeteria

q.q: What does the postcard show about Lukas?
q.a: He was grateful to be welcomed
w: He wanted to go home early
He planned to teach in China

9.text:
The Silk Road was not one road but a web of routes that stretched for thousands of kilometres across deserts, mountains and grasslands. It connected China with Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean, and for many centuries it carried both goods and ideas.
It is usually said to have begun around the second century BC, when the Han emperor Wudi sent an envoy named Zhang Qian to the west. Zhang Qian was captured and held for about ten years, but eventually he returned and reported the existence of rich and unknown lands. Trade soon followed.
Silk was the most precious cargo, because the Chinese were the only people who knew how to produce it. Wealthy Romans wore it as a sign of luxury, though they had no idea that it came from the cocoons of insects. Merchants also carried tea, paper, porcelain and spices. In the other direction came horses, grapes, walnuts and glass.
A merchant seldom travelled the whole way. Instead, goods passed from one trader to the next, becoming more expensive at every stage. Caravans of camels crossed the harsh Taklamakan Desert, resting in oasis towns such as Dunhuang and Kashgar, which became rich and lively places where many languages could be heard.
The Silk Road carried more than goods. Buddhism travelled from India into China along these routes, and the Chinese inventions of papermaking and printing slowly reached the West, where they later contributed to great changes in learning. Diseases also moved with the caravans, which is a reminder that contact can bring risks as well as benefits.
By the fifteenth century, sea routes had become cheaper and safer, and the overland trade declined. Even so, the Silk Road remains a powerful symbol of how curiosity and exchange can join distant peoples.

q.q: Why did Zhang Qian’s journey matter?
q.a: His report led to trade with the west
w: He ended a war with Rome

q.q: Why did goods become more expensive along the route?
w: Roads had to be paid for

q.q: Why did the overland trade decline by the fifteenth century?
q.a: Sea routes were cheaper and safer

9.text:
If you wanted to design an animal that is unlike a human in every possible way, you might invent something very like an octopus. It has eight arms, three hearts, blue blood and no bones at all. Yet scientists increasingly agree that it is one of the most intelligent creatures in the sea.
The octopus’s brain is surprisingly large for an animal without a backbone, and two thirds of its neurons are actually located in its arms. This means that each arm can, to some extent, decide what to do on its own, tasting and touching objects while the central brain thinks about something else.
Stories of octopus intelligence are numerous. In laboratories, octopuses have learned to unscrew the lids of jars to reach food inside. One famous octopus in New Zealand reportedly escaped from its tank at night, crossed the floor, slid down a drainpipe and returned to the sea. Aquarium workers have often found that animals which had been missing fish were being taken by an octopus that crept out and back again before morning.
Octopuses are also masters of disguise. Special cells in their skin allow them to change colour and even texture in a fraction of a second, so that they can look like a rock, a piece of coral or seaweed. When danger appears, they can squirt a cloud of dark ink to confuse an attacker, and then escape by shooting water from their body.
It is sad that these remarkable animals live very short lives, usually only one to five years, depending on the species. A mother octopus guards her eggs for months without eating, and usually dies soon after they hatch.
Perhaps this is why people who study octopuses so often speak of them with deep respect.

q.q: What is unusual about an octopus’s neurons?
q.a: Most of them are in its arms
w: There are none in its brain
They are found only in its heart

q.q: How does an octopus hide from danger?
q.a: It changes its colour and texture

q.q: What is sad about octopuses’ lives?

9.t: Marie Curie: A Life in the Laboratory
9.text:
Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in 1867 as Maria Skłodowska. At that time Poland was not an independent country, and women were not allowed to attend university there. Her father was a teacher of science, and he encouraged her curiosity, but the family was poor. Marie worked as a governess for several years to help pay for her sister’s medical studies, and then, in 1891, she travelled to Paris to study at the Sorbonne.
Life in Paris was hard. She lived in a tiny attic room, often forgot to eat, and once fainted in class from hunger. Nevertheless, she finished at the top of her class in physics and later in mathematics. She met a young physicist named Pierre Curie, and they married in 1895.
Together the Curies investigated the strange rays discovered by Henri Becquerel in uranium. Marie coined the word “radioactivity” to describe the phenomenon. Working in a cold, leaking shed, she spent years purifying tiny amounts of new substances from tons of ore. In 1898 the couple announced two new elements: polonium, named after her homeland, and radium.
In 1903, the Curies and Becquerel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. Only three years later, Pierre was killed in a street accident. Marie, heartbroken but determined, took over his teaching post and became the first female professor at the University of Paris. In 1911 she received a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry.
During the First World War she helped to organise mobile X-ray units, nicknamed “little Curies”, to treat wounded soldiers. Sadly, her long exposure to radiation harmed her health, and she died in 1934.
Marie Curie remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, and she showed that determination can open doors that society has closed.

q.q: Why did Marie work as a governess?
q.a: To help pay for her sister’s studies
w: Poland had no universities at all
She wanted to live in Paris

q.q: What was special about her Nobel Prizes?
q.a: She won in two different sciences
w: She won both in the same year
They were both shared with Pierre

q.q: How did she help during the First World War?
w: She built a new hospital in Warsaw
She tested new medicines on herself

9.text:
Interviewer: Today I’m talking with Dana, who is only sixteen and has already won a national prize for her invention. Dana, welcome. What exactly did you build?
Dana: Thank you. It is a low-cost water filter made from sand, charcoal and the shells of local crabs. It removes most of the harmful bacteria from river water, and it can be made for less than five dollars.
Interviewer: How did the idea start?
Dana: Two summers ago I visited my grandmother’s village. There was no tap water, and children often got sick from drinking from the river. I thought, surely a simple solution must exist. I spent the rest of the holiday reading about filters.
Interviewer: Was it easy?
Dana: Not at all! My first design failed completely. The water came out looking cleaner, but laboratory tests showed that it was still dangerous. I almost gave up. My science teacher told me that a failed experiment is not a waste if it teaches you something, so I kept going and tested forty different mixtures.
Interviewer: What would you say to young people who have an idea but doubt themselves?
Dana: Start small, and don’t be afraid to ask for help. I wrote to a university professor, and to my surprise she replied and let me use her laboratory on weekends. Also, be ready to hear the word “no” many times.
Interviewer: What are your plans now?
Dana: This autumn we will install fifty filters in villages near my grandmother’s home. After that, I hope to study engineering.
Interviewer: Dana, thank you, and good luck. I’m sure we will hear more about you.
Dana: Thank you so much for having me.

q.q: What gave Dana the idea for her filter?
q.a: Children in her grandmother’s village got sick from river water
w: A prize offered by the government
