q.q: What did Dana learn from her first failed design?
q.a: A failed experiment can still teach something

q.q: How did the professor help her?
q.a: She let Dana use her laboratory at weekends
w: She tested the water in the village

9.text:
Every year, on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, millions of Chinese families make sticky rice dumplings called zongzi, and thousands of teams race long, narrow boats along rivers and lakes. This is the Dragon Boat Festival, and behind its lively scenes lies an old and sad story.
Qu Yuan was a poet and minister who lived in the state of Chu more than two thousand years ago. He was honest and loyal, and he gave the king sound advice about defending the country against the powerful state of Qin. But jealous officials slandered him, and the king sent him far away from the capital.
In exile, Qu Yuan wrote beautiful, passionate poems about his love for his homeland. When he learned that Chu’s capital had fallen to the enemy, he was filled with despair. According to tradition, he walked to the Miluo River and drowned himself in sorrow.
The local people, who loved him, rushed out in their boats to look for his body. They beat drums to frighten away the fish and threw rice into the water so that the fish would not eat their hero. Later, they began wrapping the rice in leaves to keep it from dissolving, and so the first zongzi were made.
Today, dragon boat races remember those desperate rescue attempts. Each boat is decorated with a carved dragon head, a drummer sits in the front, and the paddlers stroke in perfect time. In many places, people also hang mugwort at their doors and wear perfumed pouches to keep illness away, because the season is hot and damp.
The festival was listed by UNESCO in 2009. It reminds children not only of food and fun, but also of honesty and love of one’s country.

q.q: Why was Qu Yuan sent away from the capital?
q.a: Jealous officials spoke badly of him
w: He lost a battle against Qin
He had stolen from the king

q.q: Why did people throw rice into the river?
q.a: So the fish would not eat Qu Yuan
w: To honour the king of Qin

q.q: What do the dragon boat races remember?
q.a: The attempts to rescue Qu Yuan

9.t: The Foolish Old Man Who Moved Mountains
9.text:
In the north of China, in front of the house of an old man called Yu Gong, stood two huge mountains. Yu Gong was nearly ninety years old, and every time he left his house, he had to go a long way round the mountains. “This is ridiculous,” he complained. One evening he gathered his family. “Let us dig through these mountains and open a road straight to the river!”
His sons and grandsons agreed at once, but his wife had doubts. “You are too old to move even a small hill,” she said. “And where will you put all the earth and stones?” “We shall throw them into the sea,” answered Yu Gong confidently.
So the next morning they began. The old man, his sons and a small grandson who carried baskets of earth, worked from sunrise until dark. The sea was so far away that a single trip took a whole year.
An old man called Zhi Sou, who lived by the river, laughed at them. “You must be out of your mind,” he said. “With your little strength, you cannot even remove one corner of a mountain.” Yu Gong sighed and replied, “You are not as wise as a child. When I die, my sons will continue. When they die, there will be grandsons, and so on, for ever. The mountains cannot grow any higher, but our family will always grow bigger. Why should we not succeed?”
Zhi Sou had no answer. But the gods in heaven heard this conversation, and the Emperor of Heaven was deeply moved by the old man’s determination. He ordered two powerful spirits to carry the mountains away, one to the east and one to the west.
From then on, no mountain blocked the road.
9.src: adapted from the Chinese folk tale “Yu Gong Yi Shan” (traditional, public domain)

q.q: Why did Yu Gong want to remove the mountains?
q.a: They forced him to take a long way round
w: They hid the river from view
They were full of dangerous animals

q.q: What was Yu Gong’s argument against Zhi Sou?
q.a: His family would keep working for generations
w: He had more money than Zhi Sou

q.q: How does the story end?
q.a: The Emperor of Heaven moved the mountains
w: The family gave up the work

9.text:
It is one of the oldest questions children ask: why is the sky blue? The answer lies in the way light travels through the atmosphere.
Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. A glass prism can split it, and so can raindrops, which is why we see rainbows after a storm. Each colour has a different wavelength: red light has long, gentle waves, while blue and violet light have short, quick waves.
When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it meets countless tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of light, and they scatter the light in all directions. The important point is that short waves are scattered far more strongly than long ones. The effect, known as Rayleigh scattering after the British physicist who explained it in the 1870s, means that blue light is bounced around the sky much more than red light. Wherever you look, some of this scattered blue light is travelling into your eyes.
But if violet has an even shorter wavelength than blue, why is the sky not violet? There are three reasons. The Sun produces less violet light than blue, some of the violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. Together, these facts make the sky look blue.
The same idea explains the red sunset. When the Sun is low, its light has to pass through a much thicker layer of air. Most of the blue is scattered away on the long journey, and the remaining light is orange and red.
On the Moon, which has no atmosphere, there is nothing to scatter the light, and the sky is black even in the daytime.

q.q: What happens to blue light in the atmosphere?
q.a: It is scattered more strongly than red light
w: It travels in a straight line

q.q: Why is the sky not violet?
q.a: The Sun gives less violet and our eyes see it poorly
w: Violet light cannot enter the atmosphere

q.q: Why is the sunset red?
q.a: Light passes through more air and loses its blue

9.text:
“How hard can it be?” I said. This, as I now know, is the most dangerous sentence in the English language.
It was my mother’s birthday, and my brother Ben and I had decided to surprise her with breakfast in bed. We had watched our father make pancakes a hundred times, so we felt like experts. We crept into the kitchen at six o’clock and began.
First, the flour. Ben opened the bag with such enthusiasm that a white cloud rose into the air, and for a moment we both looked like ghosts. Next, the eggs. I cracked one on the side of the bowl, and about half of it ended up on the floor, together with several bits of shell. “Fish them out,” said Ben wisely, “nobody will notice.”
Then came the milk, which we poured without measuring. The mixture turned into a thick grey paste. “Add more milk,” I suggested. Ben added too much, and suddenly it was as thin as water. So we added more flour, and we kept adding until the bowl was full to the brim and the whole kitchen was white.
The first pancake stuck to the pan. The second burned black and set off the smoke alarm, which screamed so loudly that the neighbour’s dog began to bark. The third pancake, I am proud to say, was nearly round, and Ben tossed it high into the air to celebrate. It landed on the ceiling, where it stayed.
At that moment, the kitchen door opened. Mum stood there in her dressing gown, looking at the flour, the shells, the smoke and the pancake on the ceiling. Then, to our great relief, she began to laugh.
“Best birthday ever,” she said. “Now, let me show you how to do it properly.”

q.q: Why did the boys make pancakes?
q.a: To surprise their mother on her birthday
w: They had a cooking test at school

q.q: What set off the smoke alarm?
How did the mother react?
q.a: She laughed and offered to teach them

9.text:
Saturday morning arrived, bright and fresh, and the whole world seemed to be full of summer. Everybody was cheerful except Tom Sawyer, because Aunt Polly had given him a punishment: he had to whitewash the long wooden fence in front of the house, thirty yards in length and nine feet high.
Tom sighed, dipped his brush, and painted one small section. Then he looked at the remaining fence and felt miserable. His friends would soon pass by on their way to the swimming hole, and they would laugh at him.
Just then, Ben Rogers came along, eating an apple. “Hello, old fellow! Have to work, eh?” Tom turned slowly and carried on painting with a thoughtful look. “Work? Well, it’s not exactly work. I do not know if it is work or not. All I know is that it suits Tom Sawyer.”
“Oh, come on! You don’t mean to say you like it?” “Like it? Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?” This put a new light on the matter. Ben stopped eating his apple. Tom swept his brush back and forth, stepped away to see the effect, added a touch here and there, and Ben watched every move with growing interest. “Say, Tom, let me paint a bit.”
“No, Ben. Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence. It has to be done very carefully.” At last, Ben offered his apple in exchange for a turn, and Tom, pretending to be reluctant, gave up the brush.
By the afternoon, Tom had collected a kite, a dead rat, twelve marbles and many other treasures from the boys who had queued to whitewash the fence. It had three coats, and when it ran out of paint he would have bought the whole town.
Tom had discovered a great law of human behaviour: people want what seems hard to get.
9.src: adapted from Mark Twain, “The Adventures of Tom Sawyer” (public domain)

q.q: Why did Tom have to paint the fence?
q.a: It was a punishment from Aunt Polly

q.q: How did Tom make Ben want to paint?
q.a: He pretended that painting was a special pleasure
w: He promised to give him marbles
He told him it was easy
He said Aunt Polly would pay him

q.q: What lesson did Tom discover?
q.a: People value what seems hard to get

9.text:
Ten years ago, if you had asked a computer to recognise a cat in a photograph, it would probably have failed. Today your phone can do it in an instant, and it can even translate languages, suggest music and write short poems. What changed? The answer is something called machine learning.
In traditional programming, a person writes exact rules: if this happens, do that. But nobody can write precise rules for every possible picture of a cat, because cats come in countless colours, sizes and positions. Machine learning solves the problem by reversing the process. Instead of giving the computer rules, we give it thousands of examples, each labelled “cat” or “not cat”, and let the computer discover the patterns for itself.
Most modern systems use a structure called a neural network, which is loosely inspired by the brain. It consists of many layers of simple units. Each unit receives numbers, makes a small calculation and passes the result onward. At the beginning, the network guesses at random and is mostly wrong. After every guess, it is told how wrong it was and adjusts millions of tiny settings to improve slightly. After millions of rounds, it becomes remarkably accurate.
This power brings serious questions. A system trained on poor or unfair data will repeat the same unfairness. If most of the photographs used to teach a face-recognition program show light-skinned men, the program will recognise other people badly. In addition, such programs can sound confident even when they are wrong.
That is why experts say people must check what the machines produce, and why you should not believe everything a program tells you. A machine can learn from examples, but it does not understand the world as you do. For now, thinking carefully remains a human responsibility.

q.q: How does machine learning differ from traditional programming?
q.a: The computer finds patterns from examples
w: It needs no data at all

q.q: Why can a face-recognition program treat people unfairly?
q.a: Its training data may be unbalanced

q.q: What is the writer’s main message at the end?
q.a: People must still think and check carefully

9.text:
When my grandmother turned seventy-three, my parents gave her a smartphone. She looked at it the way you might look at a small, strange animal. “What is it for?” she asked. “It is for talking to your grandchildren,” said Mum. “We already talk on the old phone,” replied Grandma, which was true, although the old phone needed a button pressed with a fingernail.
I was given the job of teaching her. The first lesson went badly. She held the phone so close to her face that I could only see her left eye. “Grandma, move it back a bit.” She moved it away, until I saw the ceiling. “Now you’re upstairs,” I laughed.
The second lesson was about touching the screen. Grandma had learned to press things hard, as if she were ringing a doorbell from the nineteenth century. Twice she accidentally closed the call. Once she called a stranger in another city, and told him very politely that she wished to speak to her granddaughter. Fortunately, he found it funny.
But Grandma is stubborn, and she practised every day. She wrote the steps on a card and stuck it to the wall: “1. Touch the green button. 2. Wait. 3. Smile.” Within a month she could call me by herself, and she began to enjoy it. She showed me the vegetables in her garden, introduced me to her new kitten, and even gave me cooking lessons, holding the phone over the pot.
Last week, she called to ask whether she could download a new game. “All my friends play it,” she explained.
I realised that I had been wrong to worry. Learning, she proved, has nothing to do with age. It only needs patience, a good reason and someone you love at the other end of the line.

q.q: What was wrong with Grandma’s first video call?
q.a: She held the phone too close, then pointed it at the ceiling
w: She forgot to charge the phone

q.q: How did Grandma remember the steps?
q.a: She stuck a card with instructions on the wall
w: She asked a neighbour each day
She made her granddaughter call first

q.q: What does the narrator learn?
q.a: People of any age can learn new skills

9.text:
Deep in the Indian jungle, on a warm evening, Father Wolf woke from his sleep and stretched. The pack was gathering at the Council Rock, and in his cave something small and brown was crawling among the wolf cubs. It was a human baby, no bigger than a loaf of bread, and it was not afraid at all.
Suddenly the entrance darkened. It was Shere Khan, the great tiger, who had followed the child’s trail. “Give me the man’s cub,” he growled. “He is mine.” But Mother Wolf lifted her head proudly. “The man’s cub is mine, Lungri. He shall live to run with the pack and to hunt with the pack. Go and look for your supper somewhere else.”
The tiger roared with anger but backed away, for he knew that a she-wolf defending her family is a dangerous enemy. “We shall see what the pack says,” he snarled, and vanished.
At the Council Rock, the wolves could not agree. Then Bagheera, the black panther, spoke. “I will buy the cub’s life with a fresh-killed bull,” he said. “Is that not the custom?” Baloo, the old brown bear who taught the young wolves the Law of the Jungle, added his support. “I shall teach him myself.” The pack accepted.
So the child was named Mowgli, which means “the little frog” because he had no fur, and he grew up among the wolves. Baloo taught him which fruit was ripe and how to talk to every creature of the forest, and Bagheera showed him how to climb trees and move without noise.
But Shere Khan never forgot. Year after year the tiger waited, and the jungle grew quiet whenever his shadow passed.
Mowgli, at ten years old, already understood a secret: the strongest member of a community is not the one with the sharpest claws, but the one who has friends.
9.src: adapted from Rudyard Kipling, “Mowgli’s Brothers” in The Jungle Book (public domain)

q.q: Why did Shere Khan come to the wolves’ cave?
w: He wished to join the pack

q.q: How did Bagheera save the child?
q.a: He offered a bull as payment
w: He carried him up a tree
He hid him in a cave

q.q: What does the last paragraph say about strength?
q.a: Having friends matters more than sharp claws

9.text:
The weather forecast had promised a clear day, which was why Ravi and his cousin Kiran set out on the hill path without a map. By noon, however, a thick mist rolled down from the summit, and the narrow path disappeared. “It’s fine,” Ravi said, trying to sound confident. “We just turn round and go back.” But after an hour of walking they reached the same strange rock twice.
Kiran, who had joined a scouting club, was the first to stay calm. “Stop,” she said. “When you are lost, the worst thing is to keep walking in circles. Let’s think.” They sat down, drank some water and checked what they had: two bottles, a bag of nuts, a torch, a thin raincoat each and a phone with only fifteen per cent battery and no signal.
“First, we turn the phone off to save power,” said Kiran. “Second, we stay together. Third, we make ourselves visible.” Ravi tied his bright yellow raincoat to a branch near a clearing, and they gathered dry wood in case they had to spend the night.
As the afternoon grew colder, they put on both coats and sat close together. Every thirty minutes Kiran blew three short blasts on her whistle, the international call for help, and then listened. Nothing came back.
Just as it began to get dark, they heard a distant bark. Then a second whistle, and a voice calling, “Hello! Is anyone there?” A forest ranger with a dog came out of the mist. “Your parents reported you missing two hours ago,” he said. “Your yellow coat was the first thing we saw.”
On the way down, Ravi apologised to his cousin. “I should have checked the route,” he said. “Next time,” Kiran replied with a tired smile, “we’ll bring a map.”

q.q: Why did the cousins realise they were lost?
q.a: They passed the same rock twice
w: Their phone showed the wrong place

q.q: Why did Kiran turn off the phone?
q.a: To save the little battery power left

q.q: What helped the ranger find them?
q.a: The yellow raincoat and the whistle

9.t: A Cup of Tea, Two Cultures
9.text:
After water, tea is the most widely drunk beverage in the world, and two countries that have shaped its story are China and Britain, although their tea habits could hardly be more different.
According to legend, tea was discovered in 2737 BC when leaves from a wild tree blew into a pot of hot water that the emperor Shennong was boiling. Whatever the truth, tea was certainly grown in China more than two thousand years ago. At first it was valued as medicine, but by the Tang dynasty it had become a refined daily pleasure, and the scholar Lu Yu wrote the first book about it, The Classic of Tea.
In China, tea is usually drunk without milk or sugar, so that the drinker can appreciate the subtle flavour and aroma. Different types, such as green, black, oolong and white tea, depend on how the leaves are processed. In a traditional ceremony, small cups are used, and the same leaves are infused several times, with each brewing revealing a slightly different taste.
Tea reached Europe in the seventeenth century, and became fashionable in Britain after Queen Catherine of Braganza, who loved it, married King Charles the Second. Because the leaves were expensive, they were locked in special boxes. By the nineteenth century, “afternoon tea” had become a social habit: a pot of strong black tea with milk, served with small sandwiches and cakes at about four o’clock.
The British also fought over tea. Heavy taxes on it contributed to the Boston Tea Party of 1773 in America, when protesters threw hundreds of chests of tea into the harbour.
Today, whether sipped slowly from a tiny porcelain cup or gulped from a mug beside a biscuit, tea brings people together. It shows that a single leaf can carry the traditions of an entire culture.

q.q: How is tea usually drunk in China?
What made tea fashionable in Britain?
q.a: A queen who loved it married the king
w: A book written by Lu Yu

q.q: What is the passage’s main idea?
q.a: Tea has different traditions but connects people
w: British tea is better than Chinese tea

9.t: Yuan Longping: The Man Who Wanted Everyone to Have Enough Rice
9.text:
Yuan Longping was born in 1930, in a China where hunger was a common experience. As a child he lived through war and had seen starving families on the roads. Later, as a young teacher of agriculture in Hunan Province, he witnessed a severe famine in the early 1960s, and the memory never left him. He made a promise to himself: he would use science to help people eat enough.
At that time most scientists believed that rice could not be improved by crossing different plants, because rice flowers pollinate themselves. Yuan challenged this belief. One day in 1964, while walking through a field, he noticed a single rice plant with unusually large, full grains. He thought it might be a natural hybrid, and he spent years searching.
The work was long and discouraging. He and his team examined thousands of plants under the hot sun, often with no result. Then, in 1970, a worker on Hainan Island found a wild rice plant whose pollen was sterile. This was the key that allowed Yuan to develop the first practical hybrid rice. By the mid-1970s farmers in China were planting it, and yields were roughly twenty per cent higher than before.
Hybrid rice has since spread to many countries in Asia and Africa, helping to feed millions of people. Yuan is often called the “Father of Hybrid Rice”, but he preferred to describe himself as a farmer. He liked to say that he had a dream: to walk among rice plants as tall as sorghum, with ears as long as brooms.
He continued to work into old age, and died in 2021 at ninety-one. Across China, thousands of people left flowers and rice at his memorial.

q.q: What experience made Yuan Longping want to help farmers?
q.a: A severe famine in the early 1960s

q.q: What was special about the wild rice plant found on Hainan?
How did Yuan describe himself?

9.text:
Every four years, thousands of runners from across the world gather to complete one of the toughest events in athletics: the marathon. Its name comes from a Greek legend, and its length comes from a royal request.
The story goes back to the year 490 BC, when a Greek army defeated a much larger Persian force near the town of Marathon. According to legend, a messenger named Pheidippides ran all the way to Athens, about forty kilometres away, to announce the victory. He gasped, “Rejoice, we have won!” and then collapsed and died. Historians now doubt this account, because the earliest sources describe a different run, of about two hundred and forty kilometres from Athens to Sparta, to ask for help before the battle. Still, the legend was too dramatic to forget.
When the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896, the organisers wanted a race that would remind people of ancient glory. The marathon was invented, and the winner was a Greek postman, Spyridon Louis, to the delight of the cheering crowd.
The exact distance varied at first. In 1908, the Games were held in London, and the course was arranged to begin at Windsor Castle, so that the royal family could watch from the start, and to end in front of the royal box in the stadium. This made the distance 26 miles and 385 yards, or 42.195 kilometres. In 1921 this distance became the official standard.
Today, ordinary people run marathons for pleasure, and many do it for charity. Most finish tired and proud, with sore legs and wide smiles. The marathon shows that the real opponent is often not another runner, but our own wish to stop.

q.q: Why do historians doubt the Pheidippides legend?
q.a: Early sources describe a different run
w: There was no battle at Marathon

q.q: Why is the marathon 42.195 kilometres long?
q.a: The 1908 London course was arranged for the royal family
w: It was the distance from Marathon to Sparta
The Greeks had measured it exactly

q.q: Who won the first modern Olympic marathon?

9.text:
When people speak of the Great Wall, they usually imagine a single, endless barrier winding over the mountains. In fact it is a collection of walls built by different states and dynasties over more than two thousand years, and, taken together, its sections stretch for more than twenty thousand kilometres.
The earliest walls were built by rival states during the Spring and Autumn period to defend themselves against each other. After the First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, united China in 221 BC, he ordered that these older walls be joined and extended to guard against nomadic tribes in the north. Hundreds of thousands of workers laboured on the project, and many suffered terribly from cold, hunger and exhaustion. The legend of Meng Jiangnu, who wept at the wall for her dead husband until a long section collapsed, reflects the hardship of those years.
Most of the wall that tourists admire today belongs to the Ming dynasty. Built from stone and large fired bricks, the Ming wall has watchtowers where soldiers could light fires or burn dung to send smoke signals, so that a warning could travel hundreds of kilometres in a few hours. Passes such as Shanhaiguan, where the wall reaches the sea, were guarded by thousands of soldiers.
Yet the Great Wall never made China completely safe. Armies sometimes broke through, or simply walked through open gates after bribing the guards. Some historians suggest that its main value was not as a military barrier but as a control on trade and migration, and a way to project power.
Today the wall is a protected monument, but long stretches are crumbling, since farmers once took the bricks to build houses.
Visitors who climb its steep steps will find it hard to believe that human hands built it, one stone at a time.

q.q: What is the Great Wall, according to the passage?
q.a: Several walls built by different states and dynasties
w: One wall built by the Qin dynasty
A wall built entirely in the Ming period

q.q: How did watchtowers send warnings?
q.a: By lighting fires and making smoke

q.q: Why did the wall not make China completely safe?
q.a: Armies broke through or guards were bribed

9.text:
Ms. Reyes: Today’s debate topic is: “Mobile phones should be banned in school.” Leo will speak for the motion, and Sofia will speak against it. Leo, please begin.
Leo: Thank you. My first point is concentration. Studies suggest that even the presence of a phone on a desk reduces a student’s attention, because part of the brain keeps wondering about messages. Secondly, phones can be used to cheat in tests or to bully classmates online. Finally, break time is supposed to be for talking and playing. Today many students sit side by side, silently staring at screens. For all these reasons, I believe a ban would improve school life.
Ms. Reyes: Thank you, Leo. Sofia?
Sofia: Thank you. Leo has raised serious problems, but a total ban is the wrong answer. First, phones are useful learning tools. We can look up words, record experiments and use educational apps. Second, parents want to be able to contact their children in an emergency, and some students travel a long way to school. Third, learning to manage technology is a life skill. If we simply forbid phones, we do not teach students self-control; we only postpone the lesson until they leave school.
Leo: But Sofia, wouldn’t a school with strong rules help students who cannot stop checking their phones?
Sofia: Yes, rules matter, Leo, and I agree that phones should be silent during lessons. A sensible compromise would be to keep phones in lockers during class but allow limited use at lunch.
Ms. Reyes: Thank you both. You have shown that a good argument needs evidence and respect for the other side. Now, let’s vote: who finds Sofia’s compromise convincing?

q.q: What is Leo’s first argument?
Why does Sofia think banning phones is the wrong answer?
q.a: Students need to learn to manage technology

q.q: What compromise does Sofia suggest?
q.a: Keep phones in lockers during class but allow limited use at lunch
w: Let teachers collect phones every week

9.text:
A honeybee colony is a remarkable society. A single hive can contain fifty thousand bees, all working together without a leader giving orders. Yet when a worker bee finds a rich field of flowers a kilometre away, she is able to tell her sisters exactly where to go. She does it by dancing.
The discovery was made by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who spent decades watching bees in glass-sided hives. He noticed that returning foragers climb onto the vertical honeycomb inside the dark hive and perform a figure-of-eight pattern. In the middle part of the pattern, the bee runs in a straight line while waggling her body from side to side. Then she circles back and repeats the performance, many times.
Von Frisch realised that the dance is a precise code. The angle between the straight run and the vertical direction on the comb shows the angle between the flowers and the Sun. If the bee waggles straight upwards, the food lies in the direction of the Sun; if she waggles to the right at sixty degrees, the flowers are sixty degrees to the right of the Sun. The longer the waggle lasts, the farther away the food is, with roughly one second meaning about a kilometre. The liveliness of the dance shows how rich the source is.
Watching the dance, other bees touch the dancer with their antennae and note the smell of nectar on her body. Then they fly out and find the place.
In 1973 von Frisch received the Nobel Prize for his work. Today, scientists build small robot bees that dance, and real bees really do follow them.
It is astonishing that a tiny brain smaller than a grain of rice can carry such a message.

q.q: What does the length of the waggle show?
q.a: How far away the food is
w: How many bees are in the hive
What time of day it is

q.q: How do the other bees get extra information?
q.a: They touch the dancer and smell the nectar
w: They follow her out of the hive

q.q: What does the writer find astonishing?
q.a: A tiny brain can carry such a message
w: Von Frisch won the Nobel Prize

9.t: The Gift of the Watch and the Combs
9.text:
Della counted her money for the third time: one dollar and eighty-seven cents. Tomorrow was Christmas, and that was all she had to buy a present for her husband Jim. She had saved every penny for months, but it was nothing.
The couple was poor. They had only two treasures. One was Jim’s gold watch, which had belonged to his father and grandfather. The other was Della’s long, brown hair, which fell below her knees like a waterfall.
Suddenly Della turned from the window. Her eyes were shining. She pulled the pins out and let her hair fall. Then she put on her old jacket and hurried out to a shop with a sign that said “Hair Goods”. “Will you buy my hair?” she asked. “I buy hair,” said the owner. “Take your hat off.” The brown waterfall fell. “Twenty dollars.” “Give it to me quickly,” said Della.
For two hours she searched the shops and at last found the perfect present: a simple platinum chain for Jim’s watch. It cost twenty-one dollars.
At seven o’clock, Jim arrived. He stopped at the door, staring at her short hair. “Don’t be angry,” she said. “I sold it. It will grow again. Say ‘Merry Christmas’, Jim.” Slowly Jim took a package out of his pocket. Inside were the beautiful combs she had admired in a shop window for months, made for her long hair.
Della laughed and cried together, and then held out the chain. “Isn’t it lovely, Jim? Give me your watch.” Jim sat down and smiled. “Della,” he said, “I sold the watch to buy the combs.”
They had each given up their greatest treasure for the other, and that, the writer says, makes them the wisest of all gift-givers.
9.src: adapted from O. Henry, “The Gift of the Magi” (public domain)

q.q: What did Della do to get money?
What irony ends the story?
q.a: Each gift was useless because of the other’s sacrifice
w: Jim did not like his gift
Della could not find the shop

q.q: Why are Della and Jim called wise?
q.a: They gave up their greatest treasure for each other
w: They saved a lot of money

9.text:
Antarctica is a continent of superlatives. It is the coldest, driest, windiest and highest continent on Earth. The lowest temperature ever measured, minus 89.2 degrees Celsius, was recorded at Vostok Station in 1983, and the interior receives so little snow that, technically, it is a desert.
But it is also a land of ice. About ninety-eight per cent of Antarctica is covered by a sheet of ice that is, on average, more than two kilometres thick, and in some places almost five. It holds roughly seventy per cent of the world’s fresh water. If all of it melted, global sea levels would rise by about sixty metres, flooding most of the world’s coastal cities.
No country owns Antarctica. Under the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 and now accepted by more than fifty countries, the continent is reserved for peaceful purposes and scientific research. Military activities and mining are banned, so scientists from many nations work side by side in research stations, studying everything from climate history to the behaviour of penguins. Ice cores drilled deep into the sheet contain bubbles of ancient air, and by analysing them, researchers have reconstructed the temperature and the amount of carbon dioxide over hundreds of thousands of years.
Life exists even here, though mostly along the coast. Emperor penguins breed during the dark winter, and the male keeps the egg warm on his feet for two months, without eating, while the female goes to sea to feed. Krill, tiny shrimp-like animals, form the foundation of the food chain, feeding whales, seals and seabirds.
Because of global warming, parts of the continent are now melting faster than ever. What happens in this remote and frozen place will eventually affect everyone on Earth.

q.q: Why is Antarctica called a desert?
q.a: Its interior gets very little snow
w: It is very hot in summer

q.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty allow?
What do ice cores tell scientists?
q.a: What the climate was like long ago
w: How thick the snow will be

9.t: Moving Your Way to a Calmer Mind
9.text:
Exams, friendships, family expectations, social media: modern teenagers face a great deal of pressure. A little stress is useful. It sharpens attention and gives us energy to meet a challenge. But when stress continues for too long, it can make us anxious, tired and unable to concentrate. Fortunately, one of the best remedies costs nothing: moving your body.
When we exercise, the brain releases chemicals called endorphins, which improve mood and lessen pain. Regular activity also lowers the level of cortisol, the main stress hormone, and helps people fall asleep more easily. Studies from several countries have found that students who exercise at least three times a week report fewer symptoms of anxiety and perform better at school than those who stay inactive.
Exercise doesn’t have to mean joining a team or running marathons. A brisk twenty-minute walk, a game of badminton, skipping rope, dancing in your room or cycling to school can all help. The important thing is to choose something enjoyable, because enjoyment helps you stick to a habit. Exercising outdoors in green places brings extra benefits, probably because nature has a calming effect on the mind.
Movement is not the only answer, however. Talking to a friend, a parent or a teacher can lift a heavy burden. Writing your thoughts in a journal, practising slow breathing or listening to quiet music can also help. If sadness or worry lasts for weeks, or makes everyday life difficult, it is wise to seek help from a doctor or counsellor. Asking for support is a sign of strength, not weakness.
So the next time your mind feels crowded, close the textbook for a few minutes and go outside. Your body will thank you, and so will your brain.

q.q: What do endorphins do?
q.a: They improve mood and reduce pain

q.q: What kind of exercise does the writer recommend?
When should someone seek professional help?
q.a: When worry lasts for weeks and affects daily life
w: Whenever they feel a little tired

9.text:
On Tuesday evening, my phone buzzed with a message from an unknown number: “Hi Grandma, I’ve got a new phone. Can you send me 500 yuan? I’ll explain later.” I stared at the screen. I am seventeen years old, and my grandmother, as far as I knew, was not exactly a person who sent text messages.
I laughed and replied: “Sorry, wrong number. I hope you find your grandmother.” To my surprise, the stranger answered within seconds. “Oh no! Sorry! I must have mistyped it. But I really need money, so if you could spare 500, I’d be extremely grateful.”
Now I was suspicious, so I played along. “What do you need the money for?” “A new pair of trainers,” came the answer. “They are limited edition.” “Then you should ask your grandmother for them for your birthday,” I wrote. The stranger said he had already tried this, and she had given him a pair of socks.
The conversation continued for twenty minutes. I discovered that he was fifteen, lived in another city, supported the same football team as me, and was terrified of his maths teacher. We argued fiercely about our goalkeeper, and I even told him about my own grandmother and her attempts to use a smartphone.
Finally, he wrote: “You are the nicest wrong number I’ve ever had. Shall we talk again?” I grinned and saved his number under “Mysterious Trainer Boy”.
We now message every week. Last month, he finally sent me a photograph of his sneakers, and, I admit, they are the ugliest shoes I have ever seen. I told him so. He said I had no taste. Thus began the best friendship that was ever caused by a typing error.

q.q: Why was the narrator surprised by the first message?
q.a: His grandmother did not send text messages
w: It arrived very late at night

q.q: What did the two boys have in common?
q.a: They supported the same football team
w: They went to the same school

q.q: How did the strange conversation end up?

9.text:
In the 1950s, the land at Saihanba, in northern Hebei Province, was a bleak place. Centuries of logging and farming had stripped away the old forest, and what remained was a windswept plateau where sand blew toward Beijing, some two hundred and fifty kilometres to the south. Dust storms that regularly covered the capital were partly blamed on this barren land.
In 1962, the government sent a group of 369 forestry workers to the plateau with a difficult mission: to create a forest from nothing. The conditions were harsh. The winters were long, with temperatures falling to minus forty degrees, and the workers lived in simple huts with little food. Their first planting failed, and so did the second, because the young trees died in the freezing wind. Only about eight per cent of the seedlings survived in the first two years.
Instead of giving up, the planters learned. They discovered that the trees needed more protection and better species, and they finally succeeded in planting Mongolian pine, which was suited to the cold. A new method of planting seedlings on slopes, ideally tilted away from the wind, gave much better results. Generation after generation continued the work, and today the forest covers about 75,000 hectares.
The results are impressive. The forest produces large amounts of clean air and oxygen every year, absorbs carbon dioxide, protects the water supply for nearby cities and has reduced the sand blown towards Beijing. In 2017, the planters were awarded a United Nations environmental prize.
They did not plant the trees to enjoy their shade, because the trees took decades to grow. They planted them for the people who would come after.

q.q: Why did the first plantings fail?
q.a: The young trees died in the freezing wind

q.q: What helped the planters to succeed?
q.a: Learning from mistakes and planting suitable trees

q.q: What is the main message of the final paragraph?
q.a: The planters worked for future generations
w: The forest was easy to build

9.text:
High in the Andes, beyond a ring of impassable mountains, lay a hidden valley where, for fourteen generations, all the people had been blind. A terrible disease had taken their sight long ago, and their children were born without it. They had forgotten that sight ever existed. For them the world was a place of touch, sound and smell, and the old stories about “seeing” had faded into nonsense.
One day a mountaineer named Nunez slipped on a glacier and tumbled down into this valley. Bruised but alive, he saw houses, neat paths and fields, and he smiled. He had heard an old proverb: “In the country of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.”
He quickly discovered that the proverb was wrong. When he called out to the villagers, they did not bow to him. They only listened, puzzled, and told him that he was clumsy. When he tried to describe the beauty of the mountains and the sky, they decided he was ill. “His brain is disturbed,” said the doctor. “These strange things he calls eyes are making him dream.”
Nunez tried to prove his advantage. He offered to fight a villager, certain that he could win by watching. But the man heard him move, and the struggle ended with a bruised Nunez. After that, he accepted that he could not rule here.
He fell in love with a young woman named Medina-saroté. Her family agreed to the marriage only on one condition: that the doctor remove his eyes, which, they said, were the cause of his madness.
Horrified, Nunez decided that sight was worth more than love. In the night, he climbed out of the valley and lay watching the stars.
9.src: adapted from H. G. Wells, “The Country of the Blind” (public domain)

q.q: Why did the villagers not understand Nunez?
q.a: They had forgotten that sight exists

q.q: What does the story show about the proverb?
q.a: Being different does not always give power

q.q: What did the family ask Nunez to do?
q.a: Let the doctor remove his eyes

9.text:
In the eighteenth century, smallpox was one of the deadliest diseases on Earth. It killed about three people in every ten who caught it, and survivors were often left blind or covered in scars. Yet people noticed a strange fact: women who milked cows and had caught the mild disease cowpox seemed never to catch smallpox.
In 1796, an English country doctor named Edward Jenner decided to test this idea. He took fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid and scratched it into the arm of a healthy eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. The boy was mildly ill for a few days. Later, Jenner deliberately exposed him to smallpox, and the boy stayed healthy. Today such an experiment would be considered unethical, but it proved a principle. The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin word for cow, “vacca”.
How does a vaccine work? Our immune system fights germs using special white blood cells. When it meets a germ for the first time, it needs days to recognise it and make weapons called antibodies, and during that time we may become seriously ill. However, the body keeps a “memory” of every enemy it has defeated. A vaccine gives the immune system a harmless sample of the germ, such as a weakened or dead virus, or just a small piece of it. The body practises, builds antibodies and stores the memory. If the real germ arrives later, the defence is ready.
Vaccination has been one of the greatest successes of medicine. In 1980, the World Health Organization announced that smallpox had been completely wiped out, the only human disease so far to disappear in this way.
Vaccines are not perfect, and a few people may feel tired or have a sore arm afterwards. But the risks of the diseases are far greater than the risks of the vaccines.

q.q: What did people notice about milkmaids?
q.a: Those who had cowpox seemed safe from smallpox

q.q: How does a vaccine help the immune system?
q.a: It lets the body practise against a harmless sample
w: It kills every germ in the blood
It gives the body extra food

q.q: What happened to smallpox in 1980?
q.a: It was declared completely wiped out

9.text:
At the beginning of the fifteenth century, the largest ships in the world were not European but Chinese. Between 1405 and 1433, a fleet commanded by the admiral Zheng He made seven great voyages across the Indian Ocean, visiting more than thirty countries, from Southeast Asia and India to Arabia and the east coast of Africa.
Zheng He was born in Yunnan into a Muslim family and was taken into the service of a prince as a boy. Years later, the prince became the Yongle Emperor, and he chose Zheng He, now a trusted official, to lead the treasure fleet. The expedition was enormous. The first voyage had about three hundred ships and nearly twenty-eight thousand men, including sailors, soldiers, doctors, translators and astronomers. The biggest “treasure ships” were said to be over a hundred metres long, though historians still argue about their real size.
The fleet carried silk, porcelain and tea to give as gifts, and returned with exotic animals, among them a giraffe from Africa that amazed the court. The aim was partly to show the power of the Ming dynasty and partly to encourage trade and friendly relations. Unlike many later European explorers, Zheng He did not conquer or colonise. His fleet used force only a few times, to deal with pirates or in local conflicts.
He navigated with a compass and star charts, and carefully recorded the monsoon winds, which carried ships across the ocean in one season and back in another.
After the Yongle Emperor died, the voyages were stopped. Officials argued that they were too costly, and most records were later lost or destroyed. Zheng He died during or soon after his last voyage, around 1433.
Today his journeys are remembered in many ports, where temples and legends still honour him as a symbol of peaceful contact between peoples.

q.q: What was the purpose of the voyages?
q.a: To show Ming power and encourage trade
w: To find a new country to conquer

q.q: How did Zheng He differ from many later explorers?
q.a: He did not conquer or colonise

q.q: Why were the voyages stopped?
q.a: Officials thought they were too costly
w: The ships were destroyed by storms

9.t: The Moon over the Mid-Autumn Night
9.text:
On the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, the moon is believed to be at its roundest and brightest. For more than a thousand years, this evening has been celebrated as the Mid-Autumn Festival, and it is second in importance among traditional Chinese holidays only to the Spring Festival.
The most famous legend is the story of Chang’e. In ancient times, ten suns appeared in the sky together, scorching the earth. A brave archer named Hou Yi shot down nine of them and saved the people. As a reward, he received a magic potion that could make someone immortal. He gave it to his wife, Chang’e, for safekeeping, but one day a greedy student tried to steal it. To protect the potion, Chang’e swallowed it, and she began to float upward until she reached the moon. There she lives with a jade rabbit, and her husband, according to the tale, leaves her favourite fruit and cakes on a table each year.
Today families return home, however far away they live, to enjoy a reunion dinner. The central tradition is eating mooncakes, round pastries filled with lotus-seed paste, red-bean paste or salted egg yolk. Their round shape represents completeness and family unity, and sharing them is a way of showing love and respect. Children may carry paper lanterns and listen to stories under the bright light of the moon.
The festival is not a Chinese tradition alone. In Vietnam, children parade with star-shaped lanterns, and in Korea families celebrate Chuseok with rice cakes. Some people believe the idea of admiring the moon was originally an ancient autumn harvest custom.
For many people, it is a moment to remember absent friends. As the famous poet Su Shi wrote, though we are far apart, we can still share the beauty of the same moon.

q.q: Why did Chang’e swallow the potion?
q.a: To stop a greedy student from stealing it
w: She wanted to live on the moon
She was ill and needed medicine

q.q: What do the round shapes of mooncakes represent?
What does the passage say about other countries?
q.a: Vietnam and Korea have similar festivals
w: They do not celebrate the moon
Their festivals take place in spring

9.text:
Buck lived in a large house in the sunny Santa Clara Valley of California. He was a huge dog, half St. Bernard and half Scottish sheepdog, and he ruled the estate like a king. Nobody had ever treated him roughly. That changed one night in 1897, when a gardener’s helper, who needed money to pay his gambling debts, sold him to a stranger.
Buck was thrown into a crate, taken by train, and then beaten by a man in a red sweater who held a heavy club. Buck learned a hard lesson there: a man with a club is a master to be obeyed, though not necessarily forgiven. Soon he was on a ship to Alaska, where gold had been found in the Klondike, and where strong dogs were suddenly worth a fortune.
Here the dog discovered a world of snow, hunger and fear. He saw one dog killed by a pack of wolfish huskies during his very first day, and understood that there was no mercy. He learned to dig a hole in the snow to sleep warm, to steal food when nobody was looking, and to pull a sled for hours across the frozen ground. Slowly the old, soft Buck faded, and ancient instincts woke inside him.
When a kind but careless team of gold-seekers took charge of him, the exhausted dogs fell through the ice. Only the intervention of John Thornton, a kind man who gave Buck rest and food, saved him. For the first time Buck felt real love.
But at night, he began to hear a call from the forest, a deep howl that stirred something in his blood. He would walk to the edge of the camp, listen, and look back toward the fire, torn between two lives.
9.src: adapted from Jack London, “The Call of the Wild” (public domain)

q.q: How did Buck come to Alaska?
q.a: He was stolen and sold because dogs were valuable
w: He was sent as a gift

q.q: What did Buck learn in the north?
q.a: To survive using hard lessons and instinct

q.q: Why was Buck torn between two lives?
q.a: He loved Thornton but heard the call of the wild
w: He wanted to return to California
He wished to become a king again

9.t: Where Does Our Electricity Come From?
9.text:
When you switch on a light, you rarely wonder about the long journey the energy has made. Yet behind every plug socket stands an enormous system of machines, wires and fuel, and the choices we make about it will decide the climate of the future.
For more than a century, most electricity has been made by burning coal, oil or natural gas. The fuel heats water into steam, the steam turns a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator. This is reliable and cheap, but it has a serious cost: burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, the main gas responsible for global warming, and other pollutants that harm health.
Renewable energy offers an alternative. Hydropower uses falling water to turn turbines, and it still provides the largest share of renewable electricity. Wind turbines turn the movement of air into power, while solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity by means of special materials called semiconductors. The costs of solar panels have dropped by around ninety per cent in ten years, and in many places they are now the cheapest way of generating new electricity.
However, wind and sun do not work to our timetable. When the air is still or the sky is dark, supply falls. For this reason, engineers are developing large batteries, pumped water storage and smarter electricity networks that can move power across long distances, and even adjust demand by charging electric cars when energy is plentiful.
Nuclear power is another low-carbon source, generating huge amounts of energy from a small amount of fuel, but it must deal with radioactive waste and high building costs, and opinions about its safety are divided.
No single solution will be enough. The challenge for your generation is to combine them, and to make energy clean, affordable and reliable for everyone.

q.q: What is the main problem of burning fossil fuels?
q.a: It releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants

q.q: Why is wind and solar power difficult to rely on?
q.a: They do not always produce power when needed
w: They cannot be built in cities

q.q: What does the writer conclude?
q.a: We need to combine several clean solutions
w: Nuclear power is the only answer
Electricity should be used less often

9.text:
Aunt Mei: So, Jun, you are sixteen now. Have you thought about what you would like to do after school?
Jun: Honestly, Auntie, I change my mind every week. Last month I wanted to be a pilot, and then a game designer, and yesterday I read about marine biologists and thought, “That’s it!”
Aunt Mei: That’s perfectly normal. I wanted to be a singer at your age. Today I am an accountant, and I’m quite happy.
Jun: Really? How did that happen?
Aunt Mei: Gradually. I discovered that I enjoyed solving problems and being organised, and I found that these skills mattered more to me than the stage. My advice is to ask different questions. Instead of “What job do I want?” try “What kind of problems do I enjoy solving? What kind of people do I like working with?”
Jun: That’s a good way to look at it. But what if I choose wrongly?
Aunt Mei: Then you will learn something and change direction. Hardly anyone keeps the same job for forty years nowadays, and many of the jobs of the future haven’t been invented yet. Skills such as clear communication, teamwork and learning new things quickly will be useful whatever you do.
Jun: So I shouldn’t worry too much?
Aunt Mei: Worry a little, because it shows you care, but experiment a lot. Try a summer course or volunteer for a charity, or ask someone who works in marine biology if you can talk to them for half an hour. Most people love to talk about their work.
Jun: I never thought of that! I will write to a professor tonight.
Aunt Mei: Good. And whatever you decide, Jun, choose something you would still enjoy on a rainy Monday morning.
Jun: I’ll remember that. Thanks, Auntie!

q.q: What does Aunt Mei suggest Jun ask himself?
q.a: What kind of problems he enjoys solving
w: What his friends want to do

q.q: Why does she say not to fear a wrong choice?
q.a: People can learn and change direction

q.q: What does she recommend as a way to experiment?
q.a: Talk to someone who works in the field

9.t: Stephen Hawking and the Questions of the Universe
9.text:
Stephen Hawking was born in Oxford on 8 January 1942, exactly three hundred years after the death of Galileo, a coincidence he enjoyed pointing out. As a boy he was a clever but untidy student, and his friends nicknamed him “Einstein”. He studied physics at Oxford and then went to Cambridge to work on cosmology, the study of the origin and structure of the universe.
At the age of twenty-one, he was diagnosed with a motor neurone disease, which gradually weakens the muscles. Doctors expected him to live only a couple of years. Hawking was devastated at first, but he later said that the diagnosis changed his attitude. Because his time seemed short, he began to work with real determination, and, to everyone’s astonishment, he lived for another fifty-five years.
In the 1960s he showed, with the mathematician Roger Penrose, that the universe may have begun from a single point of infinite density, the Big Bang. His most famous discovery came in 1974: black holes, which had been thought to swallow everything, slowly lose energy as a type of radiation, now called Hawking radiation. This suggested that they might eventually disappear.
By the 1980s he could no longer speak without a computer. He used a small device attached to his glasses and, later, a speech synthesiser which gave him his famous robotic voice. In 1988 he published A Brief History of Time, a book explaining cosmology to ordinary readers, which sold over ten million copies.
Hawking also loved humour. He appeared in a television comedy and made jokes about his own condition. He died in 2018 at the age of seventy-six, and his ashes were buried near the grave of Isaac Newton.
His motto was simple: “Look up at the stars and not down at your feet.”

q.q: How did the illness change Hawking’s attitude?
What did Hawking discover in 1974?
w: A way to travel in time

q.q: Why was A Brief History of Time important?
q.a: It explained cosmology to ordinary readers
w: It was his first scientific paper
It was written for his doctor

9.t: The Case of the Red-Headed Clients
9.text:
Mr. Jabez Wilson was a pawnbroker with flaming red hair, and he arrived at Sherlock Holmes’s rooms one morning with a most peculiar story. Two months earlier, his assistant had shown him an advertisement: the League of Red-Headed Men needed a new member, and the pay was four pounds a week for very light work.
Wilson applied and, to his delight, he won the position among hundreds of red-headed men because his hair was the brightest. His task was simple: to copy out the Encyclopaedia Britannica, from ten until two every day, in a small office. He could not leave the room, not even for a minute, or he would lose the post. For eight weeks he copied faithfully and received his wages every Saturday.
Then, one morning, he found a notice on the door: “The Red-Headed League is dissolved.” The landlord knew nothing about it, and the men had vanished.
Holmes listened carefully, with his fingertips pressed together. He asked about the assistant, who, Wilson said, had accepted low wages and was always down in the cellar developing photographs. Holmes noticed the knees of the man’s trousers, which were worn and dirty. “It is a three-pipe problem,” said Holmes, and he went off to smoke and think.
The explanation was clever. The office was only a trick to keep Wilson out of his shop for four hours each day. Meanwhile the assistant was digging a tunnel from the cellar to the vault of the bank next door. That night, Holmes and Dr. Watson waited in the dark bank cellar, and when the thieves climbed out, the police arrested them.
Holmes explained afterwards that the more unusual a crime is, the easier it is to solve, since there are fewer ways to explain it.
9.src: adapted from Arthur Conan Doyle, “The Red-Headed League” (public domain)

q.q: Why did the League want red-headed men?
q.a: It was a trick to keep Wilson away from his shop
w: To teach them to copy books

q.q: What clue did Holmes notice about the assistant?
q.a: The knees of his trousers were worn and dirty

q.q: What were the thieves really doing?
q.a: Digging a tunnel to the bank’s vault

9.t: The Day Hamlet the Hamster Escaped
9.text:
Our class pet, a golden hamster named Hamlet, had lived peacefully in his cage beside the window for two whole years. Mr. Davies, our science teacher, called him “the calmest animal in the school”. This reputation lasted until the Friday that Hamlet disappeared.
It was Sam’s turn to clean the cage. He opened the door, put Hamlet in a cardboard box, and went to fetch water. When he returned, the box was empty and there was a neat round hole chewed in the side. “Er, Mr. Davies,” said Sam in a very small voice, “we have a slight problem.”
Within minutes, thirty students were crawling on the floor, searching under desks, bookshelves and radiators. Mr. Davies suggested that we spread sunflower seeds around the room and wait quietly. Unfortunately, “quietly” is not a word that fits a class that has lost a hamster. Someone sneezed, someone giggled, and a chair fell over with a bang.
Then the headteacher walked in with a visitor from the education department, a tall woman in a grey suit. “Good morning, everybody,” said the headteacher. “May I introduce—” At that very moment, something small and golden ran straight up the visitor’s trouser leg.
She let out a scream that shook the windows. Hamlet emerged from her sleeve and sat on her shoulder, calmly cleaning his whiskers, as if nothing had happened. There was a terrible silence. Then, to everyone’s relief, the visitor began to laugh. “I used to have a hamster myself,” she said, “and he escaped, too.”
Hamlet was returned to his cage, which now has a lock on it. Every year, on the anniversary of his adventure, Mr. Davies brings in a bag of sunflower seeds, and we hold a minute of respectful applause.

q.q: How did the hamster escape?
q.a: He chewed a hole in a cardboard box
w: Sam left the cage door open

q.q: Where did Hamlet appear at the end?
How did the visitor react after her fright?
q.a: She laughed and told of her own hamster
w: She left the school at once
She demanded that Hamlet be sold

9.text:
From space, the Great Barrier Reef is one of the few living structures that can be seen. It stretches for about 2,300 kilometres along the north-east coast of Australia, and consists of nearly three thousand separate reefs and hundreds of islands. It is larger than the United Kingdom, and in 1981 it was named a World Heritage Site.
The reef is built by coral polyps, tiny soft-bodied animals related to jellyfish. Each polyp makes a hard skeleton of limestone around itself, and over thousands of years, billions of these skeletons have piled up to form great structures. Living inside the tissue of the corals are microscopic algae, which use sunlight to make food and give the coral its brilliant colours. In return, the coral gives the algae shelter, and the two partners depend on each other.
The reef is a city under the sea. It is home to about fifteen hundred species of fish, thirty kinds of whales and dolphins, six species of sea turtle and thousands of kinds of shellfish, sponges and worms. Many animals, like the clownfish that shelters among the arms of sea anemones, have unusual partnerships with others.
But the reef is in danger. When the sea becomes too warm, the corals expel their algae, turn white and may die, a process known as bleaching. Serious bleaching events have occurred in several recent years, and large areas have been damaged. Other threats include pollution washing off the land, a starfish that eats coral, and stronger storms.
People are trying to help. Farmers are encouraged to reduce the chemicals that run into rivers, scientists are breeding heat-resistant corals, and divers move baby corals to damaged areas. Yet in the end, the reef’s future depends on whether the world can slow down climate change.

q.q: How is the Great Barrier Reef built?
q.a: By tiny animals that make limestone skeletons
w: By the waves piling up sand

q.q: What is the relationship between coral and algae?
w: The algae are enemies of coral

q.q: Why do corals turn white?
q.a: The water is too warm and they expel their algae

9.text:
Ebenezer Scrooge was a tight-fisted, cold-hearted old man who hated Christmas. “Bah! Humbug!” he said to his cheerful nephew, who had come to invite him to dinner. He refused to give money to charity, and he made his poor clerk, Bob Cratchit, work in a freezing office for a tiny wage.
That night, in his dark, lonely house, the ghost of his dead partner, Jacob Marley, appeared, dragging a long chain made of cash boxes and keys. “I wear the chain I made in life,” groaned the ghost. “You still have a chance to escape it. Three spirits will visit you.”
The Ghost of Christmas Past showed Scrooge his own childhood: a lonely boy at school, and later a young man who had lost the woman he loved because he cared more for money than for her. Scrooge wept.
The Ghost of Christmas Present took him to Cratchit’s small house, where the family shared a tiny goose with great joy. The youngest child, Tiny Tim, was sick and walked on a crutch, yet he cried, “God bless us, every one!” “Will Tiny Tim live?” Scrooge asked. “If nothing changes,” said the spirit, “the child will die.”
The last ghost, silent and dark, showed Scrooge a future in which people spoke of a dead man with scorn, and nobody cried. Scrooge saw his own grave.
“I will change!” he cried, falling to his knees. “I will honour Christmas in my heart!”
He woke in his bed on Christmas morning, laughing like a child. He sent a huge turkey to the Cratchits, raised Bob’s wages and became a second father to Tiny Tim. From then on, it was said that nobody kept Christmas better than Scrooge.
9.src: adapted from Charles Dickens, “A Christmas Carol” (public domain)

q.q: What did Marley’s chain mean?
q.a: It was made of the greed he showed in life
w: It was a gift from Scrooge
It was a prison for thieves

q.q: What did the last ghost show Scrooge?
q.a: A future where he died unloved

q.q: How did Scrooge change?

9.t: A Letter to Myself at Twenty
9.text:
Dear me,
By the time you open this letter, I hope that you are twenty and that you have finished your first year at university. I am writing this at fifteen, on a cold evening at the end of the year, with a cup of hot chocolate and a pile of exam papers on my desk. This year has taught me a number of things that I do not want you to forget.
First, I learned that nobody is good at everything. I struggled with chemistry at the start of the year, and I wanted to give up. But my teacher showed me that every difficult subject is just a pile of small steps, and if you take one every day, the pile disappears. I hope you still remember that when the work seems impossible.
Second, I learned that friends matter more than marks. When my best friend Hana moved to another city, I felt as if a piece of my life had been cut out. Yet we write to each other every week, and I understand now that true friendship is not about being in the same place. Please keep writing to her. I hope that you have not become too busy.
Third, I discovered the pleasure of reading. I used to think of books as homework, but this year I found novels that made me laugh, cry and see the world differently. Keep a book beside your bed.
Finally, I made a mistake that I am still ashamed of. I laughed at a classmate’s accent, and I saw his face. Later I apologised, and he forgave me, but I will never forget how easily words can hurt. I hope you are kinder than I was.
I do not know who you will be, but I am proud of you already. Look after yourself, and remember that the best is yet to come.
With love, your fifteen-year-old self

q.q: What did the writer learn from the chemistry experience?
q.a: Difficult subjects can be solved one small step at a time
w: It is best to give up early

q.q: What does the writer say about friendship?
q.a: It does not depend on being in the same place
w: It ends when someone moves away

q.q: Why is the writer ashamed?
q.a: The writer laughed at a classmate’s accent
w: The writer lost a friend’s letter
